proof.goal: Transfer exact optimality for scaled profits to a (1−ε) guarantee without relaxing capacity.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §3.1. Assumes the minimum-weight-per-profit dynamic program is implemented with exact integer/rational arithmetic; the walk explains the loss and size bounds, not every DP implementation detail.

frames.title: Keep the original optimum feasible
frames.question: Which side of the instance may change without invalidating the capacity benchmark?

diagram.note: The same feasible subsets are compared under two objectives.

frames.claim: Rounding profits leaves O feasible for the DP.
frames.explanation: Delete overweight items first. The best remaining singleton has profit Pmax, so Pmax≤OPT; every remaining item has profit at most Pmax. Nothing in this argument rounds weights.
frames.carry: Scaled optimality can legitimately compare A with O.

frames.title: Put the rounding loss on the benchmark
frames.question: Why is the floor error charged to O rather than assumed zero on A?

diagram.note: The useful comparison points toward an upper estimate of the loss.

frames.claim: K∑O p′ᵢ>OPT−|O|K.
frames.explanation: Each item loses less than K when converted back from its scaled profit. Summing only over the original optimum controls a set the algorithm need not know.
frames.carry: A feasible benchmark loses at most nK.

frames.title: Cross through the rounded optimum
frames.question: Which link in this chain uses the dynamic program?

diagram.note: The middle inequality is algorithmic; the outside inequalities are arithmetic.

frames.claim: p(A)>OPT−nK≥(1−ε)OPT for K=εPmax/n.
frames.explanation: The final substitution uses nK=εPmax≤εOPT. It does not require A and O to contain the same items, as the worked example already demonstrates.
frames.carry: Feasibility plus the correct intermediate objective yields the approximation.

frames.title: Bound the encoded DP dimensions
frames.question: Why does a huge binary profit not force a huge profit table?

diagram.note: The table depends polynomially on n and 1/ε, rather than on Pmax.

frames.claim: Each p′ᵢ≤n/ε and the total scaled-profit range is at most n²/ε.
frames.explanation: The arithmetic must still operate on input-length weight and profit encodings. A bound on the number of states alone is not a bit-complexity proof; exact additions and comparisons have polynomial bit length.
frames.carry: The scheme is fully polynomial in input length and 1/ε.

challenges.title: Spend the error budget on feasible cardinality
challenges.skill: Refine rounding and DP size using an independently proved structural bound.
challenges.connection: The example pays a coarse nK loss. Here many input items exist, but no feasible solution can contain many of them.
challenges.prompt: Capacity is 10, every item weighs at least 3, n=60, Pmax=80, and ε=1/10. Prove a feasible-cardinality bound L, choose K=εPmax/L, and reconstruct the complete approximation chain. Then bound the largest scaled profit of any feasible subset and explain why DP columns above that bound can be discarded. State which part of the proof would fail if even one zero-weight positive-profit item were allowed without revising L.
hints: The cardinality bound concerns feasible subsets, not the number of input items.
Use L=⌊10/3⌋, bound each scaled profit by Pmax/K, and keep the exact capacity test.

probe.prompt: What upper bound on scaled profit holds for every feasible subset?
probe.feedback: At most three items fit; K=8/3 and each scaled profit is at most 80/(8/3)=30. Thus every feasible total is at most 90. Using all 60 items gives a valid but unnecessary table bound of 1800.

solution: All feasible subsets have at most L=3 items because four would weigh at least 12.
Choose K=(1/10)·80/3=8/3. The floor loss on O is smaller than 3K=8.
Exact scaled optimization and unchanged weights give p(A)>OPT−8≥0.9OPT because OPT≥80.
Every feasible subset has scaled profit at most 3·30=90, so states above 90 cannot hold a feasible weight and may be omitted.
A zero-weight positive-profit item can increase feasible cardinality beyond three. Remove and include such items separately, or derive a new bound before using the refined error budget.
rubric: Derive L from original weights and preserve original feasibility.
Show all three inequalities linking p(A), scaled optimality and p(O).
Justify the profit-index cap 90 (columns zero through 90) and handle the zero-weight exception.
challenges.mistake: Substituting L for n merely because the optimum seems small is circular. L must hold for every feasible benchmark, proved from the input.
challenges.followup: Derive the corresponding bound for capacity B and a known positive lower weight b, including the case B/b is an integer.

challenges.title: Can a tiny weight error be repaired cheaply?
challenges.skill: Construct a family separating small constraint perturbations from small objective loss.
challenges.connection: The worked example changes the winning subset while keeping feasibility exact. This proposal changes feasibility instead.
challenges.prompt: A proposed scheme rounds weights down to multiples of 0.5 and solves the rounded knapsack exactly. Capacity is 10. Item A has weight 10 and profit 1.99; B and C each have weight 5.1 and profit 1. The scheme chooses B+C, then repairs overweight solutions by deleting selected items. Identify the original optimum, prove what any deletion-only repair of this chosen subset can earn, and compare it with a 0.9 approximation claim. Extend the construction to arbitrarily small rounding units: explain why small weight error alone cannot budget the lost profit.
hints: Enumerate feasible original subsets before discussing approximation.
The repaired solution must remain a subset of {B,C}; it cannot insert A.

probe.prompt: What is the largest repaired-profit / OPT ratio on this instance?
probe.feedback: The rounded optimum has profit 2, but B+C weighs 10.2. Every feasible deletion-only repair keeps at most one item and earns 1, while the original optimum is A with value 1.99. The ratio is 1/1.99=100/199, far below 0.9.

solution: Originally B+C is infeasible, while A is feasible and better than either singleton B or C. Hence OPT=1.99.
Rounded B and C have weights 5 each; the exact rounded objective therefore prefers their profit 2 to A.
Deleting items until feasibility leaves profit at most 1, so the best deletion-only repair has ratio 100/199.
For any small unit δ dividing 5, use weights 5+δ/5 for B,C and the same profits. Both round to 5 but still cannot coexist originally.
As δ tends to zero, objective loss remains near one half of OPT. A constraint error has no automatic conversion into a relative profit error.
rubric: Identify both original and rounded optima without mixing their feasible regions.
Prove an upper bound on every deletion-only repair, not one arbitrary repair.
Give an arbitrarily small-unit family and explain the failed error accounting.
challenges.mistake: Charging removed profit to the small excess weight assumes a density bound that the input never supplied.
challenges.followup: Give an additional density condition under which deleting enough weight could be charged, and explain why it changes the theorem being proved.

proof.goal: Explain the source PTAS: round long jobs down, restore them, and insert short jobs with one—not two—slack charges.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §3.2 uses integer k≈1/ε, long jobs p>T/k, and downward rounding to T/k². The rounded long jobs are still at least T/k. The walk follows the source construction and its original-volume insertion argument.

frames.title: Turn a feasible target into a rounded candidate
frames.question: Why does the source round long processing times downward?

diagram.note: A feasible original T-schedule stays feasible after decreasing every long job.

frames.claim: If an original T-schedule exists, its rounded long jobs fit within T.
frames.explanation: A target test must not reject a genuinely feasible target merely because rounding enlarged its jobs. Downward rounding keeps the original assignment as a witness for the rounded DP.
frames.carry: The configuration problem has a valid benchmark at exactly T.

frames.title: Compress names into type multiplicities
frames.question: What must the state retain so the same job is not used twice?

diagram.note: The recurrence consumes every type count exactly once.

frames.claim: There are at most k² rounded types and (k+1)^(k²) candidate configurations.
frames.explanation: A rounded long job has size at least T/k, so no T-machine configuration contains more than k jobs. For fixed k, enumerate count vectors, reject those exceeding T, and use a count-state DP over the whole instance.
frames.carry: A feasible compressed assignment can be expanded to named jobs.

frames.title: Restore original lengths once
frames.question: How much can one machine gain when its rounded jobs are restored?

diagram.note: The restoration loss is a per-machine count bound, not a sum over all n jobs.

frames.claim: Restored long-job loads are at most (1+1/k)T.
frames.explanation: The rounded configuration uses load at most T. Each of its at most k jobs increases by less than T/k². This step does not yet insert any short job.
frames.carry: The initial large-job schedule already meets the target enlarged by T/k.

frames.title: Use original volume for the last short job
frames.question: Why need short-job insertion not add a second T/k to the restored-load bound?

diagram.note: Use the average of original processing assigned so far, rather than the maximum restored load.

frames.claim: Final makespan≤max{restored long load, short-job completions}≤(1+1/k)T.
frames.explanation: If the last finishing job is long, use the restoration bound. If it is short, its least-loaded machine starts it below T by the original-volume lower bound. These are alternative cases, so their slack terms are not added.
frames.carry: Target search and fixed-k configuration DP yield the PTAS.

challenges.title: Find the double-counted scheduling slack
challenges.skill: Choose the correct benchmark when two approximation losses appear to accumulate.
challenges.connection: The worked example decreases long-job lengths to rounded types, then restores their true load. This challenge shows why restoration and short-job insertion do not require two separate slack additions.
challenges.prompt: Let T=100, k=10, and m=3. Assume the original instance admits a T-schedule. Run the source downward-rounding configuration DP, restore long jobs, and insert all jobs of length at most 10 on the least-loaded machine using their original lengths. An examiner proposes the bound 120 by first bounding restored loads by 110 and then adding a final short job. Prove the stronger bound 110. Explain exactly why the average-load argument applies even though some restored machine may already have load above 100.
hints: Separate the last finishing long job from the last finishing short job.
At a short-job insertion, assigned original work is at most total original work minus this positive job.

probe.prompt: Which inequality correctly closes the short-job case?
options: Cⱼ≤110+pⱼ, because the largest restored load bounds the chosen machine.
Cⱼ≤(∑ᵢ≠ⱼpᵢ)/3+pⱼ<100+10, because the chosen original load is no greater than the average.
Cⱼ≤100, because downward rounding permanently removes processing time.
Cⱼ≤100+30, because all three machines contribute one slack term.
feedback: This is a valid coarse estimate but does not prove the sharper source guarantee; it uses the maximum where the minimum is chosen.
Correct. Original total work is at most 300 and the current load sum excludes j and all later jobs. The least-loaded machine is therefore below 100 before adding pⱼ<10.
Original processing times must be restored; rounded lengths are not actual execution times.
The job occupies one chosen machine, so summing slack across machines is the wrong quantity.

solution: Each rounded long job is at least 10, so a rounded T-configuration uses at most ten long jobs.
Restoring lengths increases a machine by less than ten units; hence every long-job completion is at most 110.
At insertion of short j, total original load already assigned is at most ∑ᵢ≠ⱼpᵢ<300. The least-loaded machine has load below 100, even if another machine exceeds 100.
Since pⱼ≤10, its completion is below 110. Take the maximum of the long and short cases.
The 120 estimate adds bounds belonging to different cases. It does not express the start time of a job assigned to the least-loaded machine.
rubric: Use source downward rounding and the k-job bound correctly.
Bound the minimum current original load by its average.
Combine alternative last-job cases with a maximum, not an added error.
challenges.mistake: A bound on every machine by 110 does not mean the least-loaded machine is close to 110; the original total-volume constraint is stronger.
challenges.followup: Show why this proof survives any order of short-job insertion but needs revision if the input target fails the volume lower bound.

challenges.title: A locally feasible configuration can be globally impossible
challenges.skill: Expose the integer count constraints hidden by machine descriptions.
challenges.connection: The example describes one machine by rounded types; the full algorithm must cover the instance’s entire multiplicity vector.
challenges.prompt: Two machines have target T=10. The rounded instance has three jobs of size 6 and two jobs of size 1. Its total volume is exactly 20, and configurations such as (one 6, two 1s) are individually feasible. Prove that no pair of feasible configurations covers the multiplicity vector. Give a valid linear inequality satisfied by all two-machine configuration combinations but violated by this input. Explain how a count-state DP detects the obstruction and why independent selection of a “good” local configuration cannot.
hints: Use a coefficient on the size-6 type that expresses a packing obstruction stronger than total volume.
A machine of capacity ten can contain at most one size-6 job.

probe.prompt: Which separating inequality is valid for every feasible two-machine packing here?
options: 6n₆+n₁≤20, and this inequality alone excludes the input.
n₁≤2, because every configuration has at most one short job.
n₆+n₁≤2, because every machine processes only one job.
n₆≤2, obtained by summing one large-job constraint for each machine.
feedback: The volume inequality is valid but holds with equality on this infeasible input; it does not separate it.
A machine can contain ten size-one jobs, so this is not a valid configuration inequality.
Several jobs can fit on one machine; the asserted job-count limit is false.
Correct. Each machine has 6a≤10, so its integer count a is at most one. Across two machines n₆≤2, whereas the input requires three.

solution: Any feasible configuration satisfies integer large count a≤⌊10/6⌋=1.
Adding this inequality over two machines gives total n₆≤2, contradicted by n₆=3.
The volume bound 6·3+2=20 is necessary but misses this indivisibility obstruction.
A count-state DP starting at (3,2) must subtract two feasible configuration vectors and reach (0,0). No such transition sequence exists because at most two size-6 jobs can be consumed.
Selecting locally feasible descriptions independently either leaves a large job unscheduled or duplicates some short jobs; local feasibility does not certify global counts.
rubric: Construct and justify the separating count inequality.
Explain why total volume fails to distinguish this case.
Describe the DP’s global count condition and the failure of independent local choices.
challenges.mistake: A type description compresses item identities, not item multiplicities. Forgetting the counts changes the feasible region.
challenges.followup: Generalize the certificate to jobs longer than T/r and show that each machine can contain at most r−1 such jobs.

proof.goal: Prove the APTAS bound by shifting sorted groups, paying for discarded items, and using a maximum in the small-item phase.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §3.3. Exact optimization for a bounded number of rounded types is the configuration-DP input. The walk retains both the finite additive bin and the small-volume special case.

frames.title: Shift rounded items into larger positions
frames.question: Why can rounding upward still produce a rounded instance no harder than the original?

diagram.note: Discarding the first group makes a size-dominating injection into the previous original group.

frames.claim: OPT(I′)≤OPT(Ilarge).
frames.explanation: Every rounded item in group j is no larger than every original item in group j−1. Substitute it into one distinct predecessor position of an original packing. Blocks are not asserted to be bins.
frames.carry: The rounded optimum is benchmarked by an actual feasible packing.

frames.title: Pay to restore the discarded block
frames.question: Which cost cannot vanish when the rounded instance is unpacked?

lines.reason: q discarded items, one bin each

diagram.note: The first group pays for the monotonic shift and must reappear in the final solution.

frames.claim: Large pieces can be packed in ℓ≤(1+ε)OPT bins.
frames.explanation: Replace each retained rounded item by its no-larger original item, and put each of the q discarded largest items in a separate bin. Choose q using large-item volume, with the small-volume case solved directly.
frames.carry: A feasible large-piece packing includes every input large item.

frames.title: Recognize the two small-item cases
frames.question: When is near-fullness available, and when is it unnecessary?

diagram.note: These cases are alternatives; their bounds are combined by max, not addition.

frames.explanation: If first-fit opens a new bin for a piece of size at most γ, every previous bin has insufficient slack and therefore load at least 1−γ. The final opened bin is the sole exception.
frames.carry: The original total volume bounds bins introduced by small items.

frames.title: Close the parameter and runtime bounds
frames.question: Why does γ=ε/2 suffice for the final guarantee?

diagram.note: The +1 is retained; it is not a purely multiplicative approximation.

frames.claim: For fixed ε the number of rounded types is O(1/ε²), giving an APTAS.
frames.explanation: When εVlarge≥1, q=⌊εVlarge⌋ controls the number of groups. If εVlarge<1, there are O(1/ε²) large pieces and the direct finite-type routine handles them.
frames.carry: Grouping, exact configuration optimization, and insertion each have a separate obligation.

challenges.title: Do not add two incompatible bin charges
challenges.skill: Derive the asymptotic bound from a case split rather than accumulating unrelated upper bounds.
challenges.connection: The example lists the first block and near-full small bins separately. The final proof must decide which bound applies to the actual final packing.
challenges.prompt: Set ε=1/5 and γ=1/10. Suppose the whole input has volume V=20, its large-piece rounded optimum is 21 bins, and q=4 first-block items were set aside. Restore a packing of the large items in at most 25 bins, then use first-fit for the small items. Prove the strongest integer upper bound obtained from these facts alone. An examiner adds 25 to V/(1−γ)+1; identify the exact logical error. Explain why a final packing with 26 bins would contradict the near-fullness case.
hints: First distinguish whether any new bin opens during the small-item phase.
If a 26th bin opens, at least 25 earlier bins must each have load above 0.9.

probe.prompt: What final integer upper bound follows?
probe.feedback: The no-new-bin case gives at most 25. If new bins open, B≤20/0.9+1=209/9≈23.222, so integrality gives B≤23. The combined bound is max{25,23}=25, not their sum.

solution: The restored large packing has ℓ≤21+4=25 bins.
If no new bin opens, B=ℓ≤25.
If some new bin opens, all but its final bin have load at least 0.9, so B≤20/0.9+1=209/9 and B≤23 integrally.
Thus B≤25 under either case. Adding the two bounds double-counts the original bins, which also contribute to the near-fullness volume charge.
A 26-bin result would require at least 25 bins of load at least 0.9, hence volume at least 22.5>20.
rubric: Separate the two insertion cases and account for the restored first block.
Use the volume inequality and integrality in the correct direction.
Explain the double count and explicitly rule out 26 bins.
challenges.mistake: The small-item lemma bounds all final bins when it opens a new one; it does not bound an additional set of bins to add to ℓ.
challenges.followup: Derive max{ℓ,⌊V/(1−γ)+1⌋} for arbitrary rational V and γ, noting the strictness convention at the threshold.

challenges.title: Why a tiny rounding error can double the bins
challenges.skill: Build an objective-gap counterexample to uniform size rounding.
challenges.connection: Linear grouping removes a first block so every rounded retained item has a larger predecessor. Uniform upward rounding has no such comparison.
challenges.prompt: Consider 2r items, each of size exactly 1/2. A proposed replacement rounds every size upward by an arbitrarily small positive δ<1/2, then optimally packs and maps back. Determine the original and rounded optima and their ratio. Explain why δ→0 does not make that ratio tend to one. Contrast this with the exact domination map used by linear grouping, and state where the discarded-block charge prevents the same invalid inference.
hints: Count how many original and rounded items can occupy a unit bin.
Bin count is discontinuous at the pair-sum threshold one.

probe.prompt: For r=37, what is OPT(rounded)/OPT(original)?
probe.feedback: The 74 half-items fit in 37 original bins. After any positive upward perturbation, two no longer fit, so 74 bins are needed and the ratio is 2, independently of how small δ is.

solution: Pair the original half-items to obtain OPT=r; volume r proves optimality.
Each rounded item has size 1/2+δ, so every bin can contain at most one and the rounded optimum is 2r.
The ratio is exactly two for every δ>0; a small coordinate error is not a small relative bin-count error.
Linear grouping does not compare each rounded item with itself. After dropping the first group, it injects each rounded item into a distinct larger predecessor position.
That injection proves OPT(I′)≤OPT(I), while the separately charged discarded group controls the reverse reconstruction. Uniform rounding lacks the first inequality.
rubric: Prove both optima and the δ-independent factor.
Identify the discontinuity at a bin-capacity threshold.
Describe the shifted injection and the cost it pays, rather than merely naming linear grouping.
challenges.mistake: Summing small size increases and dividing by bin capacity ignores that unused slack is distributed across indivisible bins.
challenges.followup: Construct a similar threshold example in which all original item sizes are strictly below one half and δ is specified before the input is chosen.

proof.goal: Derandomize a computable expected satisfied weight by preserving conditional expectation at every variable.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§5.1–5.3. Clauses are normalized first; variable choices follow the explicitly chosen product distribution. The walk does not assume clause indicators are independent.

frames.title: Use local expectations without fake independence
frames.question: Can two clauses share variables while their expected contributions still add?

diagram.note: The three indicators are dependent, but expectation is linear.

frames.claim: E[X]=∑C wC Pr(C satisfied)=6.
frames.explanation: Distinct variables inside a normalized clause allow its failure probability to be computed from a product. Adding clause contributions requires no independence between clauses.
frames.carry: A local formula makes the global conditional potential efficiently computable.

frames.title: Apply the weighted-average identity
frames.question: If the next bit has probability q of being one, which average relates the two branches?

diagram.note: The branch weights matter, but at least one positive-probability branch preserves M.

frames.claim: Choose a supported branch with conditional expectation at least M.
frames.explanation: For q=1/2 the children average equally; for biased rounding they do not. The identity, not a median or concentration claim, certifies that both supported children cannot lie below the parent.
frames.carry: Fixing one bit need not decrease the potential.

frames.title: Update unfinished clauses correctly
frames.question: Why does a clause already satisfied by a fixed literal contribute its full weight?

diagram.note: The x=1 branch has value seven; x=0 has value five.

frames.claim: M after the first choice can increase from 6 to 7.
frames.explanation: A satisfied clause has conditional success probability one. An unsatisfied clause with no free literals has probability zero. Only the other unfinished clauses need their remaining-literal product recomputed.
frames.carry: Each update is a genuine conditional expectation of the same objective.

frames.title: End at a deterministic certificate
frames.question: What becomes of the expectation when no random variable remains?

diagram.note: The final assignment is one concrete outcome, not a claim that every outcome is good.

frames.claim: The constructed assignment has satisfied weight at least the starting expectation.
frames.explanation: The proof certifies existence and gives an algorithm because each branch expectation is computable in polynomial time. A distribution with a hard-to-compute conditional expectation would not yield the same efficient derandomization merely from this identity.
frames.carry: The method preserves a lower bound until it becomes the actual objective.

challenges.title: Derandomize a biased, shared-variable instance
challenges.skill: Compute the same conditional potential under dependent clause indicators and biased variable marginals.
challenges.connection: The example used fair bits. Here branch probabilities are unequal, clauses share variables, and the better branch is not inferred from its probability.
challenges.prompt: Let x,y,z be independent with Pr(x=1)=3/4, Pr(y=1)=1/3, Pr(z=1)=1/2. Maximize the satisfied weight of (x∨y) of weight 6, (¬x∨z) of weight 5, and (¬y∨¬z) of weight 4. Compute the initial expectation, both x-branch expectations, and verify their weighted-average identity. Then condition on the better x branch, compute both y branches, and complete z without lowering the potential. Explain which independence assumption is used and which is not.
hints: For x=1 the middle clause reduces to z; for x=0 the first clause reduces to y.
After x=1, the y=0 branch satisfies the last clause surely.

probe.prompt: What is the initial expected satisfied weight?
probe.feedback: The failure probabilities are 1/6, 3/8 and 1/6, so expected contributions are 5, 25/8 and 10/3. Their sum is 275/24. Shared variables across clauses do not prevent this addition.

solution: The first failure probability is (1/4)(2/3)=1/6, the second is (3/4)(1/2)=3/8, and the third is (1/3)(1/2)=1/6.
For x=1 the branch value is 6+5/2+10/3=71/6; for x=0 it is 2+5+10/3=31/3. Their average with weights 3/4 and 1/4 is 275/24.
Choose x=1. Then y=0 gives 6+5/2+4=25/2, whereas y=1 gives 6+5/2+2=21/2. Their 2/3,1/3 weighted average is 71/6.
Choose y=0 and then z=1, giving all clauses satisfied with total 15. The final result is at least every earlier potential.
Variable independence computes within-clause failure products; linearity, not clause independence, adds contributions.
rubric: Compute all branch values and the unequal weighted averages correctly.
Maintain one consistent objective and conditional distribution at every step.
Distinguish within-clause variable independence from cross-clause dependence.
challenges.mistake: Averaging the x branches equally computes a different probability distribution, even though choosing the larger branch remains valid.
challenges.followup: Change Pr(x=1) to q and derive the initial expectation as an affine function of q; identify any q where the preferred branch changes.

challenges.title: A computable lower bound is not automatically a valid potential
challenges.skill: Identify the supermartingale property required for a conditional-expectation proxy.
challenges.connection: The example recomputes true conditional expectations. A proposed speedup keeps only lower estimates for unfinished clauses.
challenges.prompt: A proposed derandomization uses a lower estimate L(h)≤E[X|h] at each partial assignment h, then always chooses the child with larger L. Construct numerical parent and child estimates, consistent with two possible final objective values, showing that the sole lower-bound property does not guarantee L(child)≥L(parent) or a final value at least L(empty). State and prove a sufficient one-step inequality for a valid pessimistic estimator for a maximization guarantee. Distinguish computability, terminal correctness, and the required averaging property.
hints: Try final branch values 0 and 10; lower bounds need not be equally accurate on both branches.
A useful estimator must satisfy L(h)≤qL(h1)+(1−q)L(h0), with terminal L bounded by the actual objective.

probe.prompt: Which additional conditions suffice for the branch-maximization proof?
options: Only L(h)≤E[X|h], because a lower bound must improve under further conditioning.
Only polynomial-time computability and L(empty)>0, because the chosen branch has the larger estimate.
L(h)≤qL(h1)+(1−q)L(h0), and L(a)≤X(a) at complete assignments.
L(h)≥qL(h1)+(1−q)L(h0), and terminal estimates may exceed X(a).
feedback: Pointwise lower bounds can become arbitrarily looser on the good branch; no monotone relation follows.
Efficiently computing an unsuitable score does not give an objective guarantee.
Correct. At least one supported child has estimate at least its parent, and terminal domination transfers the preserved estimate into an actual objective bound.
The reversed inequality allows both children to fall below the parent, and overestimating terminal values destroys the final transfer.

solution: For a fair first bit let the final objectives be X(0)=0 and X(1)=10, so E[X]=5.
Take L(empty)=4, L(0)=0 and L(1)=−1. All are lower bounds on their corresponding conditional expectations.
The child maximizing L is 0, yielding objective zero, which is below the advertised initial lower bound four.
A sufficient condition is L(h)≤qL(h1)+(1−q)L(h0) at every internal node. Then a supported child has L at least the parent.
Induction preserves L(empty). If every complete assignment obeys L(a)≤X(a), the final objective is at least L(empty). Polynomial-time evaluability is a separate algorithmic requirement.
rubric: Give an explicit valid lower-bound counterexample with a failing selected branch.
State the averaging inequality in the correct direction and prove branch existence.
Include terminal correctness and efficient evaluability as distinct obligations.
challenges.mistake: The phrase “lower bound” compares two functions at the same history; it says nothing about how the lower-bound function changes between histories.
challenges.followup: Require nonnegative estimates and construct a similar example where the algorithm loses a positive target, allowing a tie-breaking rule you specify.

proof.goal: Use length-sensitive clause bounds to prove the better of fair and LP-marginal rounding is a 3/4 approximation.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§5.4–5.6. Normalize repeated literals and tautologies first; weights are nonnegative and variable rounding is independent. The LP solve and its bit-precision treatment are inputs.

frames.title: Convert a clause into a product bound
frames.question: What quantity is fixed when AM–GM maximizes the failure product?

diagram.note: The LP satisfaction value z is bounded by the sum of its literal marginals.

frames.claim: Pr(C satisfied)≥1−(1−z/k)^k.
frames.explanation: The individual truth marginals may differ. The product is largest when failure probabilities are equal at the smallest allowed total truth mass, giving a bound in terms of z alone.
frames.carry: A nonlinear clause-success lower bound can now be compared with the LP.

frames.title: Linearize using the chord, not the tangent
frames.question: Which direction of concavity gives a lower bound on z∈[0,1]?

diagram.note: A tangent is an upper bound for a concave function; the chord is the useful lower bound.

frames.claim: LP rounding contributes at least bₖz with bₖ=1−(1−1/k)^k.
frames.explanation: The LP objective is a weighted sum of z-values, so one needs coefficients multiplying z rather than a nonlinear expression that cannot simply be pulled outside the sum.
frames.carry: Each clause gets a length-dependent linear benchmark.

frames.title: Compare two algorithms before forgetting clause length
frames.question: Why is averaging their separate global worst factors too pessimistic?

diagram.note: Short clauses are LP-friendly; long clauses are fair-rounding-friendly.

frames.claim: (aₖ+bₖ)/2≥3/4 for every clause length k.
frames.explanation: For k≥3 use aₖ≥7/8 and bₖ≥1−1/e; their sum is greater than 3/2. The two small lengths attain equality and must be checked explicitly.
frames.carry: A single 3/4 coefficient survives summing all weighted LP contributions.

frames.title: Keep the better realized assignment
frames.question: Do the two generated assignments need to be independent of each other?

diagram.note: Only independence inside each assignment’s variable rounding was used in the local analysis.

frames.claim: E[best assignment]≥(3/4)OPT.
frames.explanation: The maximum inequality holds even for coupled outputs. Independence between clause events or between the two algorithms is unnecessary; confusing these assumptions makes both proof and implementation harder than needed.
frames.carry: Local compensation, then summation, produces the stronger global ratio.

challenges.title: Can changing the mixing probability beat 3/4?
challenges.skill: Solve the minimax tradeoff between clause lengths before averaging guarantees.
challenges.connection: The example averages two assignments equally. Here choose the probability of using LP rounding and test whether a universal improvement follows.
challenges.prompt: Choose LP-marginal rounding with probability λ and fair rounding with probability 1−λ. Derive the guaranteed coefficient for lengths one and two, then for all lengths at least three. Determine all λ for which this elementary analysis certifies 3/4, and prove that no λ gives a strictly greater universal coefficient using these clausewise bounds. Do not confuse a limitation of the analysis with an impossibility theorem for every MAX-SAT algorithm.
hints: For length two both methods have coefficient exactly 3/4.
Length one forces λ≥1/2; taking k→∞ forces λ≤e/4. To show this upper endpoint works, control (1−1/k)^k below e^−1 by a finite-k margin.

probe.prompt: What blocks a strictly better universal coefficient from this mixture analysis?
options: The length-two coefficient remains 3/4 for every λ, even when the unit-clause coefficient improves.
The unit-clause coefficient is 1/2 for every λ because unit clauses cannot be rounded.
The long-clause coefficient always falls below 3/4 whenever λ is positive.
The two algorithms must be independent of one another for any mixture coefficient to be valid.
feedback: Correct. A clause of length two gives (1−λ)(3/4)+λ(3/4)=3/4, so the minimum over lengths cannot exceed it.
LP rounding has coefficient one on a unit clause, so its mixture coefficient is (1+λ)/2.
For λ=1/2 the established bound exceeds 3/4 for every length at least three.
A random mixture selects one algorithm; the clause coefficients combine by total expectation, without an independence condition between hypothetical outputs.

solution: The unit coefficient is c₁(λ)=(1+λ)/2, so λ≥1/2 is necessary to certify 3/4. The length-two coefficient is c₂(λ)=3/4 for every λ, excluding any strict universal improvement from these bounds.
For general k, cₖ(λ)=1−(1−λ)2^−k−λ(1−1/k)^k. Taking k to infinity gives 1−λ/e, so λ≤e/4 is also necessary.
The preceding proof establishes that λ=1/2 works. It remains to prove λ=e/4 works for every k≥3; linearity in λ will then cover the whole interval.

At λ=e/4, the desired inequality is e(1−1/k)^k+(4−e)2^−k≤1. For k≥2, expand 1+k log(1−1/k)=−Σj≥1 1/[(j+1)k^j] and log(1−1/(2k))=−Σj≥1 1/[j·2^j·k^j]. Since j·2^j≥j+1, the first logarithm is at most the second. Hence e(1−1/k)^k≤1−1/(2k).

For k≥3, use e>8/3 and 2^k≥8k/3 to obtain (4−e)2^−k≤1/(2k). Adding this to the previous estimate proves the endpoint inequality. At k=2 the endpoint expression equals e/4+(4−e)/4=1 exactly; the unit-clause condition was already checked.
Therefore exactly λ∈[1/2,e/4] are certified by these length-sensitive bounds. No mixture has a guaranteed coefficient strictly above 3/4 because of length two.
This is a limitation of these rounding guarantees, not a hardness theorem for every MAX-SAT algorithm or stronger relaxation.
rubric: Derive both small-length coefficients and the length-two obstruction.
Give the quantified all-k condition or an explicitly labeled sufficient interval.
Distinguish this proof’s ceiling from algorithmic hardness.
challenges.mistake: Optimizing the unit-clause bound alone pushes λ toward one and can destroy the compensation on long clauses.
challenges.followup: Numerically investigate the all-k upper endpoints for k=3,…,10, then justify which additional argument would be needed to replace that investigation by a theorem.

challenges.title: Same marginals, opposite clause behavior
challenges.skill: Locate precisely where independence enters the product-of-failures proof.
challenges.connection: The example lists coefficients based on independent variable rounding. Marginals alone preserve the LP but not those success probabilities.
challenges.prompt: Take the positive clause C=x∨y with LP marginals yx=yy=1/2 and zC=1. Compare two joint roundings: (x,y) is 00 or 11 with equal probability, and (x,y) is 01 or 10 with equal probability. Compute both clause-success probabilities. Explain why each respects the same marginals but only one beats the independent guarantee. Then give a joint-condition weaker than full independence that is sufficient to preserve the AM–GM proof for every clause, including clauses with negated literals.
hints: Clause failure is the joint event that all its literals are false.
A sufficient property must control failure events for the actual signed literals, not only positive variables.

probe.prompt: What is the difference between the two clause-success probabilities?
probe.feedback: The positively coupled law succeeds only on 11, with probability 1/2. The exclusive law succeeds surely, so the difference is 1−1/2=1/2. Independent rounding would give 3/4, between the two.

solution: Both distributions give each variable true probability one half and therefore respect the same LP marginal vector.
Under {00,11}, the clause fails with probability one half and succeeds with probability one half.
Under {01,10}, it never fails and succeeds with probability one. Thus marginals alone cannot justify a success lower bound of 3/4.
It suffices that every normalized clause obey Pr(all its literals false)≤∏ᵢPr(its literal i false). The rest of AM–GM and chord analysis is unchanged.

A condition controlling only positive-coordinate events is not enough for arbitrary signed clauses; complements can reverse the relevant dependence. State the required property for all literal patterns used by the instance.
rubric: Calculate both joint success probabilities and verify identical marginals.
Identify the failed product equality in the original proof.
State a sufficient signed failure-event inequality with the correct direction.
challenges.mistake: Negative dependence is not a magic label: the theorem needs the inequality for each clause’s specific mixture of positive and negative literals.
challenges.followup: Construct a third two-bit law with the same marginals whose success probability is exactly 3/4, and relate its covariance to the independent case.

proof.goal: Use one common random threshold to balance expected tree cost against expected exclusion penalties.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §5.7. The factor-two tree-rounding theorem for the scaled terminal-cut relaxation is an explicit input; the walk proves the threshold integration and comparison with the LP.

frames.title: Use the same threshold for every terminal
frames.question: What makes one scaling x/α feasible for every retained terminal cut?

diagram.note: The common cutoff links terminal selection to one feasible fractional edge solution.

frames.claim: For retained terminals, tree cost is at most 2E/α.
frames.explanation: Every relevant cut contains a retained terminal i with yᵢ≥α, so the LP cut constraint guarantees enough edge mass after division by α. The source tree-rounding theorem supplies the factor two.
frames.carry: The only random variable in this edge-cost bound is α.

frames.title: Integrate the cost with its actual density
frames.question: Why is the edge coefficient not just its value at the mean threshold?

diagram.note: A reciprocal must be averaged as a reciprocal; replacing α by E[α] reverses the useful bound.

frames.claim: E[tree cost]≤[2ln(1/γ)/(1−γ)]E.
frames.explanation: Uniform density is 1/(1−γ). The integral of 1/α from γ to one is ln(1/γ); the positive lower cutoff keeps this finite.
frames.carry: The edge multiplier is explicit and distribution-dependent.

frames.title: Charge every excluded vertex to its LP penalty
frames.question: How is the probability bound interpreted when yᵢ lies below γ?

diagram.note: The ratio formula is an upper bound below γ, not a probability exceeding one.

frames.claim: E[penalties]≤P/(1−γ), where P=∑πᵢ(1−yᵢ).
frames.explanation: Exclusion is the upper interval α>yᵢ. For yᵢ<γ this event is certain, while (1−yᵢ)/(1−γ)>1 still gives a valid charge bound. Add penalties by linearity; their exclusion events are not independent.
frames.carry: Both random costs are now compared with the same fixed LP solution.

frames.title: Equalize the two worst coefficients
frames.question: Which equation makes one factor multiply E+P?

diagram.note: The LP objective E+P is a lower bound on the original optimum.

frames.claim: The expected factor is (1−e^(−1/2))^−1.
frames.explanation: Choosing γ after identifying both coefficients avoids optimizing edge cost alone at the expense of penalties. The balancing argument minimizes the larger of these two uniform coefficients. Increasing γ removes low thresholds, so the reciprocal edge coefficient decreases while the penalty coefficient increases; their crossing minimizes the larger coefficient.
frames.carry: A single randomized construction is certified by one combined LP lower bound.

challenges.title: Re-derive the theorem for a different threshold density
challenges.skill: Analyze a changed rounding distribution rather than importing its old coefficients.
challenges.connection: The example computes exclusion intervals under a uniform threshold. Now the density gives more weight to large thresholds.
challenges.prompt: Sample α from [γ,1] with density f(α)=2α/(1−γ²). Retain yᵢ≥α and keep the conditional tree bound 2E/α. Derive the edge multiplier A(γ), the smallest uniform multiplier B(γ) charging every expected penalty to πᵢ(1−yᵢ), including yᵢ<γ, and the γ minimizing max{A,B}. Compare this guarantee with the uniform-threshold factor without claiming either analysis is tight for every graph.
hints: Integrate (2/α)f(α), and integrate f only above y for the exclusion event.
For y≥γ, divide (1−y²)/(1−γ²) by 1−y and take the supremum over y approaching one.

probe.prompt: What is the optimized common multiplier for this density?
probe.feedback: A=4/(1+γ) and B=2/(1−γ²). They meet at γ=1/2, giving 8/3. A decreases and B increases, so the maximum is minimized at the crossing; this is weaker than the uniform-density factor about 2.541.

solution: The density integrates to one because ∫γ¹2α dα=1−γ².
The edge coefficient is ∫γ¹(2/α)·2α/(1−γ²)dα=4/(1+γ).
For y≥γ, exclusion probability is (1−y²)/(1−γ²), whose ratio to 1−y is (1+y)/(1−γ²), with supremum 2/(1−γ²).
For y<γ, the ratio is 1/(1−y)≤1/(1−γ)≤2/(1−γ²), so the same multiplier works.
A is decreasing and B increasing. Equality reduces to 4(1−γ)=2, so γ=1/2 and the factor is 8/3.
These are uniform coefficient guarantees. Instance-specific edge/penalty proportions could support a different tuning.
rubric: Normalize the density and integrate its reciprocal edge charge.
Handle both y-regimes and justify the supremum penalty coefficient.
Prove the minimax parameter choice and compare the resulting guarantees.
challenges.mistake: Using the old uniform exclusion length divides the wrong measure; a probability is an integral of the new density.
challenges.followup: For fixed known ratio E/P, minimize A(γ)E+B(γ)P instead of their maximum, and explain why the resulting bound is instance-dependent.

challenges.title: Nested exclusions: expectation survives, variance changes
challenges.skill: Distinguish linearity of expectation from an unjustified independence claim.
challenges.connection: The example sums expected penalties. A single threshold makes terminal exclusions nested rather than independent.
challenges.prompt: Let α be uniform on [1/2,1]. Two terminals have connection values 0.6 and 0.9, with penalties ten each. Derive the complete distribution of the total excluded penalty Z, compute E[Z] and Var(Z), and compare the variance with a fictitious independent-exclusion model having the same marginals. Explain why the original expected-cost proof remains correct and why concentration claims need additional work.
hints: Split [1/2,1] at 0.6 and 0.9.
The larger-connection terminal can be excluded only when the smaller-connection terminal is also excluded.

probe.prompt: What is Var(Z) under the common threshold?
probe.feedback: Z is 0, 10 or 20 with probabilities 1/5, 3/5 and 1/5. Its mean is ten and second moment is 140, giving variance 40. Independent marginals would instead give 16+16=32.

solution: Exclusion probabilities are (1−0.6)/0.5=0.8 and (1−0.9)/0.5=0.2.
The interval probabilities give Z=0 with probability 0.2, Z=10 with probability 0.6, and Z=20 with probability 0.2.
Thus E[Z]=10 and E[Z²]=60+80=140, so Var(Z)=40.
The indicators have covariance 0.2−0.8·0.2=0.04. Their individual variances are 0.16 each, and multiplying by penalty squared gives 100(0.32+0.08)=40.
Expectation still adds to 10 without independence. Only an attempted variance or exponential-tail factorization would require extra dependence control.
rubric: Derive the joint distribution from threshold intervals.
Compute the covariance and both variances correctly.
Identify exactly which proof step remains valid without independence.
challenges.mistake: Independent vertex penalties would describe a different randomized construction, even if their marginal probabilities happened to match.
challenges.followup: For y₁≤y₂ derive Cov(1{α>y₁},1{α>y₂}) symbolically and identify when it vanishes.

proof.goal: Prove feasible metric facility rounding and its expected opening-plus-connection bound from LP and dual certificates.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §5.8. Optimal primal/dual LP solutions and the support-distance complementary-slackness lemma are inputs. This is uncapacitated metric facility location.

frames.title: Open once per disjoint representative neighborhood
frames.question: Why does one probability distribution serve an entire cluster feasibly?

diagram.note: Within each representative neighborhood, ∑ᵢxᵢⱼ=1.

frames.claim: Expected opening cost is at most F*=∑ᵢfᵢyᵢ*.
frames.explanation: Use xᵢⱼ*≤yᵢ* inside each neighborhood. Disjointness allows the neighborhood sums of fᵢyᵢ* to add to at most the full LP opening cost.
frames.carry: Feasibility and the opening budget do not depend on an expected number of open facilities.

frames.title: Route a nonrepresentative through a shared support neighbor
frames.question: Which metric path relates a cluster client ℓ to the facility opened for j?

diagram.note: The intermediate facility h belongs to the LP support shared by clients ℓ and j.

frames.claim: A metric detour gives a connection bound in terms of dual prices and representative average distance.
frames.explanation: For positive LP assignment support, the dual price bounds each relevant client-support distance. The random final leg averages to Cj*. Nonmetric prices would not support the first inequality.
frames.carry: The remaining task is to control the chosen representative’s v*+C*.

frames.title: Use the actual representative priority
frames.question: Why is minimizing connection average alone insufficient?

diagram.note: The priority score contains both the dual price and connection average.

frames.claim: Each cluster client costs at most 2vℓ*+Cℓ* in expectation.
frames.explanation: Client ℓ was still unassigned when j was selected, so it was a candidate in that same minimum-score comparison. This logical timing is what licenses the substitution.
frames.carry: The detour cost is now charged to the client’s own LP/dual quantities.

frames.title: Close with primal and dual objectives together
frames.question: What prevents separately charged opening and dual prices from being counted as unrelated lower bounds?

diagram.note: Primal–dual equality relates the two budgets; both compare with the same OPT.

frames.claim: E[total]≤F*+C*+2∑vⱼ*=3LP≤3OPT.
frames.explanation: The equality of optimal LP primal and dual objectives is essential to the numerical factor. Feasible arbitrary LP/dual values would require retaining their actual values in the bound.
frames.carry: One feasible rounded solution is certified by a combined expectation bound.

challenges.title: Recover the dual charge you need not spend
challenges.skill: Sharpen an aggregate approximation proof using the distinction between representatives and their clients.
challenges.connection: The example’s sole client is itself a representative, so its expected connection is C*, not the coarser 2v*+C* bound.
challenges.prompt: Assume an optimal LP and dual have three clients with (v*,C*) equal to (3,1), (4,2), and (5,3). Their total opening contribution is F*=6. The clustering chooses client 1 as the sole representative and assigns the other two clients to its cluster. Derive the refined expected total-cost bound by charging representative connections exactly, and express the general improvement over 3LP in terms of the sum of representative dual prices. Explain why this does not establish a universal 2.5 approximation.
hints: The representative’s opened facility is sampled from its own x-distribution.
Replace 2vⱼ*+Cⱼ* by Cⱼ* only for representatives.

probe.prompt: What refined expected total-cost upper bound follows from these data?
probe.feedback: Connections cost at most C₁+(2v₂+C₂)+(2v₃+C₃)=1+10+13=24; add F*=6 for a total of 30. The generic bound is 3LP=36, and the saving is 2v₁=6.

solution: The primal LP is F*+∑C*=6+6=12, matching the dual sum 3+4+5=12.
The representative pays expected connection exactly C₁*=1 by its sampling distribution.
Other clients pay at most 2v₂*+C₂*=10 and 2v₃*+C₃*=13, so the expected total is at most 6+1+10+13=30.
For a representative set R, the same argument gives 3LP−2∑ⱼ∈R vⱼ*.
A universal factor 2.5 would require ∑R vⱼ*≥LP/4 for every instance, which this calculation neither states nor proves. Representative selection is not known here to capture that fixed fraction.
rubric: Use exact representative connection expectations and coarse bounds only for other clients.
Check primal–dual equality for the supplied numbers.
Derive the general saving and identify the missing condition for a better universal ratio.
challenges.mistake: An improved bound on one clustering is not a uniform theorem unless the saving is itself bounded below in every instance.
challenges.followup: Express the guarantee as 3−2β when representative dual mass is known to be at least βLP, and state how such a mass lemma would need to be proved.

challenges.title: The missing term in a clustering priority
challenges.skill: Diagnose the exact failed inference without overclaiming an algorithmic counterexample.
challenges.connection: The worked example needs no detour. Multi-client clustering uses a minimum v*+C* score to close that detour bound.
challenges.prompt: For a cluster client ℓ let vℓ*=7 and Cℓ*=2. A proposed rule chooses representative j by the smallest C* only, with vj*=10 and Cj*=1. The local metric path ℓ–h–j–i has lengths 7,10,1, and i is the chosen service facility. Check both support-distance inequalities and the resulting detour bound. Does the comparison needed to conclude 2vℓ*+Cℓ* hold? Decide whether these local data alone disprove the whole algorithm’s factor-three guarantee, and specify what additional construction a genuine global counterexample would require.
hints: Compare the scores vj*+Cj* and vℓ*+Cℓ*, not Cj* and Cℓ* alone.
A broken proof inequality and a fully valid bad instance are different levels of evidence.

probe.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by the stated local data?
options: The detour is bounded by 16 because Cj*≤Cℓ* implies vj*+Cj*≤vℓ*+Cℓ*.
The detour bound is 18 rather than 16, exposing a missing priority inequality; a global factor-three counterexample still needs compatible optimal LP/dual and clustering data.
The metric assumption is violated because a path can have length 18 while Cℓ*=2.
The data prove the original v*+C* rule also fails, since it must choose j.
feedback: The missing dual-price term is ten versus seven; C-ordering alone does not compare the sums.
Correct. The local substitution fails because 11>9, but these few quantities are not a complete feasible optimal primal–dual instance.
Cℓ* is an average over its own fractional assignments, not a universal upper bound on every metric path or every facility distance.
The original score rule would prefer ℓ’s score nine to j’s score eleven while both remain eligible.

solution: The support bounds c(ℓ,h)≤vℓ*=7 and c(j,h)≤vj*=10 hold at equality.
The metric detour gives c(ℓ,i)≤7+10+1=18, whereas 2vℓ*+Cℓ*=16.
The intended substitution would require vj*+Cj*=11≤vℓ*+Cℓ*=9, which fails despite Cj*<Cℓ*.
This refutes the asserted per-client proof step under the modified rule. It does not by itself establish an approximation ratio violation on a full input.

A genuine global counterexample must supply a complete metric, feasible optimal primal and dual solutions with the advertised support, the full clustering sequence, and total rounded cost compared with actual OPT.
rubric: Check both local support bounds and compute the two competing detour charges.
Identify the precise representative-order inequality that fails.
Distinguish a failed local certificate from a fully verified global bad instance.
challenges.mistake: Declaring every failed sufficient bound an algorithmic counterexample skips feasibility, LP optimality, and the global objective comparison.
challenges.followup: Investigate whether the local numbers can be embedded into a line metric with an optimal LP having the stated support; list the extra dual constraints that must be checked.

proof.goal: Show randomized midpoint ordering gives expected weighted completion at most twice the relaxed optimum.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §5.9. The lower-bounding time-indexed relaxation and its compressed polynomial implementation are source inputs. The displayed conditional calculation uses independent per-job midpoint samples.

frames.title: Normalize processing into a sampled point
frames.question: Why is a long job not given total sampling probability larger than one?

diagram.note: Sampling chooses one processing location per job, rather than selecting each occupied interval independently.

frames.claim: Xⱼ is a genuine probability distribution and Cⱼ*=E[Xⱼ]+pⱼ/2.
frames.explanation: The relaxation allocates exactly pⱼ processing units to job j. Dividing those units by pⱼ makes its occupied midpoints equally weighted by their processing fractions.
frames.carry: Every job supplies exactly one ordering key.

frames.title: Turn the sampled order into a feasible schedule
frames.question: How are release dates respected when a selected job is not yet available?

diagram.note: The order is a priority list; the machine may wait for the next job.

frames.claim: The nonpreemptive output respects all release dates in every outcome.
frames.explanation: For all jobs before j whose selected midpoint is at most x, release times are at most x−1/2. Inducting along the list bounds completion by their total processing plus their latest release, not by processing alone.
frames.carry: Conditioning on Xⱼ=x isolates a prefix whose release contribution is controlled.

frames.title: Cancel the job-length normalization
frames.question: Why does the expected preceding processing become a machine-capacity prefix sum?

diagram.note: Ties can be overcounted safely; no independence of completion times is needed.

frames.claim: Conditioned on Xⱼ=x, expected preceding work is at most x+1/2.
frames.explanation: Each job’s sampling probability divides by its own processing time, which exactly cancels its contribution pₖ to the preceding-load sum. Prefix capacity then bounds all jobs together.
frames.carry: The release and work terms sum to at most 2x.

frames.title: Average the conditional statement
frames.question: Which normalization turns pⱼ+2E[Xⱼ] into the promised factor?

diagram.note: The final step needs an optimal relaxation value, not an arbitrary feasible relaxed schedule.

frames.claim: Expected weighted completion is at most twice the integral optimum.
frames.explanation: Multiply by nonnegative weights and add by linearity. The argument does not factor any joint distribution of completion times; the sole independence used earlier concerned sampled ordering keys.
frames.carry: A conditional per-job bound becomes a global expected approximation.

challenges.title: Trace sampling, idle time, and the relaxation separately
challenges.skill: Compute a rounded schedule distribution and distinguish it from the relaxed lower bound.
challenges.connection: The two-job example has two possible orders. A third released high-density job adds a second forced interruption before the long job resumes.
challenges.prompt: Jobs A,B,C have (p,r,w) equal to (2,0,1),(1,1,4),(1,2,3). The relaxed schedule runs A on [0,1), B on [1,2), C on [2,3), and A on [3,4). Derive each sampled midpoint law and relaxed completion value. Enumerate the rounded schedules, including necessary idle time, and compute their expected weighted completion. Verify the integral optimum by comparing possible first jobs; then compare the actual result with the theorem’s factor-two upper bound.
hints: Only A has a random midpoint, at 0.5 or 3.5.
When B is first, the machine must wait until time one.

probe.prompt: What is the expected rounded weighted-completion objective?
probe.feedback: With A first, completions are 2,3,4 and cost 2+12+12=26. Otherwise the order is B,C,A, completions are 2,3,5 and cost 8+9+5=22. The two cases are equally likely, so the expectation is 24.

solution: A samples 0.5 or 3.5 with probability one half each; B samples 1.5 and C samples 2.5 surely.
Relaxed values are C_A*=2+1=3, C_B*=1.5+0.5=2, C_C*=2.5+0.5=3, giving objective 3+8+9=20.
The early A sample yields A,B,C with cost 26. The late A sample yields B,C,A, waiting until time one, with cost 22.
Thus expected output cost is 24. For this three-job instance, evaluating earliest-start schedules for all six orders gives 26,27,27,22,31,38, so OPT=22.
The theorem gives E[cost]≤2·20=40. The valid bound is much looser than both the exact expectation 24 and integral optimum 22.
rubric: Normalize A’s processing samples and calculate all C* values.
Include release-date idle time in each nonpreemptive outcome.
Verify OPT independently and separate actual expectation from the theorem’s upper bound.
challenges.mistake: Using the relaxed objective 20 as though it were an achievable nonpreemptive schedule confuses the benchmark with the output.
challenges.followup: Increase w_C while preserving the displayed relaxed order and derive how the two rounded costs and their expectation change; state when that relaxed order remains justified.

challenges.title: Does the same proof survive a shared quantile?
challenges.skill: Find a failed conditional-independence identity without falsely refuting another valid algorithm.
challenges.connection: The example’s midpoint samples are independent across jobs. The source also discusses shared α-points, but that variant needs its own justification.
challenges.prompt: Two length-two jobs have relaxed processing intervals B:[0,1) and [2,3), A:[1,2) and [3,4). Let r_B=0 and r_A=1. Choose one common U uniformly in (0,1), using the first occupied midpoint of each job when U≤1/2 and the second otherwise. Calculate Pr(X_B≤1.5 | X_A=1.5), compare it with the marginal probability, and compute the conditional preceding-work term for A. Identify the exact equality from the independent-sampling proof that no longer applies. Explain why this observation alone does not prove shared-α scheduling violates the factor-two theorem.
hints: Conditioning on the early midpoint of A reveals which half of the shared U interval occurred.
The independent proof substitutes a marginal law for another job after conditioning on X_A.

probe.prompt: What is the correct interpretation of the conditional calculation?
options: The conditional preceding work is one, because B’s marginal chance of preceding A is one half.
The conditional preceding work is zero, because both jobs choose their first midpoint together.
The conditional preceding work is two rather than the marginal expression one; this breaks that independence substitution, not necessarily the algorithmic guarantee.
The conditional preceding work is four, proving the factor-two approximation is impossible for shared quantiles.
feedback: This incorrectly replaces the conditional law under a shared random U by B’s marginal law.
B’s first midpoint is 0.5, before A’s first midpoint 1.5, so B does precede A.
Correct. X_A=1.5 forces U≤1/2 and X_B=0.5, so B contributes its full processing two. A separate proof may still establish a guarantee for shared α.
There is only one preceding job of length two; a failed proof substitution is not an impossibility theorem.

solution: The early A event is exactly U≤1/2. Under it, B’s midpoint equals 0.5 surely, so the conditional probability is one.
Marginally B’s midpoint is 0.5 or 2.5 with equal probabilities; Pr(X_B≤1.5)=1/2.
Consequently E[p_B1{X_B≤X_A}|X_A=1.5]=2, while p_BPr(X_B≤1.5)=1.
The independent proof’s step equating the conditional other-job law to its marginal law is unavailable.
Both shared-quantile outcomes actually put B before A here. The feasible schedule runs B to time two and A to time four; nothing in this instance disproves the approximation theorem.
rubric: Compute conditional and marginal laws from the shared seed.
Locate the failed equality and its independence hypothesis precisely.
Separate a proof failure from a verified bad approximation instance.
challenges.mistake: Correlated sampling can invalidate one analysis while another analysis still works; the inference “proof fails, therefore algorithm fails” is not valid.
challenges.followup: Recompute the same conditional event with independent U_A and U_B, and identify exactly where the value returns from two to one.

proof.goal: Round each commodity to a complete path and control all edge loads by a per-edge tail bound plus a union bound.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§5.10–5.11. Unit demands, independent choices across commodities, and a polynomial number of edges are assumed. Path decomposition and fractional optimization are source inputs.

frames.title: Sample routes rather than individual edges
frames.question: Why does every rounded commodity still satisfy flow conservation?

diagram.note: Dependence between edges on one path is intentional and preserves connectivity.

frames.claim: Each rounded commodity is feasible in every outcome; E[Lₑ]=μₑ.
frames.explanation: Independent rounding of edge variables could create broken routes. Sampling one path creates correlated edges within a commodity but independent commodity indicators for any fixed edge.
frames.carry: The fixed-edge load is a sum of independent bounded indicators.

frames.title: Bound the exponential moment
frames.question: Which independence permits multiplying the moment-generating factors?

diagram.note: The multiplication is over commodities, never over graph edges.

frames.claim: For a≥μₑ, choosing λ=ln(a/μₑ) gives the optimized Chernoff bound.
frames.explanation: The moment step is stronger than pairwise variance control. It is the source of the logarithmic-over-logarithmic congestion threshold at constant mean.
frames.carry: One edge now has an explicit high-load failure probability.

frames.title: Choose a tail small enough for the whole graph
frames.question: Why must a constant-probability edge bound be strengthened?

diagram.note: The constant C must absorb the polynomial number of tested edges.

frames.claim: A sufficiently large C makes each edge failure inverse-polynomially small.
frames.explanation: This asymptotic choice presumes bounded fractional mean. For large μₑ a multiplicative concentration regime is more natural; a one-size substitution should not silently discard that parameter.
frames.carry: The local failure target is calibrated to the number of constraints.

frames.title: Sum failures without inventing edge independence
frames.question: What does independence across graph edges contribute to the final step?

diagram.note: No edge-load independence is used in this inequality.

frames.claim: When |E|pmax<1, some complete path selection obeys all edge bounds.
frames.explanation: A routing path can make many edges’ loads strongly dependent. The union bound remains valid, and a sufficiently small product supplies positive success probability and a repeatable randomized construction.
frames.carry: Feasible routing and congestion control have distinct proof obligations.

challenges.title: Calibrate a global failure budget from exact tails
challenges.skill: Choose an integer congestion threshold using a local distribution and a dependent global constraint family.
challenges.connection: The four-commodity example computes one edge’s load. The algorithm must make the probability of any bad edge small enough.
challenges.prompt: Suppose there are 100 edges, and each fixed edge load has distribution Binomial(8,1/4); loads on different edges may be arbitrarily dependent. Find the smallest integer threshold a for which the union bound certifies Pr(any edge has load at least a)≤0.05. Compute the relevant exact binomial tails and explain why no independence across edges is necessary. Compare this finite calibration with inserting μ=2 into a Chernoff expression.
hints: Use a denominator 4⁸=65536 and include every term at or above the threshold.
Check a=6 and a=7; the tail is decreasing in a.

probe.prompt: What is the smallest threshold a certified by this union bound?
probe.feedback: For a=6 the local tail is (252+24+1)/65536=277/65536, yielding a global bound above 0.42. For a=7 it is 25/65536, yielding 2500/65536≈0.03815≤0.05. Thus seven is the first certified threshold.

solution: For a=6, the binomial numerator is C(8,6)3²+C(8,7)3+1=252+24+1=277.
The union bound is then 27700/65536≈0.42267, so a=6 is not certified. Any smaller a has an even larger tail.
For a=7, the local numerator is 8·3+1=25 and the global bound is 2500/65536≈0.03815.
Thus a=7 is the smallest threshold this information certifies. The actual global failure may be smaller because the union bound need not be tight.
Chernoff bounds are valid under the within-edge commodity independence, but may be looser here. The final summation works under arbitrary cross-edge dependence.
rubric: Compute exact inclusive binomial tails and use the correct failure event.
Prove minimality relative to the union-bound certificate, not the unknown true global probability.
State the two distinct independence issues clearly.
challenges.mistake: Using Pr(L=a) instead of Pr(L≥a) drops higher loads, while multiplying independent edge-success probabilities assumes dependence information not supplied.
challenges.followup: If the 100 load variables are identical in every outcome, compute the true global failure at a=6 and explain how much the union bound wastes.

challenges.title: Pairwise independent routing bits can have a heavy tail
challenges.skill: Construct a high-order dependence obstruction to an exponential-moment argument.
challenges.connection: The example’s binomial law comes from mutual independence across commodities. Pairwise independence preserves mean and variance but not the same tail.
challenges.prompt: Let R be uniform in F₂⁴. For every nonzero a∈F₂⁴ define B_a=1 when a·R=0, with dot product modulo two. There are fifteen load indicators. Prove that distinct indicators are independent fair bits, derive the exact distribution of L=∑B_a, and calculate Pr(L≥12). Explain why the Chernoff product-of-moments step is unjustified even though every pair is independent. Generalize the rare high-load probability to r seed bits.
hints: Two distinct nonzero vectors over F₂ are linearly independent.
When R≠0, its orthogonal hyperplane contains 2³ vectors including zero.

probe.prompt: What is Pr(L≥12) for the four-bit seed?
probe.feedback: R=0 gives all fifteen indicators one, with probability 1/16. Every nonzero R has exactly seven nonzero orthogonal vectors, so L=7 otherwise. Pairwise independence does not remove the atom at load fifteen.

solution: For nonzero a, the functional a·R is uniform, so B_a has mean one half.
For distinct nonzero a,b, the map R↦(a·R,b·R) has rank two. Its four outputs are equally likely, proving pairwise independence.
If R=0 then L=15. If R≠0 its kernel has eight vectors, seven nonzero, so L=7.
Consequently Pr(L≥12)=1/16, although mean is 15/2 and variance still equals 15/4 as pairwise independence predicts.
The exponential moment involves products of all fifteen indicators. Pairwise independence does not factor that product.
For r bits, L=2ʳ−1 with probability 2^−r and L=2^(r−1)−1 otherwise; the extreme-load probability is 1/(n+1), not exponentially small in n.
rubric: Prove pairwise independence using rank, not just state it.
Derive the complete two-point load distribution and its tail.
Identify why high-order moment factorization requires more than pairwise independence.
challenges.mistake: A correct variance computation is not a Chernoff proof. Exponential tails use a family of higher moments that pairwise independence does not determine.
challenges.followup: For r=4 compare the exact extreme-load probability with the fully independent Binomial(15,1/2) probability of load fifteen.

proof.goal: Use a logarithmic dominating sample, enumerate its proper colors, and reduce each extension to 2SAT.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §5.12. Assumes a 3-colorable graph with minimum degree at least δn for fixed δ>0. The finite tripartite picture illustrates extension; probability and enumeration bounds concern the general dense input.

frames.title: Make every unsampled vertex lose a color
frames.question: Why does domination reduce the extension to lists of size at most two?

diagram.note: Every outside vertex must meet the sample; otherwise it retains three choices.

frames.claim: A properly colored dominating sample leaves at most two allowed colors per outside vertex.
frames.explanation: A color appearing on a sample neighbor is forbidden at the vertex. Domination guarantees at least one such forbidden color, independent of which correct candidate sample coloring is being tested.
frames.carry: Each remaining vertex can be encoded by at most one Boolean choice.

frames.title: Bound a failed domination event
frames.question: How does minimum degree make a logarithmic sample sufficient?

diagram.note: Repeated sample vertices cause no problem; the number of distinct sampled vertices is at most s.

frames.claim: With high probability the sample dominates the whole graph.
frames.explanation: Each draw misses a fixed vertex’s neighborhood with probability at most 1−δ. Independence concerns the sample draws; domination events for different vertices need not be independent.
frames.carry: One sampled set supports all candidate-coloring tests.

frames.title: Enumerate the promised restriction
frames.question: Why does trying exponentially many colors of a small sample remain polynomial?

diagram.note: The polynomial exponent depends on fixed density; this is not a practical small constant assertion.

frames.claim: At least one tested sample coloring is the restriction of a valid global coloring.
frames.explanation: Reject improperly colored sample candidates. The promise ensures some remaining candidate agrees with one true coloring, even though most candidates may fail extension.
frames.carry: For that candidate, the residual Boolean constraints are satisfiable.

frames.title: Encode forbidden edge-color pairs locally
frames.question: Why does an edge constraint produce a 2-clause rather than a global coloring guess?

diagram.note: Each forbidden simultaneous choice uses at most the two endpoint Boolean variables.

frames.claim: Solving a satisfiable extension 2SAT formula yields a proper full 3-coloring.
frames.explanation: Add a clause for every edge and every common permitted color. Satisfying all clauses excludes every monochromatic outside edge; lists already exclude sample-edge conflicts.
frames.carry: Sampling, enumeration, and exact extension each have a precise role.

challenges.title: Turn a domination failure target into an enumeration cost
challenges.skill: Calibrate the probability bound and interpret fixed-parameter polynomial time honestly.
challenges.connection: The small tripartite example chooses a helpful sample deliberately. This challenge derives how large a genuinely random sample must be.
challenges.prompt: Let n=1000 and minimum degree be at least 0.2n. Take s independent uniform vertex draws with replacement. Find the smallest integer s for which the displayed union-bound analysis guarantees domination failure at most 0.01. Derive a symbolic expression for general n,δ,η. Then express the corresponding 3^s color enumeration as a power of n when η=n^−c, and explain why fixed-density polynomial time does not imply a small practical search.
hints: Require n(1−δ)^s≤η, and remember ln(1−δ) is negative.
With η=n^−c, the numerator becomes (c+1)ln n.

probe.prompt: What is the smallest s certified for the given numerical parameters?
probe.feedback: The inequality is 1000·0.8^s≤0.01, so s≥ln(10^−5)/ln(0.8)≈51.594. The smallest integer is 52; rounding down would not meet the requested certificate.

solution: For a fixed vertex, all s draws miss its neighborhood with probability at most 0.8^s.
The union bound gives failure at most 1000·0.8^s, so s≥ln(0.01/1000)/ln(0.8).
Taking the ceiling gives s=52. This is the smallest sample size certified by this worst-case bound, not necessarily by the graph’s true failure probability.
In general s=⌈ln(n/η)/(−ln(1−δ))⌉. For η=n^−c this is (c+1)ln n/(−ln(1−δ)) up to rounding.
Therefore 3^s≤3n^((c+1)ln3/(−ln(1−δ))). For fixed δ,c this is polynomial, but its exponent and finite search can be enormous.
rubric: Derive the per-vertex and global probabilities with the correct logarithm direction.
Use the ceiling and distinguish the certificate from the unknown exact probability.
Translate the enumeration into a parameter-dependent polynomial exponent.
challenges.mistake: Writing O(log n) without its δ-dependent constant hides the very term that controls the enumeration cost.
challenges.followup: Repeat the calculation with sampling without replacement and derive an equal or stronger per-vertex miss bound.

challenges.title: A proper sample coloring can leave an unsatisfiable extension
challenges.skill: Construct the Boolean implication obstruction corresponding to a residual odd cycle.
challenges.connection: The tripartite example extends cleanly. Here a locally proper partial coloring forces two-color lists that are globally inconsistent.
challenges.prompt: Consider a five-cycle v0,…,v4, and attach a distinct pendant sample vertex s_i to each v_i. Color every s_i with color 1. This partial coloring is proper, but each cycle vertex now has list {2,3}. Introduce b_i=1 for color 3. Write all edge clauses, exhibit an implication path from b0 to ¬b0 and the reverse, and conclude that this candidate cannot extend. Show that the original graph nevertheless is 3-colorable. This local gadget illustrates the extension step, not the dense-sampling probability theorem.
hints: For an edge, forbid both endpoints choosing 2 and both choosing 3.
Alternating around an odd cycle flips the starting Boolean value after five edges.

probe.prompt: What is the length of a shortest implication path from b0 to ¬b0 in this formula?
probe.feedback: Each edge forces the opposite Boolean value. Going once around the five-cycle yields b0→¬b1→b2→¬b3→b4→¬b0, length five. A shorter path would correspond to a shorter odd closed walk in C5.

solution: Each edge i,i+1 contributes (b_i∨b_(i+1)) and (¬b_i∨¬b_(i+1)), enforcing opposite endpoint bits. There are ten 2-clauses.
The implication path b0→¬b1→b2→¬b3→b4→¬b0 follows five edges.
Starting with ¬b0 gives the reverse-parity path ¬b0→b1→¬b2→b3→¬b4→b0. Thus b0 and ¬b0 lie in the same strongly connected component.
The 2SAT formula is unsatisfiable: a five-cycle cannot be colored with only 2 and 3.

The original graph is still 3-colorable: color the cycle with three colors and each pendant leaf with any color different from its neighbor. The failing condition is this particular sample restriction, not the original promise.
rubric: Encode both same-color prohibitions for every residual edge.
Exhibit both implication paths and the strongly connected contradiction.
Give a global 3-coloring argument and state the local gadget’s limited role.
challenges.mistake: Properly coloring the sample checks only its induced edges; it does not establish that the partial coloring extends to the whole graph.
challenges.followup: Replace the five-cycle with an even cycle and describe both satisfying Boolean assignments and their interpretation as residual colorings.

proof.goal: Relax sign products to a Gram matrix and transfer an angle-by-angle separation inequality into an expected cut guarantee.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§6.1–6.2. Nonnegative edge weights are assumed. Polynomial-time SDP optimization and the numerical minimization defining αGW are inputs; the geometric probability and objective comparison are explained.

frames.title: Embed every integral cut in the relaxation
frames.question: Why is the SDP optimum an upper bound rather than a lower bound?

diagram.note: Every sign solution has a feasible rank-one Gram matrix.

frames.claim: SDPopt≥OPTcut.
frames.explanation: The relaxation enlarges the feasible set of a maximization problem. Its objective has the same value on every embedded integral cut, so the inequality direction is fixed.
frames.carry: A good rounding ratio against SDPopt also implies one against OPTcut.

frames.title: Read cut probability from the angle
frames.question: What fraction of hyperplane normal directions separate one pair?
