diagram.note: Only the projection of the random normal onto the pair’s plane affects separation.

frames.claim: Pr(edge is cut)=θ/π.
frames.explanation: In the two-dimensional span, the separating normals occupy total angular measure 2θ out of 2π. Rotational symmetry supplies the probability even when different edge events are dependent.
frames.carry: The rounded and relaxed edge expressions can be compared pointwise in θ.

frames.title: Choose the worst angular ratio
frames.question: Why must one prove the inequality for every possible edge angle?

diagram.note: A finite test at a few convenient angles cannot certify the universal constant.

frames.claim: Every edge’s expected rounded contribution is at least αGW times its relaxed contribution.
frames.explanation: Different instances and different optimal vector solutions can use different angles. The minimum ratio creates one coefficient valid across all of them; the source gives approximately 0.87856.
frames.carry: The local inequality is uniform enough to sum over the graph.

frames.title: Sum before demanding a good outcome
frames.question: Why is independence between cut edges unnecessary?

diagram.note: A random hyperplane defines one valid cut in every outcome.

frames.claim: Expected cut weight is at least αGWOPTcut.
frames.explanation: All edge events share one random normal and are usually dependent. Feasibility is supplied by global vertex signs, while linearity combines their marginal guarantees.
frames.carry: One coherent cut, not independently rounded edge decisions, realizes the theorem.

challenges.title: A tight SDP can still lose value during rounding
challenges.skill: Use symmetry and PSD eigenvalues to separate relaxation loss from rounding loss.
challenges.connection: The triangle example exhibits an SDP gap. On K4 the relaxation is exact, yet the same rounding still has a nontrivial loss.
challenges.prompt: For the unit-weight complete graph K4, symmetrize any feasible Gram matrix over all vertex permutations, giving diagonal one and common off-diagonal c. Derive its eigenvalues and the allowed interval for c. Compute the SDP optimum and the integral maximum cut. For the regular-simplex optimum c=−1/3, compute the expected hyperplane cut weight and its ratio to OPT. Explain why equality of relaxation and integral optima does not force the rounded solution to be optimal.
hints: The all-ones direction has eigenvalue 1+3c; the orthogonal subspace has eigenvalue 1−c.
K4 has six edges, each separated with probability arccos(−1/3)/π.

probe.prompt: What is the expected rounded-cut / OPT ratio?
probe.feedback: PSD forces c≥−1/3. The objective 3(1−c) is maximized at four, equal to the 2-by-2 integral cut. Hyperplane rounding yields 6·arccos(−1/3)/π in expectation, so dividing by four gives (3/2)arccos(−1/3)/π≈0.91226.

solution: Averaging feasible matrices preserves PSD, unit diagonal and objective, so an optimum may be taken with common off-diagonal c.
Its eigenvalues are 1+3c once and 1−c three times; hence −1/3≤c≤1.
The SDP objective is six times (1−c)/2=3(1−c), with optimum four at c=−1/3.
The largest integral cut partitions four vertices 2+2 and has four edges, so the relaxation is exact on this input.
The regular-simplex vectors have pair angle arccos(−1/3). Linearity gives expected rounded cut 6 arccos(−1/3)/π, strictly below four.
An exact relaxation certifies that an optimal integral solution exists at that objective; the rounding distribution need not concentrate on those optimal solutions.
rubric: Justify symmetrization and both PSD eigenvalues.
Compute and compare integral and relaxed optima.
Derive the rounding expectation and explain the distinct source of loss.
challenges.mistake: A zero integrality gap does not make every optimal fractional representation an optimal integral output under an arbitrary rounding rule.
challenges.followup: Compare this expectation with rounding an optimal rank-one cut matrix; explain why different optimal SDP solutions can have different rounded performance.

challenges.title: Why independently correct edge probabilities do not define a cut
challenges.skill: Derive joint constraints imposed by a single global hyperplane.
challenges.connection: The triangle’s three edge probabilities are each two thirds. Their dependence is essential to cut feasibility.
challenges.prompt: Use the equiangular triangle vectors from the example. Determine the distribution of the three cut-edge indicators up to probability-zero boundary events. Compute the covariance of two distinct edge indicators and the variance of their sum. Compare with independently sampling three Bernoulli(2/3) edge decisions. Identify an impossible event produced by the independent scheme and explain why the original expected-value proof never needed that independence.
hints: A nontrivial cut of a triangle always cuts exactly two edges.
Rotational symmetry makes the three possible two-edge cut sets equally likely.

probe.prompt: What is the covariance of two distinct cut-edge indicators?
probe.feedback: Each edge is cut with probability 2/3, but any specified pair is jointly cut with probability 1/3. Thus covariance is 1/3−4/9=−1/9. The negative covariances cancel the individual variances so the cut-edge count is always two.

solution: The vectors sum to zero, so a generic hyperplane cannot put all three on the same side. Thus exactly two triangle edges are cut in every nonboundary outcome.
Symmetry gives probability one third to each of the three two-edge cut sets.
For distinct indicators Xi,Xj, E[XiXj]=1/3 and E[Xi]E[Xj]=4/9, so Cov=−1/9.
Each indicator has variance 2/9. Therefore Var(X1+X2+X3)=3·2/9+2·3·(−1/9)=0.
Independent Bernoulli decisions would cut all three edges with probability 8/27, impossible for any vertex bipartition of an odd cycle.
The actual theorem sums marginal expected edge weights. Global signs ensure feasibility; edge independence is neither assumed nor desired.
rubric: Derive the three supported joint patterns and their probabilities.
Compute covariance and total variance consistently.
Use odd-cycle parity to identify why independent edge decisions can be infeasible.
challenges.mistake: Matching every edge marginal is not sufficient to preserve the combinatorial feasible set.
challenges.followup: For unequal triangle edge weights, derive the three possible cut weights and their variance under these same vectors.

proof.goal: Combine independent hyperplane signatures, repair, high-degree neighborhood removal, and repeated semicolorings.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §6.5. A feasible vector 3-coloring and its polynomial-time computation are inputs. Maximum degree bounds apply to the remaining graph; high-degree removal uses the promise that every neighborhood is bipartite.

frames.title: Make collisions exponentially rarer
frames.question: What changes when the hyperplanes are independent rather than repeated?

diagram.note: An edge survives as a collision only if all independently sampled planes fail to separate it.

frames.claim: Pr(edge endpoints share a signature)≤3^−t.
frames.explanation: Adjacent vectors have angle at least 2π/3, so each hyperplane has collision probability at most one third. Multiplying these failures uses independence across hyperplanes, not across edges.
frames.carry: The palette grows as 2^t while expected repair cost shrinks as 3^−t.

frames.title: Convert collisions into a large colored subset
frames.question: Why must a failure-probability target be distinguished from an expectation bound?

diagram.note: Every remaining edge has different endpoint signatures, so the remaining subgraph is properly colored.

frames.claim: With t=Θ(log₃Δ), a useful constant fraction survives with constant probability.
frames.explanation: Choose t with enough additive slack for the desired constant success probability. Expected few collisions alone does not mean every sample has few collisions; resampling can select a useful semicoloring.
frames.carry: The bounded-degree subroutine uses O(Δ^(log₃2)) colors.

frames.title: Remove high degree using the promise
frames.question: Why may the open neighborhood use two fresh colors?

diagram.note: N(v) excludes v itself; under a global 3-coloring its vertices use only the other two colors.

frames.claim: The high-degree phase costs O(n/σ) colors and leaves maximum degree below σ.
frames.explanation: Bipartiteness can be checked and colored algorithmically. Different removed batches receive distinct palettes, so edges between batches cannot become monochromatic.
frames.carry: The total semicoloring cost has two competing powers of σ.

frames.title: Balance the terms, then finish the graph
frames.question: How does a semicoloring become a full coloring without cross-round conflicts?

diagram.note: Repeat on uncolored vertices and use fresh palettes; a constant surviving fraction gives O(log n) rounds.

frames.claim: The full coloring uses O(n^(log₆2)log n) colors under this analysis.
frames.explanation: The final logarithm records repeated semicolorings, not a change in the local collision exponent. Palettes must remain distinct across phases unless an additional conflict-handling argument is supplied.
frames.carry: Probability amplification, degree splitting and palette accounting are all necessary.

challenges.title: Choose signatures for a specified success probability
challenges.skill: Calibrate collision expectation, vertex repair and Markov failure rather than merely count colors.
challenges.connection: The example fixes four planes and computes an expectation. This question starts with a demanded success probability.
challenges.prompt: Let n=72 and maximum degree Δ=27. Delete both endpoints of every signature-collision edge. Using only the displayed worst-case edge count and Markov inequality, choose the smallest integer t that certifies at least probability 3/4 of retaining at least half the vertices. Compute the palette size and expected deletion bound. Explain why dependence between collisions does not invalidate this certificate, and why t−1 is not certified by the same estimates.
hints: There are at most 72·27/2=972 edges.
The bad event D>36 is bounded by E[D]/36≤2·972/(36·3^t).

probe.prompt: What is the smallest certified number t of independent planes?
probe.feedback: The Markov bound is 54/3^t and must be at most 1/4, requiring 3^t≥216. Thus t=5 works (243≥216), while t=4 gives 54/81=2/3. The palette has 32 colors and E[D]≤8.

solution: The maximum number of edges is 972, hence E[bad edges]≤972·3^−t.
Deleting both endpoints gives E[D]≤1944·3^−t, without needing collision independence.
Markov gives Pr(D>36)≤54·3^−t. Requiring this at most 1/4 gives 3^t≥216.
The smallest integer is t=5. Then E[bad edges]≤4, E[D]≤8, and the failure bound is 2/9<1/4.
With t=4, this analysis gives failure at most 2/3, not the requested quarter. This is a limitation of the certificate, not proof that four planes always fail.
rubric: Carry the endpoint-deletion factor two correctly.
Choose the smallest t meeting the stated Markov target and count 2^t colors.
Distinguish dependence-free expectation/Markov reasoning from a true failure lower bound.
challenges.mistake: Setting expected deleted vertices below half does not by itself give success probability three quarters.
challenges.followup: Derive the formula for arbitrary required failure η and retained fraction 1−β.

challenges.title: Reconstruct the degree split rather than quote its exponent
challenges.skill: Optimize a two-regime algorithm and preserve color feasibility across its phases.
challenges.connection: The bounded-degree example omits the high-degree batches and the repeated rounds that produce a full coloring.
challenges.prompt: Assume the bounded-degree semicoloring uses O(σ^a) colors, where a=log₃2, and high-degree neighborhood removal uses O(n/σ) colors. Derive the optimal cutoff and exponent. Specialize to n=6^12 and calculate the common scale of the two terms. Then explain why only the open neighborhood is bipartite under the promise, why each batch can be found without knowing the promised 3-coloring, and why reusing the same palette across arbitrary batches is unjustified.
hints: Set n/σ=σ^a, then use 1+a=log₃6.
A neighborhood’s bipartition is found by a standard graph search; the promise proves that search will succeed.

probe.prompt: For n=6^12, what is the common scale n/σ=σ^a at the balanced cutoff?
probe.feedback: The cutoff is σ=n^(1/(1+log₃2))=3^12. Both n/σ and σ^log₃2 equal 2^12=4096. Constants such as the two colors per high-degree batch are separate from this common growth scale.

solution: Balancing n/σ and σ^a gives σ^(1+a)=n, hence σ=n^(1/(1+a)).
The color exponent is a/(1+a)=log₆2. At n=6^12, σ=3^12 and both growth terms are 2^12.
In a promised 3-coloring, no neighbor of v uses v’s color, so G[N(v)] is bipartite. Adding v itself can create a triangle and need a third color.
A breadth-first bipartiteness algorithm finds the two-coloring without being handed the original 3-coloring. At least σ vertices are removed in a high-degree batch.
Distinct palettes prevent conflicts across arbitrary removed batches. Repeating semicoloring on the remainder adds O(log n) palettes because each successful round removes a constant fraction.
rubric: Derive the cutoff, exponent and numerical specialization.
Justify the exact neighborhood object and its constructive two-coloring.
Account for cross-batch and cross-round palette separation.
challenges.mistake: A correct coloring inside every batch does not control edges joining different batches when color names are reused.
challenges.followup: Suppose a stronger low-degree routine used O(σ^b) colors. Derive the new exponent and identify what happens as b tends to zero.

proof.goal: Use negative edge covariance to make selected-edge repairs cheaper than the selected-vertex benefit.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §13.2. A vector 3-coloring and standard Gaussian tail bounds are explicit inputs. The threshold calculation concerns its asymptotic large-degree regime; small degrees require separate treatment.

frames.title: Read all covariances from one Gaussian direction
frames.question: Why are adjacent projections not independent standard normals?

diagram.note: Each marginal is standard normal, but the pair geometry carries the useful dependence.

frames.claim: For an edge, Var(Zᵢ+Zⱼ)≤1.
frames.explanation: Expand the variance as 1+1+2Cov. The negative inner product makes a large common positive excursion unusually expensive.
frames.carry: A two-coordinate event can be bounded by a stronger one-dimensional tail.

frames.title: Enlarge the bad event in the useful direction
frames.question: Which sum event is guaranteed by two threshold exceedances?

diagram.note: Containment supplies an upper bound on harm, not an equality of events.

frames.claim: An adjacent pair’s tail has exponential scale e^(−2t²), versus e^(−t²/2) for one vertex.
frames.explanation: A centered normal with variance no larger than one has no larger positive upper tail than a standard normal. This comparison would fail in this form if the covariance constraint were weakened.
frames.carry: Bad-edge benefit decays much faster with threshold than good-vertex benefit.

frames.title: Repair before claiming an independent set
frames.question: Why may selected vertices be counted even though selection itself is not independent-set feasible?

diagram.note: A deletion can repair several edges, so charging one deletion to every selected edge is safe but possibly loose.

frames.claim: E[|I|]≥nQ(t)−mQ(2t).
frames.explanation: Delete one endpoint from each still-present selected edge. At most the original selected-edge count is removed, producing an actual independent set in every outcome. Linearity then subtracts expected harm.
frames.carry: The objective lower bound concerns a feasible repaired object.

frames.title: Choose a threshold that absorbs the degree factor
frames.question: What balances one-vertex and two-vertex tail exponents?

diagram.note: The 1/t marginal prefactor remains in the selected-vertex benefit.

frames.claim: A suitable threshold gives expected size Ω(nΔ^−1/3/√lnΔ).
frames.explanation: Use quantitative tail inequalities, not only exponent notation, to choose the additive constant so repair consumes at most a fixed fraction. The display describes growth and does not replace the source’s constants and regime checks.
frames.carry: Negative covariance is converted into a degree-dependent independent-set guarantee.

challenges.title: Derive the exponent for a weaker vector separation
challenges.skill: Recompute the degree exponent from covariance and Gaussian tail scales.
challenges.connection: The example uses covariance at most −1/2. This task changes the geometric constraint and follows its effect through the entire proof.
challenges.prompt: Suppose adjacent unit vectors instead satisfy vᵢ·vⱼ≤−β, where 0<β<1 is fixed. Using two-sided Gaussian tail estimates Q(x)=Θ(e^(−x²/2)/x) for x≥1, derive a valid pair-selection tail bound, the coefficient of lnΔ in the threshold t² needed to control repairs, and the resulting exponent of Δ in the independent-set size. Recover the original β=1/2 case and evaluate β=1/3. State which constants and degree regime the asymptotic notation suppresses.
hints: The sum variance is at most 2(1−β), so standardize the sum threshold before using Q.
Compare exp(−t²/(1−β)) with exp(−t²/2).

probe.prompt: What is the power a in nΔ^−a/√lnΔ for β=1/3?
probe.feedback: The exponent is a=(1−β)/(1+β). For β=1/3 it is (2/3)/(4/3)=1/2. The required threshold coefficient is 2(1−β)/(1+β)=1, so t² is lnΔ plus a suitable constant.

solution: Var(Zᵢ+Zⱼ)≤2(1−β), hence pair selection is at most Q(2t/√(2(1−β))).
Its exponential scale is exp(−t²/(1−β)); the single-vertex scale is exp(−t²/2).
Their ratio is Θβ(exp(−t²(1+β)/(2(1−β)))); the 1/t factors cancel up to β-dependent constants.
Choose t²=[2(1−β)/(1+β)]lnΔ+Cβ with a sufficiently large constant Cβ so the degree-weighted repair term is at most a fixed fraction of vertex benefit.
The marginal benefit is then Ωβ(nΔ^−(1−β)/(1+β)/√lnΔ). For β=1/2 the exponent is one third; for β=1/3 it is one half.
These estimates assume t≥1 and sufficiently large Δ; constants may depend on fixed β, and small-degree cases need another direct bound.
rubric: Standardize the Gaussian sum with its new variance.
Derive both the threshold coefficient and independent-set exponent.
Recover known cases and state the asymptotic restrictions honestly.
challenges.mistake: Changing covariance changes the pair-tail exponent before threshold optimization; merely keeping t²=(2/3)lnΔ imports a bound no longer proved.
challenges.followup: Investigate what the formula predicts as β tends to zero and explain why fixed-β constants cannot be treated uniformly near every endpoint.

challenges.title: Turn an expected size into an honest repetition guarantee
challenges.skill: Use bounded integer output to obtain a success probability without assuming independent vertex choices.
challenges.connection: The example’s 22.4332 is an expectation, not a deterministic independent-set size.
challenges.prompt: Let the repaired independent-set size R be integer-valued in [0,1000], and suppose the previous calculation rigorously gives E[R]≥22.4332. Prove existence of an outcome with at least 23 vertices. Using only this expectation and the range, derive a lower bound on Pr(R≥12) and an upper bound on the expected number of independent runs until such a set is found. Explain why these facts do not justify saying a single run succeeds with probability one half.
hints: On failure of R≥12 the integer R is at most eleven.
Bound the mean above by 11(1−p)+1000p and solve for p.

probe.prompt: What lower bound on Pr(R≥12) follows from this range-and-mean argument?
probe.feedback: If p=Pr(R≥12), then E[R]≤11+989p. Thus p≥(22.4332−11)/989=28583/2472500≈0.01156. An expectation near 22 does not imply a median near 22.

solution: If R≤22 in every outcome, its expectation would be at most 22, contradicting the assumed lower bound. Thus some outcome has R≥23.
Let p=Pr(R≥12). On the complementary event R≤11; on success R≤1000. Hence E[R]≤11(1−p)+1000p.
Combining with 22.4332≤E[R] yields p≥28583/2472500.
Independent repetitions have expected waiting time 1/p, at most 2472500/28583, about 86.5 runs.
The information permits highly skewed distributions: rare large outputs can supply the mean. A probability-one-half assertion requires a stronger distributional or second-moment argument.
rubric: Use integrality to prove the 23-vertex existence statement.
Derive the success-probability lower bound with correct failure maximum eleven.
Justify the repetition bound and identify the unsupported median claim.
challenges.mistake: Markov bounds upper tails from above; it cannot be reversed to claim a large lower-tail success probability from the mean alone.
challenges.followup: Derive the optimal range-and-mean bound for Pr(R≥h) for an arbitrary integer h≤E[R], and construct an extremal two-point distribution.

proof.goal: Grow feasible element prices, buy tight sets, and bound total cost by frequency-weighted dual charges.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §7.1. Every element must be coverable, costs and dual prices are nonnegative, and f denotes maximum element frequency. This is the bounded-frequency primal–dual method, not greedy’s harmonic bound.

frames.title: Spend the slack of a containing set
frames.question: What limits the next price increase of an uncovered element?

diagram.note: Uncovered elements are the only growing coordinates.

frames.claim: The price vector stays feasible for every set constraint.
frames.explanation: Increasing yₑ affects all sets containing e. Stop at the minimum remaining slack among them; this maintains all inequalities and produces a tight set covering e.
frames.carry: Each processed element becomes covered without losing the dual lower bound.

frames.title: Freeze the purchased set’s total price
frames.question: Why does a purchased set stay tight after later iterations?

diagram.note: A set may remain selected even if a later purchased set covers its elements too.

frames.claim: Every purchased set’s cost equals its final element-price sum.
frames.explanation: The algorithm never raises prices of covered elements. Once S is bought, all its elements become covered, so no future update can alter its dual sum.
frames.carry: The actual selected-set cost can be expanded exactly into price incidences.

frames.title: Count each price by its multiplicity
frames.question: What does the frequency bound count, and what does it not count?

diagram.note: Set size does not bound how often one element can be charged.

frames.claim: cost(selected)=∑ₑfselected(e)yₑ≤f∑ₑyₑ.
frames.explanation: Swap the order of summation over purchased sets and their elements. Every selected set belongs to the input family, so each element appears in at most f such sets.
frames.carry: The approximation loss is an overlap charge, not a slack violation.

frames.title: Use a genuinely feasible dual lower bound
frames.question: Why does a large price sum mean anything about integral OPT?

diagram.note: If any set budget were exceeded, the lower-bound certificate would disappear.

frames.claim: The returned cover costs at most fOPT.
frames.explanation: Feasibility makes every integral cover pay for all required element prices, even when it covers elements repeatedly. Nonnegative prices ensure repeated coverage cannot reduce this lower bound.
frames.carry: Growth, persistent tightness and overlap accounting close the proof.

challenges.title: Build a frequency-two family approaching factor two
challenges.skill: Construct and analyze a near-tight charging example rather than quote f.
challenges.connection: The worked example’s sequential purchases may look better than the worst-case frequency factor. This family makes the overlap charge explicit.
challenges.prompt: There are m elements. For each element e_i there is a singleton of cost one, and one universal set U has cost m−δ, where 0<δ<1. Process e1,…,em in order, raising only its price while uncovered; retain every bought set. Derive the selected sets, final dual prices, actual OPT, and approximation ratio. Specialize to m=6 and δ=0.1. Explain what reverse deletion would do on this family and why that improvement is not part of the specified buy-and-retain algorithm.
hints: The first m−1 elements each have slack one in their singleton.
Before processing e_m the universal set has residual slack 1−δ.

probe.prompt: For m=6 and δ=0.1, what is selected cost divided by OPT?
probe.feedback: Five singleton purchases cost five, then U costs 5.9, so selected cost is 10.9. OPT is 5.9 and the final dual sum is also 5.9. The ratio is 109/59, tending to two for large m with fixed δ.

solution: For the first m−1 elements, raising to one makes the singleton tight before U is tight, so those singleton sets are bought.
The final element can rise only to 1−δ before U becomes tight; buying U covers everything.
Final dual sum is (m−1)+(1−δ)=m−δ. U alone has that cost, so weak duality proves OPT=m−δ.
The retained solution costs (m−1)+(m−δ)=2m−1−δ, with ratio (2m−1−δ)/(m−δ) approaching two.
Each of the first m−1 prices is charged twice; the final price is charged once. This realizes the frequency-two accounting.
Reverse deletion would discard all singleton purchases after U is present, returning OPT on this family; that is an extra algorithmic step, not a consequence of the original purchase analysis.
rubric: Trace the stopping events and all final prices.
Prove OPT by a matching feasible primal and dual certificate.
Derive the limiting ratio and distinguish retaining from pruning selected sets.
challenges.mistake: Using the maximum set size m as the approximation factor misses that every element here belongs to only two input sets.
challenges.followup: Choose deterministic tie-breaking and δ depending on m to quantify the difference between the actual ratio and two.

challenges.title: Two numerical errors can multiply in a proof certificate
challenges.skill: Repair approximate tightness and approximate dual feasibility without silently dropping either error.
challenges.connection: The exact example uses tight equalities and feasible dual budgets. Numerical implementations may supply two distinct approximate statements.
challenges.prompt: Let η≥0. Suppose a returned cover and nonnegative prices satisfy ∑e∈S yₑ≤(1+η)cS for every input set, while every purchased set satisfies cS≤(1+η)∑e∈S yₑ. Maximum element frequency is f. Derive a rigorous approximation guarantee from exactly these statements by rescaling the dual. Evaluate f=3,η=0.1, and explain why claiming only f(1+η) ignores one error. State what stronger certificate would remove one factor.
hints: First use approximate purchased-set tightness to charge the output to ∑y.
The given y is not dual feasible; y/(1+η) is.

probe.prompt: What factor follows for f=3 and η=0.1?
probe.feedback: Approximate tightness gives cost≤(1+η)f∑y. Rescaling y by 1+η makes a feasible dual, so ∑y≤(1+η)OPT. Together the factor is f(1+η)²=3.63.

solution: Sum purchased-set inequalities to get cost≤(1+η)∑ₑfselected(e)yₑ≤(1+η)f∑ₑyₑ.
Define zₑ=yₑ/(1+η). Every set satisfies ∑e∈S zₑ≤cS, so z is a feasible dual.
Weak duality gives ∑y=(1+η)∑z≤(1+η)OPT.
Combining yields cost≤f(1+η)²OPT, equal to 3.63 in the numerical case.
Exact dual feasibility would remove the rescaling factor. Exact purchased-set tightness would instead remove the first factor. Neither follows from the two approximate assumptions as stated.
rubric: Use both approximate statements in their correct inequality directions.
Construct a feasible rescaled dual and apply weak duality.
Identify the independent source of each multiplicative error.
challenges.mistake: Calling an almost-feasible price vector a lower bound without rescaling makes the final comparison with OPT invalid.
challenges.followup: If feasibility error and tightness error are different η and τ, derive the factor and specify which error should be controlled most tightly in a numerical certificate.

proof.goal: Grow feasible cut prices and prune a tight tree to a path whose cost equals the dual lower bound.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §7.3. Nonnegative edge costs and reachable t are assumed. The exactness proof uses connectedness inside the constructed tree, not merely inside the input graph.

frames.title: Grow the reached component to tightness
frames.question: Which edges can become tight at the first two growth events?

diagram.note: The first cut is {s}; after buying s–a the reached cut becomes {s,a}.

frames.claim: Stop each price increase before any edge’s accumulated cut charge exceeds its cost.
frames.explanation: The first event is y({s})=2. Then s–b has residual slack one and a–b has slack one, so the second growth interval ends in a tie. A consistent choice attaches b without creating a cycle.
frames.carry: Dual feasibility survives events; bought edges connect the reached tree.

frames.title: Keep the prices attached to their actual cuts
frames.question: If the tie chooses s–b, what is the final dual certificate?

diagram.note: The target enters when b–t becomes tight; the dual objective is five.

frames.claim: All edges of the bought tree are tight for the final cut-price vector.
frames.explanation: The path edges have charges 2+1=3 on s–b and 2 on b–t. The branch s–a has charge two. Other input edge budgets remain feasible; tightness alone does not yet say which edges are needed.
frames.carry: The whole bought tree has cost seven, while the useful dual sum is five.

frames.title: Remove the branch that serves no s–t connection
frames.question: Why can a tight branch be deleted without weakening feasibility?

diagram.note: The unique tree path is s–b–t. Tightness does not make the a-branch necessary.

frames.claim: Pruning leaves a feasible path of cost five.
frames.explanation: Every reached set used for a positive cut is connected inside the bought tree and contains s. Its intersection with the unique s–t path is therefore an initial segment: leaving and later reentering would create a second tree route.
frames.carry: The pruned path crosses each positive-price cut exactly once.

frames.title: Match the two objective values
frames.question: Which equality turns an approximation argument into exact optimality?

diagram.note: The same feasible dual and feasible path squeeze OPT to one value.

frames.claim: cost(P)=∑SyS=OPT.
frames.explanation: Without pruning, a positive cut can have extra branch crossings and its price may be charged more than once. Exactness comes from the structural path property, not from every purchased edge merely being tight.
frames.carry: A path and equal-valued dual lower bound are an inspectable optimality certificate.

challenges.title: Resolve a tie and certify both the branches and the path
challenges.skill: Trace residual cut slack and compare feasible primal and dual objectives.
challenges.connection: The example uses unit-cost branches. Here unequal costs and simultaneous tight edges require checking all dual budgets.
challenges.prompt: Use edges s–a=2, s–b=3, a–b=1, a–t=5, b–t=2. Grow reached cuts from s and, when s–b and a–b tie, choose s–b to attach b. Record every positive cut and its price, verify every input edge budget, list all bought edges, and prune to an s–t path. Show that retaining every bought edge would fail the equality certificate even though the path found is optimal.
hints: After y({s})=2, the next cut is {s,a}, and both candidate attachments have slack one.
The edge a–t sees the second and third cuts but not the first.

probe.prompt: Which final price vector, listed for {s}, {s,a}, {s,a,b}, matches the growth and certifies the optimal path?
options: (2,3,2), with value seven matching the entire tight tree.
(2,1,4), because a–t has cost five.
(2,0,2), which is feasible and therefore makes every bought edge tight.
(2,1,2), with value five matching s–b–t after deleting s–a.
feedback: The edge s–b would receive charge five, exceeding its cost three, so this is not dual feasible.
The edge b–t would receive charge four, exceeding its cost two.
This is feasible but s–b has charge two rather than cost three; it neither records the actual second event nor matches the chosen path.
Correct. The five edge charges are 2,3,1,3,2, respectively, all within costs; the pruned path costs 3+2=5.

solution: Grow {s} by two and buy s–a. Both s–b and a–b then have one remaining unit of slack for the cut {s,a}.
Grow {s,a} by one and choose s–b. The reached set is {s,a,b}.
Grow this last cut by two until b–t is tight. Prices are (2,1,2).
Edge charges for s–a,s–b,a–b,a–t,b–t are 2,3,1,3,2; all satisfy costs 2,3,1,5,2.
The bought tree costs 2+3+2=7. Delete branch s–a to obtain s–b–t of cost five.
The path equals the dual objective five, so weak duality proves OPT=5. Tightness of an unnecessary branch did not justify charging it once to that same dual total.
rubric: Trace all growth intervals and verify every edge constraint.
Respect the stated tie choice and prune the actual resulting tree.
Prove exactness by equal feasible objective values, not a visual shortest-path guess.
challenges.mistake: A feasible dual price vector need not be the vector generated by a proposed growth trace; both the trace and its final certificate must be checked.
challenges.followup: Choose a–b instead at the tie and derive the different bought tree and equal-cost optimal path.

challenges.title: Connected in the input is not connected in the bought tree
challenges.skill: Identify the exact structural invariant required for a single-crossing argument.
challenges.connection: The proof prunes a tree whose grown sets are connected in that tree. Replacing that invariant by input-graph connectedness sounds similar but is weaker.
challenges.prompt: Take the unit-cost path s–a–b–t and add an edge s–b of cost ten. Let S={s,b}, which is connected in the input by the expensive chord, and assign its cut price yS=1 with all other cut prices zero. Verify dual feasibility and tightness of the three unit path edges. Count the crossings of S by that path and compare path cost with dual value. Explain why this is not a counterexample to the source algorithm and formulate the correct connectedness invariant.
hints: The chord lies inside S, so it receives no cut charge.
The unique path in the bought unit-edge tree connects s to b through a, which is outside S.

probe.prompt: What exactly fails in the proposed single-crossing argument?
options: Dual feasibility fails because the expensive chord must receive cut price one.
S is connected in the input but not in the bought tree; the path crosses it three times, so its one price is charged three times.
The path is infeasible because s and b belong to the same cut side.
Every connected input cut must be grown by the source algorithm, so the source theorem is false.
feedback: The chord has both endpoints in S and receives zero charge; the dual is feasible.
Correct. All three unit edges cross S and are tight. Input connectedness does not make the intersection with the bought tree a connected subtree.
A path may enter and leave a set several times and remain a perfectly feasible s–t route.
The source grows its actual reached component, a much stronger and algorithm-dependent condition.

solution: The three unit path edges each cross S once and receive total charge one; the internal chord receives zero. Thus the dual is feasible and all path edges are tight.
The path leaves S at s–a, reenters at a–b, and leaves again at b–t: three crossings. Its cost is three while the dual objective is one.
The input-induced S is connected by the cost-ten chord, but S is disconnected inside the bought unit-edge path tree.
Therefore “connected in the input” does not imply a path crosses once.

The source invariant is that each grown reached set is connected in the constructed tree and contains s. The tree’s unique path cannot leave that connected subtree and return without creating a second tree route.
rubric: Check the complete dual certificate and all three crossings.
Distinguish input connectedness from bought-tree connectedness.
State the actual invariant and explain why the constructed example does not arise from that growth trace.
challenges.mistake: Two statements using the word “connected” are not interchangeable when they refer to different edge sets.
challenges.followup: Add a second expensive chord making the complement connected too. Does that repair the single-crossing claim? Give a proof or a counterexample.

proof.goal: Use uniform moat growth, safe pruning, and an aggregate contracted-forest degree bound to obtain factor two.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §7.4. Demand-pair feasibility and the source reverse-deletion/forest invariant are assumed precisely. The degree bound is aggregate; no pointwise degree-at-most-two claim is made.

frames.title: Grow all active cuts at the same rate
frames.question: Why can one edge’s slack decrease twice as fast as one moat price?

diagram.note: An edge is charged by every active component cut it crosses.

frames.claim: Uniform growth stops at the first zero-slack edge event.
frames.explanation: Activity means some required pair is still separated by the component. Uniform time does not mean every edge sees one growing cut; it may see two, which determines the next event.
frames.carry: The final tight-edge cost can be decomposed into contributions of common growth intervals.

frames.title: Prune before using the degree lemma
frames.question: Why is a large degree at an active component not a contradiction?

diagram.note: The active-degree sum is eight across five active components, despite the center’s degree four.

frames.claim: Only a sum of active degrees is bounded by twice the number of active components.
frames.explanation: Pruning deletes edges unnecessary for required pair connections. After contracting the current components in the final pruned forest, a nonisolated inactive component cannot be a useless leaf.
frames.carry: Inactive nonisolated vertices supply degree at least two in the contracted forest.

frames.title: Subtract the inactive degree budget
frames.question: How does the full forest identity leave a bound on active vertices?

diagram.note: Remove isolated inactive components before counting; active isolated vertices cause no harm.

frames.claim: ∑active deg≤2·number(active).
frames.explanation: The full forest has no cycles, so each of its q components has one fewer edge than vertices. The pruning invariant makes inactive degrees large enough to subtract them rather than pay for them.
frames.carry: Every common growth interval increases primal charge at most twice as fast as dual value.

frames.title: Integrate the interval-wise charge
frames.question: Why does the sum bound suffice despite changing components over time?

diagram.note: The set of active components changes only at events; the bound is valid within every interval.

frames.claim: The feasible pruned forest is a two-approximation.
frames.explanation: Uniform growth lets every active incidence receive the same dτ factor. Feasible dual prices supply the lower bound, and safe pruning supplies both connectivity and the needed degree invariant.
frames.carry: The theorem combines algorithm timing, structural pruning, and charging.

challenges.title: Compute the stronger forest charge with inactive components
challenges.skill: Reconstruct the aggregate degree lemma and expose its pruning hypothesis.
challenges.connection: The star example has no inactive vertices. Here inactive contracted components must be subtracted explicitly.
challenges.prompt: At a growth interval the pruned contracted forest consists of exactly eight vertices: five active and three inactive, with two connected components. Every inactive vertex is nonisolated and has degree at least two. Derive the strongest active-degree upper bound from these facts, and construct a forest realizing it. Then remove the inactive-degree condition and build a family showing why no bound by twice the number of active vertices follows from acyclicity alone.
hints: The forest has 5+3−2 edges.
For the sharp example, use two paths and place each inactive vertex internally.

probe.prompt: What is the strongest active-degree upper bound supplied by these data?
probe.feedback: The total degree is 2(8−2)=12. The three inactive vertices consume at least six, leaving active degree at most six. The coarser 2A bound would be ten, but the component count saves four.

solution: A forest on eight vertices with two components has six edges and total degree twelve.
Inactive degree is at least 2·3=6, so active degree is at most six.
Use one path A–I–A–I–A and another A–I–A. These have five active and three inactive vertices, two components, and active degree six, attaining the bound.
Without the inactive-degree condition, a star with one active center and r inactive leaves is a forest with active degree r, which exceeds 2A=2 for r>2.
Such inactive leaves would be useless in the required pruned invariant. This is exactly why acyclicity alone does not close the approximation proof.
rubric: Use both component count and inactive-degree subtraction.
Construct a realizing forest with exactly the stated counts.
Give an unbounded inactive-leaf family and relate it to pruning.
challenges.mistake: The forest identity bounds total degree by total vertices, not active degree by active vertices unless inactive degrees are accounted for.
challenges.followup: Derive 2A−2q for arbitrary counts and determine how active isolated components affect the formula.

challenges.title: A feasible dual can become too weak under nonuniform growth
challenges.skill: Identify where a common growth rate is essential to aggregate charging.
challenges.connection: The star example grows all five active prices together. Changing rates preserves feasibility but can destroy that particular factor-two certificate.
challenges.prompt: Consider a unit-cost star with q leaves and demands connecting the center to every leaf. Instead of growing all active singleton prices uniformly, grow only the center price until all q edges become tight. Compute the dual value, bought cost, and true optimum. Compare with uniform singleton growth. Explain why the failed bound against this dual does not itself prove the nonuniform algorithm outputs a bad approximation, and locate the equality in the interval analysis that required uniform rates.
hints: Center-only growth reaches price one.
With uniform growth, every edge sees two growing singleton cuts and becomes tight at time one half.

probe.prompt: For q=7, what dual objective does uniform singleton growth obtain before buying the star?
probe.feedback: There are eight active singleton cuts, each reaching price one half, so the dual objective is four. Center-only growth yields value one. The same optimal seven-edge star therefore has very different primal–dual charge ratios.

solution: Under center-only growth, y_center=1 makes every unit edge tight. The dual is feasible and has value one.
All q edges are required to connect every leaf, so the bought cost and OPT both equal q. The assertion cost≤2·this dual fails for q>2, although the output is optimal.
Uniform growth reaches time one half because every edge crosses the center and its leaf cut. The dual sum is (q+1)/2.
Then cost q≤2·(q+1)/2, matching the aggregate degree analysis.

With arbitrary rates r_C, incremental primal charge is ∑C r_C deg(C)dτ while dual increase is ∑C r_Cdτ. An unweighted degree-sum inequality does not control that weighted ratio when all rate is placed on a high-degree center.
The example refutes a reused certificate proof, not the approximation quality of the particular returned star.
rubric: Check dual feasibility and compute the actual optimum in both growth schedules.
Write the weighted-rate charging expression.
Separate a weak dual certificate from a genuinely poor primal output.
challenges.mistake: Weak duality gives a lower bound, but not every feasible lower bound is strong enough for a particular approximation proof.
challenges.followup: State a sufficient weighted degree inequality for nonuniform rates and explain why it is stronger than the source’s uniform forest lemma.

proof.goal: Transfer a fixed original capacity plan into a random dominating tree, charge merged loads by concavity, and include the map-back cost.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§8.5–8.6. The hierarchical expected-stretch theorem and controlled treatment of auxiliary tree vertices are explicit inputs. The cycle picture is illustrative, not a derivation of FRT.

frames.title: Fix the benchmark before drawing the tree
frames.question: Which object is allowed to depend on the sampled tree in the expectation comparison?

diagram.note: Linearity applies to fixed original edge charges; the tree optimum is bounded above by their induced feasible routing.

frames.claim: For each sampled tree, OPTtree is at most the cost induced by the fixed original optimum.
frames.explanation: Map each original edge’s capacity along its unique tree path. This preserves all demanded routes after concatenation. The benchmark’s original capacities are fixed before the tree is random.
frames.carry: We can now charge tree cost to deterministic original-edge coefficients.

frames.title: Merge loads with the correct cost direction
frames.question: Why is concavity useful when many original edges share one tree edge?

diagram.note: The diagram compares one merged capacity with the charges assigned before routes overlap.

frames.claim: Merged capacities cost no more than separately charging every original routed capacity.
frames.explanation: For a+b>0, apply concavity to a and b as mixtures of zero and a+b, then add. The normalized nonnegative concave cost ensures the merge cannot reverse this upper bound.
frames.carry: Separate charges expose original pairs, exactly the level of the expected-stretch theorem.

frames.title: Apply stretch pair by pair, then add
frames.question: Why is the maximum stretch of a sampled tree the wrong random variable?

diagram.note: Every sampled tree still has a worst adjacent pair of stretch five.

frames.claim: E[induced tree cost]≤α·original benchmark cost.
frames.explanation: Subadditivity bounds tree cost by ∑e f(c_e)dT(u_e,v_e). For each fixed original edge, expected distance is at most αdG(u_e,v_e). Sum these inequalities; no bound on a tree’s simultaneous maximum stretch is needed.
frames.carry: E[OPTtree]≤αOPToriginal for the fixed benchmark transfer.

frames.title: Include the map-back theorem explicitly
frames.question: What additional fact turns a cheap tree solution into an original-network solution?

diagram.note: κ records any auxiliary-vertex elimination or edge-realization loss; it cannot be silently set to one.

frames.claim: Expected stretch alone is only one part of the final approximation factor.
frames.explanation: Original-point tree edges can often be realized by shortest paths. Auxiliary vertices need the source’s separate structural treatment, since domination of terminal-pair distances is not by itself a whole-network cost mapping theorem.
frames.carry: Every transfer direction and constant must be justified.

challenges.title: Compute the gap between merged and separate charges
challenges.skill: Trace a fixed capacity plan through a random tree and identify the exact role of concavity.
challenges.connection: The example averages one six-cycle pair and separately checks sqrt-capacity subadditivity. This task puts routing overlap and distortion in the same calculation.
challenges.prompt: Take a unit four-cycle with one unit of installed capacity on every original edge and cost f(c)=√c per unit length. Delete a uniformly chosen cycle edge to form a tree, and route every original edge’s capacity along its tree path. Compute the capacity on each retained tree edge, the actual merged tree cost, and the separate-charge upper bound. Compare with expected stretch times original cost. Then replace f by c² and show exactly which claimed transfer inequality fails.
hints: The deleted edge’s unit capacity travels along all three retained edges, each of which already carries its own original unit.
Compute merged and unmerged costs separately before averaging.

probe.prompt: For sqrt cost, what is actual merged tree cost divided by original capacity-plan cost?
probe.feedback: Every retained edge carries two units, so merged tree cost is 3√2. Original cost is four. The ratio is 3√2/4≈1.06066, below the separate-charge stretch upper bound 6/4=1.5.

solution: Whichever edge is removed, its routed unit traverses all three retained edges. Each also carries its own original unit, giving capacity two everywhere.
Original cost is 4f(1)=4 and merged tree cost is 3f(2)=3√2.
Separate routed charges cost three for the removed edge plus one for each retained original edge, totaling six.
For a fixed adjacent pair, expected tree distance is (1/4)·3+(3/4)·1=3/2. Thus α times original cost is (3/2)·4=6, exactly the separate-charge expectation.
With f(c)=c², original cost remains four but merged tree cost becomes 3·4=12, exceeding the separate charge six. The subadditivity step fails because f(2)=4>2f(1).
rubric: Derive each tree-edge capacity from overlapping routed original edges.
Separate actual merged cost from the distortion-based upper charge.
Identify the failed inequality under convex cost, rather than blaming the embedding.
challenges.mistake: Multiplying every original cost by a pairwise stretch does not directly price merged capacities; concavity is the bridge that makes that upper bound valid.
challenges.followup: Repeat with f(c)=c^p for p∈(0,1] and find the exact merged/original ratio as a function of p.

challenges.title: Exact terminal distances do not give a free network map-back
challenges.skill: Distinguish pair-distance domination from realizability of a shared auxiliary junction.
challenges.connection: The cycle trees use only original vertices. General tree embeddings can introduce a junction that has no original-network location.
challenges.prompt: The original graph is a unit triangle on terminals a,b,c. Two unsplittable unit commodities go from a to b and from a to c, with concave capacity cost f(x)=min{x,1} times edge length. A comparison tree adds auxiliary center o and three edges of length 1/2. Verify that all terminal distances equal the original metric, compute the optimum tree network cost and optimum original network cost, and prove that no cost-nonincreasing map-back can exist for this solution. Explain what separate lemma is needed in a general embedding proof.
hints: The a–o edge carries two units; the other two star edges carry one each.
In the original graph every used edge carries a positive integer number of unit paths, so its capacity cost is one.

probe.prompt: What minimum multiplicative map-back loss is forced by this example?
probe.feedback: The auxiliary star costs three halves, while any original path-based network connecting all three terminals uses at least two unit edges and costs at least two. Thus any map-back for this tree solution loses at least 2/(3/2)=4/3, despite exact terminal distances.

solution: Each tree terminal distance is 1/2+1/2=1, exactly the unit-triangle metric, so domination and terminal distortion are perfect.
The tree’s unique demand routes use all three star edges; their loads are two, one, one. Since f is one on every positive integer load, cost is 3/2.

Any original unsplittable routing supports a connected subgraph containing all three terminals, hence at least two unit edges. Each used edge has positive integer load and cost one, so total cost is at least two.
Two direct edges a–b and a–c attain cost two. Therefore the original optimum is two and a cost-nonincreasing map-back from the 1.5-cost tree solution is impossible.
The obstacle is the new shared auxiliary junction, not pairwise metric distortion. The general proof needs a controlled auxiliary-vertex elimination or realization lemma and must include its factor.
rubric: Check all terminal-pair distances and all routed capacities.
Prove both network optima under the stated path-routing convention.
Explain why pairwise domination alone cannot justify whole-network cost preservation.
challenges.mistake: A junction shared by several routes has a cost effect that cannot be inferred from checking one pair of terminals at a time.
challenges.followup: Replace three terminals by k equidistant terminals and derive the analogous star-versus-original spanning-network ratio.

proof.goal: Lose only a small fraction of a fixed optimum by deleting one layer residue, then optimize the surviving bounded-width graph exactly.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §10.2. The bounded-outerplanarity/treewidth theorem for the specified planar layers and a valid tree decomposition are explicit inputs. Arbitrary layer definitions are not assumed equivalent.

frames.title: Partition the fixed optimum, not the algorithm’s output
frames.question: Why do the deletion losses add to exactly OPT?

diagram.note: Every vertex of one fixed optimum has exactly one layer residue.

frames.claim: Some residue loses at most OPT/k.
frames.explanation: The algorithm does not know the optimum or these counts. Their sum is OPT, so averaging proves a good shift exists among the k shifts the algorithm explicitly tries.
frames.carry: One reduced graph retains a large feasible subset of the original optimum.

frames.title: Keep the comparison direction when deleting
frames.question: Can the reduced optimum contain replacement vertices?

diagram.note: Deleting vertices cannot add an edge, but reduced optimization may improve on this restricted witness.

frames.claim: The reduced optimum is bounded below, not asserted equal to the surviving part of O.
frames.explanation: The entire point of exact optimization is that it may choose different vertices. Equality with the restricted original optimum is unnecessary and can be false.
frames.carry: The approximation proof needs no reconstruction of the unknown O.

frames.title: State the structural theorem before using DP
frames.question: Which step uses planarity rather than elementary averaging?

diagram.note: Averaging works in any graph; bounded width is what makes exact optimization efficient here.

frames.claim: For fixed k, independent-set bag-state DP solves each reduced component exactly.
frames.explanation: A valid decomposition covers every edge and keeps each vertex’s bags connected. These axioms enforce compatibility between child solutions and explain why a join counts the selected bag only once.
frames.carry: The reduced optimum can actually be computed without another objective loss.

frames.title: Try all shifts and choose the best feasible output
frames.question: Why need the algorithm not recognize the analytically good residue?

diagram.note: Pick k so 1/k≤ε; structural and DP costs may depend exponentially on k but polynomially on n for fixed ε.

frames.claim: The algorithm is a PTAS for planar maximum independent set.
frames.explanation: All outputs are independent sets in induced subgraphs and therefore in the original graph. Comparing their actual sizes selects a result at least as good as the unknown good shift.
frames.carry: Averaging, width, exact DP and shift selection remain separate obligations.

challenges.title: Extend the proof to weights and repair a join-node double count
challenges.skill: Transfer the layering benchmark to additive weights and justify a tree-decomposition recurrence.
challenges.connection: The example counts surviving optimum vertices. The same proof must be rebuilt carefully when vertices contribute different weights.
challenges.prompt: Extend the layer-deletion argument to nonnegative vertex weights. At a join bag containing adjacent vertices u,v with weights 7 and 11, consider state I={u}. The two child optima consistent with I have weights 31 and 29, each counting the selected bag. Derive the parent state value and prove the subtraction rule using the decomposition axioms, including why no edge joins two private child vertices. Explain why I={u,v} must be rejected before any arithmetic.
hints: The overlap consists exactly of the selected bag vertices, whose contribution is weight seven here.
If an edge joined private vertices from the two children, some bag would have to contain both despite their separated occurrence subtrees.

probe.prompt: What value should the join assign to state I={u}?
probe.feedback: The child values both include u’s weight seven, so the parent value is 31+29−7=53. Subtracting one vertex or the entire bag’s weight gives the wrong weighted objective.

solution: Partition the weight of a fixed optimal independent set by layer residue. The k losses sum to OPTweight, so one is at most OPTweight/k.
The surviving weighted optimum remains a feasible benchmark, and exact weighted bag DP preserves that lower bound.
At a join, the child vertex sets intersect in the bag; a vertex occurring in both child subtrees must occur along their connecting path of bags.
No graph edge can join private vertices of the two children: edge coverage would require a bag containing both, contradicting their separated occurrence subtrees.
Thus compatible independent child solutions combine, with the selected bag counted twice. Subtract w(I)=7, giving 31+29−7=53.
The state selecting both u and v is infeasible because their bag edge is present. An arithmetic recurrence cannot rescue a nonindependent state.
rubric: Reprove the weighted averaging benchmark using nonnegative additive weights.
Justify child overlap and absence of cross-private edges from decomposition axioms.
Apply the weighted subtraction and reject illegal bag states.
challenges.mistake: Replacing a vertex count by weights requires changing the overlap correction as well as the final comparison; subtracting |I| would overcount heavy bag vertices.
challenges.followup: Allow zero and negative weights. Which can be ignored safely in maximum independent set, and which parts of the averaging argument need explicit reformulation?

challenges.title: How accurate must each reduced-instance solver be?
challenges.skill: Compose a structural loss and an optimization loss without pretending either is exact.
challenges.connection: The example uses exact DP. A proposed faster routine approximates each reduced graph too.
challenges.prompt: Suppose the layer theorem is unchanged, but the reduced-graph solver returns an independent set of size at least (1−η) times its reduced optimum. Derive the whole-graph factor and the smallest integer k certifying a 0.9 approximation when η=0.04. Compare with the naïve k=10 choice and explain why independently budgeting ten percent loss for both steps is invalid. State what feasibility guarantee the reduced solver must retain.
hints: The second guarantee multiplies the surviving-optimum benchmark.
Solve (1−η)(1−1/k)≥1−ε for k before rounding to an integer.

probe.prompt: For η=0.04 and desired factor 0.9, what is the smallest certified k?
probe.feedback: The combined factor is 0.96(1−1/k). Requiring it at least 0.9 gives 1/k≤0.06/0.96=1/16, so k=16 is minimal. At k=10 the factor is only 0.864.

solution: The good shift retains a feasible benchmark of size at least (1−1/k)OPT.
Its reduced optimum is at least that benchmark; the approximate solver therefore returns at least (1−η)(1−1/k)OPT.
For target 1−ε, solve 1/k≤(ε−η)/(1−η), requiring η<ε for a finite meaningful k.
At ε=0.1 and η=0.04, the bound is k≥16. With k=10, 0.96·0.9=0.864, which does not meet the target.
The reduced solver must return an actual independent set, not just an approximate objective estimate. Otherwise the best-shift comparison need not produce a feasible original solution.
rubric: Derive the product factor through the surviving benchmark.
Solve and round the k inequality correctly, including η<ε.
Distinguish feasible approximate solutions from numerical objective estimates.
challenges.mistake: Separate relative guarantees compose multiplicatively through their benchmarks; assigning the same full error budget to both steps overspends the target.
challenges.followup: Given a cost model for the reduced solver as a function of k and η, formulate the tradeoff needed to choose them for minimum runtime at a fixed final ε.

proof.goal: Preserve global proof consistency and exact gadget values, then choose error parameters giving a strict target-objective gap.
proof.scope: Williamson–Shmoys §§16.1 and 16.3. PCP existence and tunable completeness/soundness predicates are deep source inputs. The walk proves the reduction accounting conditional on those promises.

frames.title: Enumerate tests while preserving one global proof
frames.question: Why does logarithmic randomness matter to the reduction size?

diagram.note: Local tests may overlap; every occurrence of one proof bit must refer to the same variable.

frames.claim: A polynomial-size constraint instance represents the acceptance rate of one global proof.
frames.explanation: Soundness maximizes over one proof string. Giving each test unrelated local variables would allow incompatible answers and change that maximization problem.
frames.carry: The verifier gap is meaningful only for globally consistent assignments.

frames.title: Keep satisfied and unsatisfied gadget baselines
frames.question: What does a failed source predicate still contribute to the target objective?

diagram.note: Auxiliary gadget choices must attain the stated values and not exceed them in either case.

frames.claim: The target objective is an affine function of source satisfaction, not a simple multiple.
frames.explanation: Dropping the unsatisfied baseline changes both completeness and soundness numerically. A gadget proof needs a lower-bound construction and an upper bound for every auxiliary assignment.
frames.carry: Translate the source promises into the target’s own units.

frames.title: Compare the approximation’s YES lower bound with the NO ceiling
frames.question: Which inequality makes the reduction decide a promise problem?

lines.reason: strict separation for max ratio ρ

diagram.note: The approximation output is feasible, so a NO input can never exceed its true optimum.

frames.claim: A ρ-approximation distinguishes the promises when ρc>s.
frames.explanation: On YES inputs the approximation guarantees at least ρ times the optimum lower bound. On NO inputs every feasible output is at most the soundness ceiling. Equality does not supply a separating threshold.
frames.carry: Approximation conventions and a strict numerical gap are both essential.

frames.title: Tune source errors before claiming the target threshold
frames.question: Why can a ratio above a limiting threshold fail on a coarse finite gap?

diagram.note: The limiting 7/8 threshold is approached only after choosing sufficiently small source error.

frames.claim: Select the PCP error and gadget parameters to enforce the desired strict gap.
frames.explanation: The deep PCP input allows a family with suitable constant errors. A single numerical illustration with larger errors does not prove every ratio above the limiting barrier is excluded.
frames.carry: Size, consistency, gadget values and parameter choice jointly support hardness.

challenges.title: How small must the source error actually be?
challenges.skill: Derive a strict finite hardness gap rather than appeal to its limiting ratio.
challenges.connection: The example’s 98-versus-51 promise fails to separate ratio 0.88. This task solves for the source accuracy needed to repair that argument.
challenges.prompt: Assume a source promise with M predicates, YES satisfiable fraction at least 1−ε and NO fraction at most 1/2+ε. A four-clause gadget yields value four for a satisfied predicate and three otherwise. For a maximization algorithm with ratio 22/25, derive the exact allowable ε range and explain why its endpoint is excluded. Then take M=10000 and ε=0.01 and compute the guaranteed YES output versus the NO ceiling, retaining all baseline terms.
hints: The target coefficients are 4−ε and 7/2+ε.
Require (22/25)(4−ε)>7/2+ε before substituting numerical errors.

probe.prompt: What is the supremum of allowable positive ε values for this strict-gap argument?
probe.feedback: The inequality becomes 88/25−(22/25)ε>7/2+ε, or 1/50>(47/25)ε. Thus ε<1/94. At the endpoint the lower and upper thresholds coincide, so the supremum is not itself allowed.

solution: The YES target value is at least [4(1−ε)+3ε]M=(4−ε)M.
The NO target value is at most [4(1/2+ε)+3(1/2−ε)]M=(7/2+ε)M.
A ratio 22/25 distinguishes only if (22/25)(4−ε)>7/2+ε, which simplifies to ε<1/94.
At ε=1/94 equality holds, so this worst-case promise accounting provides no separating threshold.
For M=10000 and ε=0.01, YES optimum is at least 39900, algorithm output at least 35112, and NO optimum at most 35100. The strict gap is twelve clauses.
These calculations assume the promised source family and correct gadget proof; they do not construct a PCP from scratch.
rubric: Include the unsatisfied-predicate baseline in both target coefficients.
Solve the rational strict inequality and handle its endpoint correctly.
Verify the finite integer thresholds and state the theorem inputs.
challenges.mistake: A ratio above the limiting 7/8 barrier is insufficient unless the actual completeness and soundness errors are small enough.
challenges.followup: Derive the allowable source error symbolically for every ρ>7/8, and explain its behavior as ρ approaches 7/8 from above.

challenges.title: Equivalent optima can have inequivalent approximation ratios
challenges.skill: Translate approximation conventions under an additive objective complement.
challenges.connection: The gadget example includes unavoidable baseline clauses. Such additive shifts are harmless for exact optimization but can dominate an approximation ratio.
challenges.prompt: A constraint instance has M clauses. Let S be the number satisfied and U=M−S the number unsatisfied. Show that a maximization guarantee S_alg≥ρS_opt yields only an additive-form bound for U_alg, and derive its relative minimization factor in terms of U_opt/M. Evaluate M=10000, U_opt=200 and ρ=0.88. Then give a family with U_opt=1 showing why no fixed minimization factor follows uniformly from the maximization guarantee alone. Distinguish this limitation of a guarantee from constructing an algorithm that always realizes the worst permitted value.
hints: Substitute S_opt=M−U_opt before taking complements.
The additive term (1−ρ)M does not shrink with U_opt.

probe.prompt: What relative upper factor on U follows for the numerical case?
probe.feedback: The guarantee permits U_alg≤M−0.88(M−200)=1376. Dividing by U_opt=200 gives 6.88, rather than 1/0.88. Additive complements do not preserve multiplicative approximation ratios.

solution: Substitution gives U_alg=M−S_alg≤M−ρ(M−U_opt)=(1−ρ)M+ρU_opt.
For U_opt>0 this is U_alg/U_opt≤ρ+(1−ρ)M/U_opt. The factor depends on the optimum’s scale relative to M.
At M=10000,U_opt=200,ρ=0.88, the permitted unsatisfied count is 1200+176=1376 and the factor is 6.88.

When U_opt=1 and M grows, the resulting factor bound is ρ+(1−ρ)M, which is unbounded. Such instances exist: take one contradictory unit-clause pair x,¬x and M−2 positive unit clauses on distinct fresh variables. Every number of additional failures from zero to M−2 is realizable by choosing the fresh bits.
For U_opt=0 a finite-factor minimization guarantee would require U_alg=0, whereas a fixed maximization ratio below one permits a positive unsatisfied count.
The argument describes what follows from the stated guarantee, not the actual behavior of every algorithm meeting it. A stronger algorithm could perform much better on this family.
rubric: Translate the complemented objective before dividing by U_opt.
Calculate the finite factor and exhibit an unbounded-scale family.
Handle U_opt=0 and distinguish a weak guarantee from a proven bad output.
challenges.mistake: Taking a reciprocal ratio is appropriate for neither an additive shift nor an objective complement; only positive multiplicative rescaling preserves the same approximation ratio directly.
challenges.followup: For a gadget objective aM+bS with a,b>0, derive the exact target ratio produced by a source ρ guarantee and analyze how a large baseline a dilutes the gap.

proof.goal: Track a false permanent claim through expansion and random compression until a directly checked scalar is false.
proof.scope: This develops LFKN's false-claim invariant and root-bound soundness. The full protocol's polynomial bookkeeping and integer-to-field representation are inputs from the assigned paper.

frames.title: Expansion cannot repair every false child
frames.question: If the checked row expansion equals a false parent value, why must at least one supplied minor value still be false?

diagram.note: These numerical values illustrate the invariant: a passing sum of correct children would give the correct parent.

frames.claim: A passing expansion of a false parent leaves at least one false minor claim.
frames.explanation: The verifier checks q=Σᵢ a₁ᵢqᵢ. If every supplied qᵢ equaled per(Bᵢ), the permanent expansion identity would force q=per(B), contradicting the false parent. The argument needs no random choice.
frames.carry: The current list still contains a lie, although the verifier need not know which entry is false.

frames.title: The endpoint witnesses a nonzero discrepancy
frames.question: Which fact rules out g−f being the zero polynomial before the verifier samples a?

diagram.note: The prover's g must satisfy the announced endpoints and be fixed before the fresh challenge.

frames.claim: If a compressed pair contains a false endpoint, h=g−f is nonzero and deg(h)≤r.
frames.explanation: Each permanent term is a product of r entries linear in t, so f has degree at most r. The checked prover polynomial has the same degree bound. A false announced endpoint makes g differ from f at 0 or 1, certifying nonzeroness without evaluating the permanent everywhere.
frames.carry: The next bad event is a root of one fixed, nonzero, low-degree polynomial.

frames.title: Charge only the first loss of every lie
frames.question: Why does adaptivity not prevent a root bound followed by a union bound?

lines.reason: g is fixed; a is fresh and uniform

diagram.note: Round-to-round dependence is allowed. A uniform bound after fixing the prior transcript is the needed statement.

frames.claim: The probability that the list first loses all false claims is at most the sum of the compression degree bounds divided by |F|.
frames.explanation: If another false entry remains outside the compressed pair, this compression cannot lose every lie. Otherwise the pair includes a false endpoint, so the conditional root bound applies. Summing over possible first-loss positions is valid even for an adaptive prover.
frames.carry: Except for the explicitly budgeted root events, at least one lie reaches the terminal list.

frames.title: End with an independently computable claim
frames.question: What makes the final check non-circular?

diagram.note: The verifier never needs an efficient algorithm for the original large permanent.

frames.claim: A surviving false scalar is rejected, so false acceptance requires an earlier charged loss event.
frames.explanation: At dimension one the permanent is the matrix entry itself. If the sole remaining claim is false, direct comparison detects it. This connects the probabilistic invariant to the final accept/reject decision rather than merely asserting that most intermediate polynomials were well behaved.
frames.carry: Soundness is a causal chain: expansion preserves a lie, compression rarely erases it, and the base case detects it.

challenges.title: An explicit cubic lie and an adaptive second compression
challenges.skill: Compute the actual collision set, then distinguish an exact local error from a conditional global bound.
challenges.connection: The scalar example has one explicit root. Here a genuine diagonal-matrix restriction has three collision points and is followed by an adaptive lower-dimensional check.
challenges.prompt: Over F₁₃ let C=I₃ and D=2I₃, so f(t)=per(C+t(D−C))=(1+t)³. A prover announces g(t)=4t³+6t²+5t. Compute the announced endpoint claims, factor g−f, and identify every challenge that erases this lie. After a noncolliding challenge, suppose the only remaining random compression has conditional discrepancy degree at most 2, whatever the preceding transcript. Prove a valid total false-accept upper bound using these facts alone; explain why an exact global probability is not determined.
hints: Reduce coefficients modulo thirteen before factoring. Try the candidate roots 2, 4 and 6.
A first-loss event can happen at the cubic compression or at the later degree-two compression. The latter guarantee is conditional, not an independence assertion.

probe.prompt: What total upper bound follows by adding the two stated degree budgets? Enter the fraction.
probe.feedback: g−f=3(t−2)(t−4)(t−6), giving exactly 3/13 at the first compression. The later conditional bound contributes at most 2/13, so 5/13 is a valid union bound. Neither multiplying exact probabilities nor claiming equality at 5/13 is justified by the supplied second-step bound.

solution: The true endpoints are f(0)=1 and f(1)=8. The announcement has g(0)=0 and g(1)=2 modulo thirteen, so both endpoint claims are false.
Subtracting gives 3t³+3t²+2t+12=3(t−2)(t−4)(t−6) in F₁₃. The three distinct roots are exactly 2,4,6.
The first compression loses this pair's discrepancy with probability 3/13. On every surviving false history, the later degree-two discrepancy loses its lie with probability at most 2/13.

A union bound gives total loss probability at most 5/13. A sharper 3/13+(10/13)(2/13)=59/169 is also justified when the later check is reached only after first-step survival; 5/13 is the requested additive degree-budget bound.
The second discrepancy and its number of roots are unspecified. These bounds do not identify an exact final acceptance probability.
rubric: Exhibit the modular factorization and all three roots, not only the degree bound.
Keep announced endpoints separate from true endpoint permanents.
Use a conditional soundness statement and label the final expression as an upper bound rather than an exact probability.
challenges.mistake: Treating 3/13 as the probability the lie survives reverses the event: collisions erase the discrepancy, whereas the other ten challenges preserve it.
challenges.followup: Derive the sharper sequential bound 59/169 and state which reachability assumption makes it available.

challenges.title: Move the random challenge before the polynomial
challenges.skill: Construct an adaptive cheating polynomial and identify the quantifier reversal that defeats the root argument.
challenges.connection: The example compares one fixed false line with a random point. This task changes only when the line may be selected.
challenges.prompt: Work over F₁₇ with the true scalar restriction f(t)=2+3t. The prover must keep the false endpoint claim g(0)=3 and must send a polynomial of degree at most one, but a defective verifier first reveals a uniform challenge a and only then accepts the polynomial. For every a≠0 construct gₐ with gₐ(0)=3 and gₐ(a)=f(a). Determine the best possible pass probability, including a=0. Explain precisely why the ordinary degree-one root bound cannot be applied to this strategy.
hints: Write gₐ(t)=3+bt and solve for b using the revealed nonzero a.
The statement for each fixed polynomial followed by a random point has a different quantifier order from choosing a polynomial after seeing that point.

probe.prompt: What is the defective verifier's exact maximum acceptance probability?
probe.feedback: For a≠0 choose gₐ(t)=3+(3−a⁻¹)t; it passes at a. At a=0 the fixed false endpoint cannot match f(0)=2. Thus exactly sixteen of seventeen challenges can pass. The discrepancy polynomial changes with a, so it is not one polynomial with sixteen roots.

solution: For nonzero a solve 3+ba=2+3a, obtaining b=3−a⁻¹ in F₁₇.
This legal degree-one polynomial retains gₐ(0)=3 and satisfies gₐ(a)=2+3a, so each nonzero challenge passes.
When a=0 the two required values are 3 and 2 at the same point, which is impossible. Hence the upper bound 16/17 is attained.
The valid root theorem says: fix nonzero h, then sample a, and Pr[h(a)=0]≤1/17. The defective protocol instead lets the prover choose hₐ after seeing a.
Commitment to the coefficients before fresh randomness restores the relevant order without making the prover computationally bounded.
rubric: Construct a valid polynomial for every nonzero a using its field inverse.
Handle zero separately and prove optimality, not only a lower bound.
State the fixed-polynomial versus adaptive-polynomial quantifier distinction explicitly.
challenges.mistake: A degree-one polynomial has at most one root, but this strategy uses a different degree-one polynomial for every challenge. Counting those roots as if they belonged to one polynomial is invalid.
challenges.followup: Require a second endpoint g(1)=d fixed before a. Determine how that extra constraint changes the possible degree-one adaptive strategy.

proof.goal: Explain why a polynomial number of adaptive counting checks yields an interactive simulation of a deterministic counting-oracle computation.
proof.scope: Permanent completeness, amplification, and Toda's containment are named external inputs. The visual proof establishes the adaptive error-accounting step rather than reproving those inputs.

frames.title: Correct replies determine one computation path
frames.question: Why is agreement with the true oracle needed only along the path actually followed?

diagram.note: The verifier need not know all possible oracle replies in advance. It checks the numerical values supplied on the current path.

frames.claim: If every accepted reply on the executed path is correct, the simulated machine makes the same decision as the true oracle machine.
frames.explanation: Induct on query positions. The initial state is fixed. A correct reply sends the simulated deterministic machine to the same next state and therefore to the same next query or halt. Adaptivity is handled by this induction, not removed from the machine.
frames.carry: A wrong final decision must be preceded by an accepted false reply.

frames.title: Freeze the history before applying soundness
frames.question: What must a local checker guarantee for a query selected using all prior replies?

diagram.note: A bound averaged over random queries would not justify the worst-case query now fixed by the transcript.

frames.claim: For every fixed reachable history, a false current numerical claim is accepted with conditional probability at most δᵢ.
frames.explanation: The current query may be unusual or adversarially induced. The permanent-verification soundness theorem must hold for each false instance and each cheating continuation, after the earlier transcript has been fixed. Fresh local randomness is then sampled.
frames.carry: Every possible first false accepted reply has an applicable conditional error budget.

frames.title: Sum positions rather than assume independence
frames.question: Why can a prover answer honestly for a long time without escaping the error bound?

lines.reason: condition on all earlier true replies
some false reply must have passed

diagram.note: This covers a late first lie as well as a lie at the first query. No product of independent error events is required.
