frames.claim: Choosing local budgets with sum at most ε bounds the complete simulation's soundness error by ε.
frames.explanation: Assign every false accepting transcript to its first accepted false answer. The positions form a union of events, each controlled after conditioning on its history. Amplification makes their sum small while using only polynomial resources for polynomial Q.
frames.carry: The interactive oracle simulation stays polynomial and has controlled overall error.

frames.title: Attach consequences to their actual inputs
frames.question: Which arrow is supplied by a separate counting theorem rather than by the preceding error calculation?

diagram.note: The arrows encode different theorems. Algebraic checking does not by itself prove Toda's theorem or a relativized counting-completeness statement.

frames.claim: Combining PH⊆P^#P with the verified counting-oracle simulation gives PH⊆IP.
frames.explanation: The containment on the left is Toda's theorem. The local reduction to permanent verification uses counting completeness. The work just done explains how to compose a polynomial number of those checks even when later queries depend on earlier replies.
frames.carry: Defend each consequence by naming its separate reduction, algebraic protocol, and error-composition ingredient.

challenges.title: An error budget with adaptive stopping
challenges.skill: Bound bad events using both conditional soundness and the probability of reaching a query position.
challenges.connection: The worked example budgets every possible query equally. Here independently sampled stopping coins make later positions less likely to be reached.
challenges.prompt: A checker makes at least one and at most four numerical checks. After each of the first three accepted checks it tosses a fresh fair continuation coin; on tails it stops, and on heads it may make the next query, chosen adaptively from the transcript. For every fixed history and false current claim the local acceptance probability is at most 1/16. Bound the probability that any false numerical claim is accepted by using a separate reach-probability bound for each position. Do not assume independent claim errors or use a distribution of honest queries.
hints: Reaching position i requires i−1 continuation coins to be heads, even if all prior acceptance tests are favorable.
Bound Pr[reach i and false pass at i] by Pr[reach i]/16, then sum four terms.

probe.prompt: What weighted union-bound value do these reach probabilities give?
probe.feedback: The reach probabilities are at most 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8. Multiplying their sum 15/8 by 1/16 gives 15/128. The unweighted value 4/16 is valid but misses the stated stopping structure; multiplying four errors would bound a different event.

solution: Let Rᵢ be the event that check i is reached. Independent fair continuation coins imply Pr[Rᵢ]≤2^{−(i−1)}; earlier rejections can only lower this probability.
Condition on any history in Rᵢ. If its current claim is false, local soundness bounds acceptance by 1/16; if it is true, this position contributes no false-pass event.
Averaging over those histories gives Pr[Rᵢ and false pass]≤2^{−(i−1)}/16.
Union-bound the four possible positions to obtain (1+1/2+1/4+1/8)/16=15/128.
The estimate allows arbitrary adaptive queries and correlated local errors. It is an upper bound, not a claim that this probability is attained.
rubric: Prove each reach bound from the independent continuation coins.
Condition on the reached transcript before applying local soundness.
Sum the probabilities of any false pass rather than multiplying probabilities of four false passes.
challenges.mistake: An expected query count measured only against the honest prover would not suffice. The reach bound here holds for every cheating strategy because the stopping coins remain fresh and independent.
challenges.followup: Replace the fair continuation coins by probability p and cap the number of checks at Q. Derive the geometric-series budget, including the case p=1.

challenges.title: Average-query soundness is the wrong quantifier
challenges.skill: Construct a complete checker with excellent average error but catastrophic error on one adaptively selected query.
challenges.connection: The example's local bound is stated after every possible history. This task tests what breaks when that uniform guarantee is replaced by an average.
challenges.prompt: Construct a checker for the constant counting function f(q)=0 on ten-bit queries with these properties: every true claim is accepted, a false claim passes with probability at most 1/1024 when q is uniform, yet a deterministic one-query computation can select a false claim that is accepted with probability one. Give the checker explicitly and explain why amplification of the average statement does not supply the conditional theorem used in the LFKN composition argument.
hints: Make one exceptional query q*=0¹⁰ accept the false value 1, and reject false values at every other query.
The average experiment samples q. The composition proof instead fixes the query produced by the preceding computation.

probe.prompt: Which local guarantee would repair the composition proof?
options: For a uniform q, every false claim has small acceptance probability on average over q.
For every fixed reachable history and current false claim, every prover continuation has small conditional acceptance probability.
For every cheating prover there exists a distribution of queries on which its average error is small.
For every current query, the honest prover's claimed value is accepted with high probability.
feedback: A machine may select the exceptional query deterministically, so averaging over an unrelated uniform query hides precisely the dangerous case.
This is the needed order of quantifiers: the history and false instance are fixed first, and the checker must withstand every cheating continuation using fresh coins.
An existentially convenient query distribution says nothing about the distribution induced by the computation actually being verified.
This states completeness only. It supplies no bound on acceptance of a false numerical answer.

solution: Define f(q)=0 for all ten-bit q. Accept every claim 0. Also accept claim 1 at q*=0¹⁰; reject every other false claim.
The checker is perfectly complete. For a uniform q, the worst false claim is accepted only at q*, which has probability 1/1024.
An outer machine that queries q* can be supplied the false answer 1 and sees acceptance with certainty.
Repeating this defective checker on that fixed query repeats acceptance with certainty. The randomness of a different average-query experiment is not available to amplify this instance.
The conditional worst-case guarantee is what permits the first-false-answer argument. Counting completeness and the genuine LFKN verifier provide that stronger type of guarantee.
rubric: Specify a checker that is complete on every true claim.
Compute the average bound and the selected-query error for the same checker.
Explain why repetition does not repair a fixed exceptional instance with error one.
challenges.mistake: Confusing average error over inputs with probability over fresh verifier coins changes the theorem being composed. A small average can conceal a deterministic fatal input.
challenges.followup: If only a δ fraction of query addresses are exceptional, state an additional restriction on the outer query distribution that would make an average-case argument applicable.

proof.goal: Preserve Boolean semantics while controlling degree, then check the resulting sequence of algebraic claims in reverse order.
proof.scope: The visual mechanism covers Boolean gate identities, Boolean-preserving degree reduction, and the committed-polynomial root argument. Shamir's complete operator schedule and PSPACE-completeness of QBF are inputs.

frames.title: Start with identities that are true on bits
frames.question: Why must the arithmetic operations be checked on Boolean inputs before any degree argument matters?

diagram.note: The product and sum-minus-product identities reproduce the Boolean truth tables. This is a semantic condition, not merely a degree bound.

frames.claim: On Boolean inputs, arithmetic conjunction and disjunction encode the corresponding Boolean gates.
frames.explanation: The four table rows establish the gate identities. Consequently, replacing each Boolean gate by its arithmetic expression preserves the formula's value on the Boolean cube. For a quantified variable, universal elimination multiplies its two endpoint values; existential elimination uses their arithmetic OR.
frames.carry: The polynomial computation has the intended Boolean meaning before off-cube challenges are introduced.

frames.title: Reduce degree by retaining endpoint information
frames.question: Does degree reduction preserve the whole formal polynomial, or only its Boolean endpoint values?

diagram.note: At zero and one the columns agree. Their different value at seven is allowed; the degree-reduced extension is a new polynomial.

frames.claim: RₓP=(1−x)P(0,…)+xP(1,…) is linear in x and agrees with P at x∈{0,1}.
frames.explanation: Substitution of x=0 or x=1 selects the appropriate endpoint exactly. Thus the operator preserves all remaining Boolean evaluations even when it changes values elsewhere in the field. The verifier must follow the specified sequence of polynomial identities rather than demand equality of these different extensions at arbitrary points.
frames.carry: One can replace a high-degree extension by a Boolean-equivalent low-degree extension.

frames.title: Repeat reduction before degree can accumulate
frames.question: Why is a single reduction at the start insufficient for a long quantifier elimination?

diagram.note: The bound is achieved by the full reduction schedule, not by assuming multiplication preserves multilinearity.

frames.claim: Frequent Boolean-preserving reductions prevent repeated elimination from causing exponential degree growth.
frames.explanation: Multiplication can double a surviving variable's degree. A variable made linear once can become quadratic at a later product and grow again at subsequent products. Applying the prescribed reductions to surviving variables restores low degree while retaining the Boolean values needed for the next elimination.
frames.carry: Every univariate restriction checked later has a known degree budget.

frames.title: Check the operator chain in reverse
frames.question: What order of events allows a nonzero discrepancy to be bounded by its number of roots?

diagram.note: The current polynomial is fixed by the transcript before the random restriction. Future prover messages may still adapt to earlier challenges.

frames.claim: A false committed restriction becomes accidentally consistent with probability at most its degree divided by the field size.
frames.explanation: After fixing the preceding transcript, a false restriction differs from the correct bounded-degree restriction by a nonzero polynomial. A fresh uniform point hits a root with the degree-over-field bound. Summing conditional first-error bounds across the polynomially many scheduled checks controls overall soundness.
frames.carry: Boolean semantics, degree control, and message order are separate necessary ingredients.

challenges.title: A false quantified formula has a nonzero off-cube value
challenges.skill: Separate Boolean semantics, formal polynomials, and randomly evaluated extensions.
challenges.connection: The example's P and RₓP agree at Boolean endpoints but differ off the cube. This task makes the distinction affect an actual quantified Boolean predicate.
challenges.prompt: Over F₁₇ let P(x,y)=x+y−2xy, the XOR predicate on Boolean inputs. First eliminate ∀y by forming U(x)=P(x,0)P(x,1). Compute U, its Boolean-preserving reduction RₓU, and their values at x=3. Evaluate the Boolean sentence ∃x∀y P(x,y). An examiner says that an honest proof must be rejected because U(3) differs from (RₓU)(3). Explain the exact false premise in that objection and which operator relation a correct verifier should check instead.
hints: The two y-endpoints are x and 1−x. The result is not a multilinear polynomial in x.
Rₓ uses U(0) and U(1), both of which are zero. Reducing degree does not claim equality away from those endpoints.

probe.prompt: What is U(3)−(RₓU)(3) as the standard residue 0,…,16?
probe.feedback: U(x)=x(1−x), while RₓU=0. At x=3, U(3)=−6≡11 modulo seventeen. The nonzero residue is compatible with the Boolean sentence being false: off-cube extension values are not direct truth values of the quantified formula.

solution: On bits P is XOR. For y=0 its restriction is x, and for y=1 its restriction is 1−x.
Universal elimination gives U(x)=x−x². Since U(0)=U(1)=0, its Boolean linear reduction is the zero polynomial.
At x=3, U(3)=−6=11 in F₁₇, while the reduced value is zero.
For each Boolean x one of the two y-values makes XOR false. Hence ∀y P(x,y) is false for both x, and the existentially quantified sentence is false.
The correct algebraic relation is RₓU=(1−x)U(0)+xU(1), not the formal identity U=RₓU. The protocol verifies the actual operator sequence with its corresponding endpoint identities.
rubric: Compute the unreduced and reduced polynomials, not only the two Boolean truth values.
Evaluate the quantified sentence by the order of its Boolean quantifiers.
Identify the invalid formal-identity assumption and write the valid reduction identity.
challenges.mistake: Nonzero values at a random non-Boolean point need not mean a Boolean formula is true. Those values serve as algebraic consistency claims inside the verifier's operator chain.
challenges.followup: Repeat with existential elimination of y. Derive its polynomial and explain why its reduced extension represents a different Boolean function.

challenges.title: When can reduction commute with universal elimination?
challenges.skill: Derive an exact condition for an operator interchange rather than relying on Boolean agreement.
challenges.connection: The worked reduction preserves endpoints. This challenge asks whether that fact licenses moving reductions past a multiplication step.
challenges.prompt: Fix all other parameters and work over a field F of size greater than two. Suppose the two y-restrictions of a polynomial already linear in x are A₀+B₀x and A₁+B₁x, where Aᵢ,Bᵢ are field elements. Compare Rₓ((A₀+B₀x)(A₁+B₁x)) with (Rₓ(A₀+B₀x))(Rₓ(A₁+B₁x)) as formal polynomials. Derive a necessary and sufficient condition for equality. Give an explicit counterexample using XOR and explain why both orders nevertheless agree at Boolean x.
hints: Expand the product. Its only possible quadratic coefficient is B₀B₁.
Reduction replaces the contribution of x² by that of x while preserving the values at zero and one.

probe.prompt: What condition is necessary and sufficient for the two formal polynomials to be identical?
options: B₀+B₁=0, because opposite slopes cancel before multiplication.
A₀A₁=0, because one endpoint product must vanish.
B₀B₁=0, because exactly that coefficient multiplies x²−x in the difference.
B₀=B₁, because equal slopes make the product multilinear.
feedback: Opposite slopes still produce the quadratic coefficient B₀B₁. For XOR the slopes are 1 and −1, and the product is not linear.
The constant coefficient does not determine whether a quadratic term remains. A₀=A₁=0 and nonzero slopes already give a counterexample.
The unreduced product minus its reduction is B₀B₁(x²−x). This is the zero formal polynomial exactly when B₀B₁=0.
Equal nonzero slopes produce a nonzero square term rather than remove it. Equality of slopes is not a multilinearity condition.

solution: Expanding the product gives A₀A₁+(A₀B₁+A₁B₀)x+B₀B₁x².
Its Boolean linear reduction is A₀A₁+(A₀B₁+A₁B₀+B₀B₁)x.
The difference is B₀B₁(x²−x), so formal equality holds exactly when B₀B₁=0.
For XOR the restrictions are x and 1−x, with B₀=1 and B₁=−1. Their product x−x² is nonzero formally, while its reduction is zero.
The difference vanishes at x=0 and x=1 regardless of the coefficients. Boolean equivalence alone does not justify swapping operators inside a protocol that checks off-cube claims.
rubric: Expand both formal polynomials and isolate the coefficient of x²−x.
Prove both necessity and sufficiency of the coefficient condition.
Give an explicit counterexample and distinguish formal equality from Boolean agreement.
challenges.mistake: Applying Rₓ separately to two already linear factors changes nothing, but their product can still be quadratic. Reduction is not a multiplicative homomorphism on formal polynomials.
challenges.followup: For three affine factors, characterize the two independent high-degree coefficients that must vanish for the product to equal its Boolean linear reduction.

proof.goal: Explain the IP⊆PSPACE evaluation recurrence while respecting indistinguishable verifier-private histories.
proof.scope: This is a supplied upper-bound argument accompanying the assigned interactive-proof papers, not a claim that LFKN contains this full private-information proof. Normalize and pad the protocol to a fixed polynomial message and termination schedule, with explicit verifier-message symbols, so each visible-message child partitions the compatible private tapes.

frames.title: Group tapes by what the prover can observe
frames.question: Why cannot the prover choose a different current answer for every private tape?

diagram.note: The optimization is over strategies defined on visible histories. A private random tape is not a question shown to the prover.

frames.claim: Every compatible tape in one visible-history class receives the same prover message.
frames.explanation: A legal deterministic prover's next message is a function of its input and visible interaction history. If two private verifier executions induce the same visible history, the prover cannot distinguish them. Optimizing separately inside each hidden-tape branch would give it information absent from the protocol.
frames.carry: The maximum over the next message belongs outside the sum over compatible private tapes.

frames.title: Count compatible tapes by replay
frames.question: How can an exponential class of private tapes be represented without an exponential list?

diagram.note: The normalized schedule includes halt and padding symbols, so histories and visible-message partitions are unambiguous.

frames.claim: Compatibility with a private tape can be checked using polynomial space by deterministic replay.
frames.explanation: Fix a candidate verifier tape and simulate its computation along the proposed transcript. Reject compatibility if any visible verifier message or termination symbol disagrees. A counter enumerating 2ᴿ tapes needs only R bits, and a count up to 2ᴿ needs R+1 bits.
frames.carry: Exact class sizes and acceptance numerators can be recomputed as needed with small memory.

frames.title: Optimize one message over an entire class
frames.question: Which recurrence would illegally give the prover its opponent's hidden random tape?

lines.reason: one legal message versus hidden-tape choices

diagram.note: The right-hand expression can be strictly larger. Weighted classes must be counted, not averaged as equally likely history labels.

frames.claim: The recurrence chooses a common prover reply first, then averages its consequences across compatible verifier tapes.
frames.explanation: At a verifier-message position, the normalized visible messages partition the compatible tapes. Each child receives its actual tape-count weight. At a prover-message position, enumerate possible polynomial-length messages and maximize over their correctly weighted continuation values. The order of the sum and maximum preserves the information constraint.
frames.carry: The recurrence evaluates the optimal legal interaction rather than a stronger clairvoyant game.

frames.title: Trade recomputation for memory
frames.question: Why does exponential branching not force exponential space?

diagram.note: Runtime may be exponential. PSPACE bounds simultaneously stored information rather than the number of recomputed branches.

frames.claim: Depth-first evaluation uses polynomial space even when it explores exponentially many tapes and messages.
frames.explanation: The protocol has polynomially many scheduled message positions and polynomial message lengths. Each frame stores a polynomial transcript, counters, and exact counts. There are only polynomially many frames. Enumerating alternatives sequentially and recomputing discarded branches keeps the total working storage polynomial.
frames.carry: The proof gives IP⊆PSPACE; it does not give an efficient polynomial-time strategy algorithm.

challenges.title: A visible signal with unequal posterior class sizes
challenges.skill: Compute the optimal legal response under partial information and identify the weighted max/sum order.
challenges.connection: The worked example hides the secret completely. This task reveals a signal whose two possible values have different probabilities.
challenges.prompt: Eight verifier tapes are equally likely. On six tapes the prover sees signal A, with secret counts (3,2,1) for secrets (0,1,2). On the other two tapes it sees signal B, both with secret 1. It then makes one guess and is accepted exactly when the guess equals the secret. Compute the optimal legal acceptance probability, compare it with ignoring the signal and with revealing the full secret, and derive the correct formula using class counts. Explain why averaging the two posterior maxima with weight one half is invalid.
hints: For A the best conditional success is 3/6. For B it is 2/2. The signals themselves are not equally likely.
Sum the largest secret count in each visible class and divide by eight.

probe.prompt: What is the optimal legal acceptance probability with the stated visible signal?
probe.feedback: Choose 0 after A and 1 after B. This wins on 3+2 of eight tapes, hence 5/8. The value 3/4 incorrectly averages the two signal labels equally. Ignoring the signal gives 4/8, while learning the entire secret would give one.

solution: Conditioned on A, the secret distribution is (1/2,1/3,1/6), so guessing zero is optimal and succeeds with probability 1/2.
Conditioned on B, the secret is one with certainty. The signal probabilities are 6/8 and 2/8.
The weighted optimum is (6/8)(1/2)+(2/8)(1)=5/8, equivalently (max{3,2,1}+max{0,2,0})/8.
Without the signal the total secret counts are (3,4,1), so the best fixed guess wins with probability 1/2. Full revelation gives probability one.
The illegal per-tape optimization also yields one, but it uses unavailable private information. Equal weighting of A and B yields 3/4 and corresponds to a different experiment.
rubric: Compute the two posterior distributions and weight them by actual signal probabilities.
Give an explicit optimal response rule and justify its optimality within each visible class.
Distinguish no information, partial information, and the illegal/private-tape-informed optimization.
challenges.mistake: A history label is not a random tape. Two visible histories can have unequal numbers of compatible tapes, so a simple average over labels changes the probability measure.
challenges.followup: For an arbitrary partition of R-bit tapes into visible classes, prove the analogous sum-of-class-maxima formula for a one-message guessing verifier.

challenges.title: Does a randomized prover evade the information restriction?
challenges.skill: Prove deterministic strategies suffice for a finite interaction without giving them access to verifier-private randomness.
challenges.connection: The example optimizes a deterministic guess. An examiner now permits an arbitrary private random tape and asks whether moving the maximum inside hidden branches becomes legal.
challenges.prompt: Consider a fixed input and a finite polynomially scheduled protocol. A prover may use private random coins independent of the verifier's coins and remember its entire local history. Prove that its acceptance probability is no larger than that of some deterministic visible-history strategy. Explain why this does not justify independently selecting the best prover random tape for each verifier-private tape. Then describe how this observation fits the polynomial-space recurrence without storing a full exponential strategy table.
hints: Fixing the prover's entire random tape fixes one coherent deterministic strategy on every possible visible history.
The acceptance probability of the randomized prover is an average of the acceptance probabilities of those coherent strategies, with the verifier's randomness still inside each term.

probe.prompt: Which operation is valid in the determinization argument?
options: For each verifier-private tape, select a different prover tape that wins on that hidden branch.
Resample a prover tape after learning which secret verifier state is most favorable.
Select one full prover tape independently of verifier coins; its fixed visible-history strategy is at least as successful as the average for some tape.
Replace every weighted compatible-tape class by its most favorable private verifier tape.
feedback: This chooses a strategy using information that the prover does not receive. It interchanges the legal maximum and the verifier's expectation.
The prover may sample private coins, but it cannot condition that sampling on an unrevealed verifier state.
Fixing a full prover tape gives a coherent legal deterministic strategy. The average over such tapes cannot exceed their maximum, while verifier coins remain independent.
The compatible class must be averaged with its actual weights. Choosing only its most favorable tape changes the verifier's distribution.

solution: Fix the prover's complete private random tape s. With input and visible history supplied, all its messages are now deterministic; call that legal strategy Pₛ.
Independence of prover and verifier coins gives Pr[accept]=Eₛ[Prᵣ[Vᵣ interacts with Pₛ and accepts]]. An average cannot exceed the largest term.
Thus some fixed tape s produces a deterministic visible-history strategy with at least the randomized prover's success.
The expression Eᵣ[maxₛ acceptance] permits s to depend on the hidden verifier tape r and need not equal maxₛ Eᵣ[acceptance]. The guessing example shows a strict gap.

The depth-first recurrence needs to optimize one reply per visible-history class and recursively recompute continuations. Determinization is an existence argument, not a requirement to store a full strategy table.
rubric: Fix an entire prover random tape, producing a coherent strategy across all histories.
Use independence and the average-versus-maximum argument in the correct order.
Explain why the PSPACE computation can enumerate local choices without retaining an exponential global table.
challenges.mistake: Randomization does not create access to another machine's secret coins. A mixture of legal strategies remains a legal information-limited strategy, not a mixture chosen separately after each hidden outcome.
challenges.followup: Extend the argument to multiple separated classical provers with shared randomness, and state why replacing shared randomness by entanglement requires a different analysis.

proof.goal: Explain how separated local answers can be constrained to describe one oracle, then a structured encoding of a valid computation.
proof.scope: The three-point affine test is a finite illustration of consistency, not BFL's robust soundness theorem. The actual local-to-global testing/decoding theorem and computation encoding are named inputs with their prescribed question distribution and parameters.

frames.title: A local strategy must ignore the other prover's question
frames.question: Which piece of context must be absent from the restriction prover's view for this comparison to constrain its whole answer?

diagram.note: Pre-agreed strategies and shared classical randomness are allowed; communication or leaking the hidden question changes the test.

frames.claim: For fixed local deterministic strategies, the point answers define a table f, and a restriction answer must be chosen without seeing the comparison point.
frames.explanation: A prover's answer may depend on its own received question, not on an unseen part of the verifier's choice. Fixing shared classical coins first reduces the analysis to such local deterministic strategies. The question design is what lets one reply be checked against several possible hidden comparisons.
frames.carry: The agreement event can be analyzed against one fixed point table rather than a separate table for each unseen context.

frames.title: An affine restriction cannot fit an arbitrary table
frames.question: Why can no single affine polynomial match all three listed values over F₅?

diagram.note: The first two points force an affine line, whose third value disagrees. The best agreement is two of the three addresses.

frames.claim: Over F₅, the table (0,1,0) on addresses 0,1,2 has maximum affine agreement 2/3 under uniform sampling.
frames.explanation: An affine polynomial is fixed by its values at two distinct points. If it matches the first two displayed points, it is x and fails at the third. No line fits all three; some line fits any selected pair. This is a small consistency obstruction, not a general robust testing proof.
frames.carry: Agreement tests have force only when the same restriction answer faces multiple possible comparison points.

frames.title: Consistency and algebraic structure are different obligations
frames.question: Why does agreement between two arbitrary tables not already provide the structured object needed by the computation checker?

diagram.note: Each transition has hypotheses. A convenient finite affine example does not supply BFL's full quantitative decoding theorem.

frames.claim: The soundness proof needs a robust local-to-global statement for the verifier's actual test distribution.
frames.explanation: Noncommunication alone does not force arbitrary local tables to be low degree. BFL's testing and decoding machinery connects high test success to a globally meaningful algebraic object. Its field, encoding, error parameters, and sampled questions must match the verifier that invokes it.
frames.carry: A decoded structured oracle is available only after the relevant local-to-global theorem has been applied.

frames.title: A structured oracle still has to encode a true computation
frames.question: Which remaining check distinguishes a valid encoding from a well-structured encoding of the wrong object?

lines.reason: arbitrary consistent answers may be false

diagram.note: The second row denotes combining two proof obligations, not adding numerical error terms.

frames.claim: Only after computation checks are checked does local consistency contribute to a sound proof of the claimed language statement.
frames.explanation: A genuine multilinear or low-degree table can still encode Boolean values that violate the intended witness relation. The verifier must check those constraints using decoded values, and charge the relevant consistency/decoding errors. Algebraic form is not itself truth.
frames.carry: Defend BFL as a chain from legal local strategies to a decoded object to a valid computation.

challenges.title: Weighted comparison points change the best cheating line
challenges.skill: Combine a polynomial intersection bound with the actual comparison distribution.
challenges.connection: The worked example uses three uniformly sampled addresses. Here the oracle table is quadratic, the restriction must be affine, and two addresses have twice the sampling weight.
challenges.prompt: Over F₇ consider addresses x=0,1,2,3,4,5 with point table f(x)=x². Their sampling weights are respectively (1,1,1,1,2,2)/8. A restriction prover must announce one affine g before learning x. Determine the maximum agreement probability, prove an upper bound for every affine polynomial, and exhibit a polynomial attaining it. State exactly why this finite calculation would not by itself prove BFL's global decoding theorem.
hints: The nonzero polynomial x²−g(x) has degree two, so at most two of the six addresses can agree.
The largest possible total weight of two addresses is carried by 4 and 5. Interpolate their table values.

probe.prompt: What is the exact maximum weighted agreement probability?
probe.feedback: Any affine g matches at most two points of x². The two largest address weights total 4/8, attained by g(x)=2x+1 at x=4,5. The uniform estimate 2/6 applies to a different distribution; a degree bound must be combined with actual sampling weights.

solution: Because the quadratic coefficient of x²−g is one, the discrepancy is nonzero and has at most two field roots.
Therefore agreement can occur at no more than two of the sampled addresses. Their total probability is at most the sum of the two largest weights, 2/8+2/8=1/2.
At x=4 and x=5 the squared values are 2 and 4. The line through them has slope two and intercept one, so g(x)=2x+1.
Its discrepancy x²−2x−1 has roots 4 and 5 in F₇, attaining agreement probability one half.
This proves only the stated local restriction bound. BFL also needs the legal-question model, robust global consistency, decoding, and computation checks.
rubric: Prove the at-most-two agreement claim from a nonzero formal quadratic.
Use weighted addresses rather than the uniform fraction of matching points.
Give and verify a maximizing affine polynomial and clearly delimit the finite result.
challenges.mistake: A root-count bound controls the number of agreeing points, not automatically their probability mass under a nonuniform distribution.
challenges.followup: For arbitrary positive address weights, derive the analogous sum-of-largest-two bound and determine when a line can attain it.

challenges.title: No communication, but the questions leak a context bit
challenges.skill: Construct local separated strategies that pass a defective consistency test without describing a context-independent oracle.
challenges.connection: The existing example hides the comparison address from the restriction prover. This new defect sends a shared context label to both provers, allowing the same address to be interpreted differently.
challenges.prompt: A verifier samples independent uniform c∈{0,1} and x∈F₇. It sends c to the restriction prover, which returns an affine g_c, and sends (c,x) to the point prover, which returns a bit a(c,x). It accepts when g_c(x)=a(c,x). Construct separated deterministic strategies that pass with probability one but for which no context-independent f:F₇→{0,1} agrees with a(c,x) on more than half of all pairs (c,x). Prove this last claim and identify the missing question-design property.
hints: Both provers can legally use the context they were actually sent, without communicating.
Try the constant restriction g_c(t)=c and the point reply a(c,x)=c. For each fixed address, the two contexts demand opposite values.

probe.prompt: For those strategies, what is the best possible agreement probability of a single context-independent bit-valued oracle f(x)?
probe.feedback: For each x, the two equally likely contexts return zero and one. Whichever bit f(x) chooses, it agrees in exactly one context. Thus agreement is exactly 1/2 even though the defective two-prover comparison accepts with probability one.

solution: Let the restriction prover send the constant polynomial g_c(t)=c. Let the point prover answer a(c,x)=c.
Each strategy uses only its own question. They are separated, deterministic, and always satisfy g_c(x)=a(c,x).
For any fixed x and bit f(x), one of c=0 and c=1 matches and the other does not. Since c is independent and fair, agreement is exactly one half at every address.
Averaging over x preserves this one-half bound for every single global f.

The defect is that the supposed point-oracle question contains the context whose influence the test was meant to rule out. Noncommunication does not erase information explicitly present in both local questions.
rubric: Give legal local strategies without an illicit communication channel.
Prove the one-half global-oracle agreement bound for every f.
Identify the leaked common context and distinguish this faulty test from BFL's actual consistency construction.
challenges.mistake: Saying separated provers must describe one table without analyzing their questions is too strong. A shared question component can legally index incompatible tables.
challenges.followup: Modify the verifier so the point prover receives only x, then derive its optimal acceptance probability against the two constant context restrictions.

proof.goal: Explain the separate roles of coordinate tests, robust proximity, self-correction, and verification of the decoded computation.
proof.scope: The robust BFL testing theorem is used with its own hypotheses and parameters, not reproved by the finite examples. The random-line interpolation below is a self-contained illustration of why proximity enables correction; it is not a replacement for BFL's full decoder.

frames.title: Exact multilinearity gives affine coordinate lines
frames.question: Why is a coordinate-line restriction affine, while an arbitrary line restriction may have higher degree?

diagram.note: Multilinear means degree at most one in each coordinate separately. It does not mean total degree one.

frames.claim: An exact multilinear function passes the prescribed coordinate-restriction identities.
frames.explanation: Fixing all coordinates but one leaves an affine polynomial in that remaining coordinate. Moving several coordinates together can combine their degrees; a d-variable multilinear polynomial has total degree at most d. This distinction determines the correct interpolation degree in a self-correction procedure.
frames.carry: Coordinate testing and arbitrary-line interpolation use different degree statements.

frames.title: High test success needs a robust global theorem
frames.question: What stronger statement is needed to move from a few passing restrictions to one useful decoded polynomial?

diagram.note: Exact passing examples do not establish a quantitative robust theorem. The actual BFL statement supplies that implication under its specified conditions.

frames.claim: The verifier can use proximity to a single global polynomial only after invoking the appropriate robust testing result.
frames.explanation: Passing some chosen lines is weaker than being close to one multilinear object. The source's local-to-global analysis supplies the required proximity statement. Altering the sampled line distribution or dropping a hypothesis can invalidate that invocation.
frames.carry: Assume a decoded P with a controlled fraction η of corrupted table positions, with the theorem's applicable parameters.

frames.title: Reconstruct one target from random restrictions
frames.question: Why can a union bound control corrupted interpolation queries even though the queried points are dependent?

lines.reason: r uniform; each nonzero tᵢ gives a uniform point

diagram.note: Use d+1 distinct nonzero tᵢ, so the field needs at least d+2 elements. If all answers are correct, interpolation returns q(0)=P(z).

frames.claim: Closeness allows a random-line interpolation to recover a target value with a controlled error budget.
frames.explanation: For fixed target z and a uniform direction r, each z+tᵢr with nonzero tᵢ is uniform on the grid. Thus each query has corruption probability at most η. When all d+1 distinct samples are uncorrupted, degree-d interpolation determines q and its value at zero. Dependence among samples does not obstruct the union bound.
frames.carry: A decoder's errors must be budgeted when its recovered values are used in further verification.

frames.title: Check the decoded object against the statement
frames.question: Why might an exact multilinear oracle still have to be rejected?

diagram.note: Structure, recoverability and truth are logically different properties.

frames.claim: A sound proof must use the decoded values to check the encoded computation, in addition to establishing multilinear structure.
frames.explanation: Even a perfectly consistent low-degree encoding can represent the wrong Boolean witness. The computation checks connect the decoded polynomial's designated values to a valid accepting computation. Robust testing and self-correction make those accesses meaningful; they do not themselves supply witness validity.
frames.carry: The full argument combines a proximity theorem, a correction guarantee, and semantic constraints, each with its own error contribution.

challenges.title: Exact failure probability of a correlated self-corrector
challenges.skill: Analyze interpolation errors using shared random directions rather than falsely independent sample points.
challenges.connection: The worked example counts bad coordinate lines. Here a target is reconstructed from three points on one random line, so the error events share the same direction.
challenges.prompt: Over F₇² let P(x,y)=x+y. Change only f(1,0) from 1 to 2. To recover P(0,0), choose a uniform direction r∈F₇², query f(r), f(2r), f(3r), interpolate the unique polynomial of degree at most two through those three t-values, and output its value at t=0. Find every direction that leads to a wrong output, compute the interpolation error in each case, and determine the exact failure probability. Compare it with the three-query union bound using η=1/49.
hints: A query is corrupted only when tᵢr=(1,0). The inverses of 1,2,3 modulo seven are 1,4,5.
The Lagrange interpolation coefficients at zero for samples t=1,2,3 are 3,−3,1 modulo seven.

probe.prompt: What is the exact failure probability of this decoder?
probe.feedback: The bad directions are (1,0), (4,0), and (5,0). Each corrupts exactly one sample by +1, producing nonzero output errors 3,4,1 respectively. All other directions return zero, so the exact failure is 3/49, attaining the stated union bound in this example.

solution: The polynomial P(tr)=t(rₓ+rᵧ) is actually linear, so three correct samples reconstruct it exactly as a polynomial of degree at most two.
The only corrupted address is a=(1,0). It is hit at t=1,2,3 precisely for r=a,4a,5a. These are three distinct directions among 49.
For the three sample positions, interpolation at zero uses coefficients 3,−3,1, which are 3,4,1 in F₇.
Each bad direction changes exactly one queried value by +1, so its corresponding nonzero coefficient is the output error. No cancellation can occur.
Thus failure probability is exactly 3/49. The queried positions are dependent, but their bad-direction sets are disjoint here, so the marginal union bound happens to be tight.
rubric: Identify all three bad directions using field inverses.
Compute the interpolation coefficients and show that every identified direction really gives a wrong value.
Separate the exact enumeration from the generally valid union bound and avoid an independence assumption.
challenges.mistake: The expression 1−(48/49)³ treats the three queried addresses as independent. They all depend on the same r and in this example their corruption events are disjoint.
challenges.followup: Move the unique corruption to the target (0,0). Compute the new exact failure probability and explain why the same marginal union bound is no longer tight.

challenges.title: A biased line tester accepts a far-from-multilinear table
challenges.skill: Prove distance from the global code and identify the test-distribution hypothesis a robust theorem needs.
challenges.connection: The example samples both coordinate directions uniformly. This examiner changes the sampling distribution while keeping an easy-to-test table.
challenges.prompt: Over F₅² let f(x,y)=x². A defective tester chooses a vertical line (fix x, vary y) with probability 9/10 and a horizontal line with probability 1/10, then accepts exactly when the complete restriction is affine. Compute its acceptance probability. Prove that f has distance exactly 3/5 from the set of multilinear polynomials a+bx+cy+dxy, where distance is the fraction of differing grid points. Explain why high success of this biased test cannot be substituted for the hypotheses of the standard prescribed tester.
hints: Every vertical restriction is constant. Every horizontal restriction is the same non-affine quadratic over five points.
For each fixed y, any multilinear polynomial is affine in x and can match x² at at most two x-values.

probe.prompt: What is the exact relative distance to the nearest multilinear polynomial?
probe.feedback: Each of the five horizontal rows can agree with an affine function at at most two of five positions, so agreement is at most 2/5. The multilinear polynomial P=x attains two matches per row, at x=0 and x=1. Therefore distance is exactly 3/5, despite acceptance 9/10 under the biased tester.

solution: A vertical restriction fixes x and therefore has constant value x², so it always passes.
A horizontal restriction equals x² on all five field points. No affine polynomial agrees with that quadratic everywhere, since their nonzero discrepancy has degree two, so it always fails.
The tester consequently accepts with probability 9/10.
For any multilinear P and every fixed y, P(·,y) is affine. The discrepancy x²−P(x,y) is a nonzero quadratic in x and has at most two roots, giving at most ten matches across 25 grid points.

The choice P(x,y)=x matches exactly x=0,1 in every row, attaining ten matches. Hence the distance is 15/25=3/5. A theorem for a different test distribution cannot be imported without a quantitative comparison.
rubric: Analyze both sampled directions and compute the biased test's acceptance.
Prove a distance lower bound for every multilinear P, not just for a proposed candidate.
Exhibit a matching candidate and identify the altered sampling distribution as the missing hypothesis.
challenges.mistake: A high acceptance rate has meaning only relative to the specified test. Heavily undersampling the direction containing all violations can make a far table look good.
challenges.followup: Give the acceptance probability as a function of the horizontal-line sampling probability α, and derive the distance/acceptance relationship for this particular table.

proof.goal: Distinguish the elementary exponential-time upper bound from the algebraic lower bound establishing classical MIP=NEXP.
proof.scope: The visual argument proves how to represent and evaluate classical local strategies. BFL's NEXP encoding, robust consistency theorem, and the stated circuit-complexity consequences are separate theorem inputs. Entangled provers are outside this model.

frames.title: A local strategy is a table on local histories
frames.question: Why does the strategy description remain exponential rather than requiring a joint answer for every tuple of hidden questions?

diagram.note: A complete classical strategy specifies answers for every possible local history. The tables cannot depend on another prover's unseen current question.

frames.claim: Polynomially long local histories and replies give an exponential-size description of each deterministic classical strategy.
frames.explanation: If a local history has at most p(n) bits, it has at most 2^{p(n)} possible indices. Each table entry has polynomial length. There are polynomially many scheduled rounds and a fixed or polynomially bounded number of provers, so the entire profile still has size 2^{poly(n)}.
frames.carry: A nondeterministic exponential-time machine can guess one coherent local strategy profile.

frames.title: Evaluate a guessed profile by enumerating verifier coins
frames.question: Why is guessing one table profile different from deterministically enumerating every profile?

diagram.note: The evaluator guesses a single strategy profile and loops over random tapes; it does not enumerate all possible strategy profiles.

frames.claim: The acceptance probability of a guessed profile can be computed exactly in exponential time.
frames.explanation: Enumerate every polynomial-length verifier random tape, simulate the fixed verifier and the guessed local strategies, and count accepting executions. The number of tapes, table size, and each simulation cost are all exponential or smaller. Their product remains exponential in a polynomial of the input length.
frames.carry: This proves classical MIP⊆NEXP without needing BFL's low-degree machinery.

frames.title: The reverse containment needs local-to-global algebra
frames.question: What is missing from the claim that short addresses alone let two provers certify an exponential witness?

diagram.note: A prover that chooses a different witness for each local check must be ruled out. That is the hard role of consistency and decoding.

frames.claim: NEXP⊆MIP requires the full algebraic encoding and consistency soundness construction.
frames.explanation: An exponential accepting computation cannot simply be sent to a polynomial-time verifier. Short-address queries help access it, but legal local answers must be forced to agree with one global witness satisfying all the computation checks. BFL supplies this difficult construction.
frames.carry: Combining the elementary upper bound with the imported lower-bound construction yields the equality.

frames.title: A circuit hypothesis can make the strategy publishable
frames.question: Why do arbitrary wrong circuits not need a separate correctness certificate in the MA simulation?

lines.left: any circuits on a false input

diagram.note: BFL's circuit consequence uses hypotheses about the complexity of the honest prover functions; it is not an unconditional circuit lower bound.

frames.claim: Under the stated small-circuit hypothesis for honest prover functions, a multiple-prover proof can yield an MA proof.
frames.explanation: Merlin supplies circuits before Arthur's fresh random coins. Honest circuits ensure completeness. On a false input, any supplied circuits still describe some legal local strategy, already covered by MIP soundness. Arthur therefore need not verify that each circuit computes the intended honest function.
frames.carry: Keep the classical strategy model and all circuit hypotheses attached when stating the theorem's consequences.

challenges.title: A separated-prover game with incompatible local equations
challenges.skill: Prove a classical strategy bound from local-table consistency, then repeat it conditionally.
challenges.connection: The worked example evaluates a supplied pair of tables. This task optimizes over every possible local table and exposes why a joint-question table would be an illegal stronger model.
challenges.prompt: A verifier samples independent fair bits x,y, sends x to P₁ and y to P₂, receives bits a(x),b(y), and accepts when a(x) XOR b(y)=xy. Prove that every separated classical strategy succeeds on at most three of four input pairs, and give a strategy attaining that bound. Next run three fresh sequential rounds, revealing the whole previous transcript before each round but keeping the current x hidden from P₂ and current y hidden from P₁. Prove the exact maximum probability that all three rounds pass. Explain why an evaluator allowed to use joint answers a(x,y),b(x,y) would compute the wrong game value.
hints: Write the four required equations and XOR all their left sides. Each local answer appears twice.
After any preceding transcript, fix a legal current strategy. The next two question bits are still fresh, so the same one-round bound applies.

probe.prompt: What is the exact maximum probability that all three sequential rounds pass?
probe.feedback: The four local equations cannot all hold, so the conditional one-round optimum is 3/4. Fresh sequential questions give an upper bound (3/4)³=27/64, attained by always answering zero. A joint-question strategy could set a=0,b=xy and pass with probability one, but P₂ does not receive x.

solution: The four acceptance requirements are a₀⊕b₀=0, a₀⊕b₁=0, a₁⊕b₀=0, and a₁⊕b₁=1.
XORing the four left sides gives zero because each answer appears twice; XORing the right sides gives one. At least one equation must fail.

The constant-zero strategy satisfies the first three equations and fails only at x=y=1, attaining success 3/4. Shared classical randomness cannot improve an average beyond the best deterministic strategy.

Conditioned on any full previous transcript, the next independent question pair has the same distribution and the local information restriction is unchanged. Therefore all-pass probability is at most (3/4)³.
The constant strategy attains 27/64 across the independent rounds. Allowing b to depend on x would remove the inconsistent local-table requirement and change the model.
rubric: Prove the four-equation contradiction for all local deterministic tables.
Justify the same bound after conditioning on previous rounds, rather than simply asserting independent errors.
Give an attaining strategy and identify the precise illegal dependence in the joint-question solution.
challenges.mistake: The verifier knows both questions, but neither prover does. Evaluating a strategy table indexed by both questions silently grants extra communication or information.
challenges.followup: Analyze why the sequential conditioning proof does not automatically prove the same product formula for a verifier sending all three question bits simultaneously.

challenges.title: Why Merlin need not certify the strategy circuits
challenges.skill: Derive an MA containment under explicit circuit hypotheses while maintaining the correct quantifier order.
challenges.connection: The example guesses explicit tables. This task compresses honest strategy descriptions into circuits and asks which obligations transfer to Arthur's one-message simulation.
challenges.prompt: Assume a classical multiple-prover protocol for a language L has polynomial communication and polynomial-time verification, and that for every true input its honest local prover functions have polynomial-size circuits, with one fixed polynomial size bound. Merlin sends a circuit for each local strategy before Arthur samples the verifier's coins. Prove completeness and soundness of the resulting MA protocol. Explain why Arthur need not check that the circuits are the honest ones, why the circuit-size hypothesis is used only on true inputs, and why a generic nondeterministic exponential witness cannot simply be assumed to have such circuits.
hints: On a false input, a wrong circuit still defines an allowed local answer function.
Completeness needs existence of compact honest strategies. Soundness already quantifies over all legal strategies, including those described by malicious circuits.

probe.prompt: Which statement is the soundness argument for Arthur's simulation?
options: Every supplied circuit must first be proved equal to the canonical honest-prover function.
The circuit-size hypothesis guarantees that Merlin never supplies a dishonest circuit.
Arthur can reveal his random tape before receiving the circuits because the underlying verifier is randomized.
Every bounded circuit tuple defines legal local strategies, so the original false-input soundness bound applies to every tuple.
feedback: Such an equivalence test is unnecessary and may be hard. The original soundness theorem already protects against arbitrary dishonest local functions.
A nonuniform existence hypothesis supplies good circuits on true inputs; it does not constrain Merlin to send them.
Merlin's circuits must be fixed before Arthur's fresh randomness. Otherwise they could be tailored to the sampled verifier tape.
This is exactly the needed universal statement on false inputs. The circuits need not compute the intended honest functions to be covered by soundness.

solution: Fix a polynomial bound on circuit sizes and reject descriptions exceeding it. Evaluating the permitted circuits during a polynomial-time verifier simulation is polynomial time.
On each true input, the hypothesis supplies circuits implementing the honest local strategy functions, so Merlin can send them and achieve the protocol's completeness probability.
On a false input, each circuit tuple describes one legal classical local strategy profile because each circuit sees only its prescribed local input/history.
Original soundness quantifies over every such profile, hence Arthur's acceptance probability is bounded for every Merlin message. No certificate of circuit correctness is needed.

The circuit description precedes Arthur's coins, as MA requires. General NEXP witnesses and their response functions need not have polynomial-size circuits; the stated compactness hypothesis cannot be dropped.
rubric: State a fixed polynomial description bound and Arthur's polynomial simulation cost.
Use the circuit hypothesis for completeness and the universal strategy quantifier for soundness.
Keep the Merlin-before-randomness order and avoid assuming compact circuits for arbitrary exponential witnesses.
challenges.mistake: Confusing 'there exists an honest compact strategy' with 'every compact strategy is honest' obscures why the original soundness theorem is essential.
challenges.followup: Apply this argument to the precise honest-prover complexity hypothesis in BFL's circuit corollary, and identify the additional hypothesis needed to conclude EXP=MA.

proof.goal: Explain how the graph-isomorphism simulator reproduces a malicious verifier's full view using fair hidden guesses and consistent rewinding.
proof.scope: This develops the valid-bit challenge case and the source's expected-time simulation mechanism. The paper's handling of verifier deviations, auxiliary information, and expected-time machines supplies the complete formal zero-knowledge theorem.

frames.title: The guessed source bit is hidden by graph symmetry
frames.question: Why can a verifier that inspects H still not infer which isomorphic source the simulator used?

diagram.note: Composing a uniform permutation with a fixed graph isomorphism preserves uniformity, including graphs with automorphisms.

frames.claim: On a true GI instance, the simulator's fair source guess remains uniform after conditioning on the relabeled graph H.
frames.explanation: A fixed isomorphism maps the permutations of G₀ bijectively to those of G₁ that produce corresponding labeled graphs. Therefore both source choices induce the same distribution on H, so H reveals no information about the independent fair guessed source bit.
frames.carry: For a fixed verifier tape and prior transcript, the verifier's challenge is a function of H while the hidden guess is still fair.

frames.title: A fair match does not bias which graph is kept
frames.question: Why is success probability one half for every possible H more useful than merely one half on average?

diagram.note: The verifier's challenge can depend on H. The hidden fair guess matches that fixed challenge with probability one half at each H.

frames.claim: Conditioning on a guessed challenge matching the verifier's challenge preserves H's distribution.
frames.explanation: Fix the verifier's tape and prior conversation. For each H, its valid challenge bit is fixed, and the independent fair guess equals it with probability one half. Rejection sampling therefore multiplies every H probability by the same factor before renormalization; no graph-dependent selection bias appears.
frames.carry: The simulator retains the correct distribution of first messages rather than only a plausible accepting transcript.

frames.title: The opened isomorphism must also have the right distribution
frames.question: Why is matching the graph distribution alone not enough to establish simulation of the verifier's view?

diagram.note: For a fixed H, the producing permutations form equal-size fibers related by isomorphism composition. The response distribution must be compared, not only its validity.

frames.claim: On a matching trial, the graph, challenge, and response have the same joint distribution as in the real GI protocol.
frames.explanation: The simulator knows the relabeling from its guessed source to H. Once the challenge matches, that is the needed response. Isomorphism composition gives a bijection between the relevant permutation fibers, so the response is distributed as the honest response, including any automorphism multiplicities.
frames.carry: The complete view, including correlations between messages and verifier coins, is the distribution being simulated.

frames.title: Rewind one fixed verifier, not new independent verifiers
frames.question: What must remain fixed when a guessed challenge fails?

lines.reason: fresh fair guess; identical H laws
geometric retry with fresh simulator coins

diagram.note: The verifier's random tape and accepted transcript prefix persist across retries. Only simulator trial randomness is refreshed.

frames.claim: Correctly restored rewinding gives expected polynomial-time simulation with the required full-view correlations.
frames.explanation: The simulator rolls back the verifier to its pre-round state after an unsuccessful guess and tries fresh simulator randomness against the same tape and prior transcript. Each trial succeeds with conditional probability one half. Summing expected polynomial costs over polynomially many rounds remains polynomial.
frames.carry: A proof of zero knowledge needs both a distributional argument and a runtime argument.

challenges.title: A biased guess creates a measurable selection bias
challenges.skill: Compute the accepted simulator distribution and its statistical distance from the real view.
challenges.connection: The worked example's hidden source guess is fair. Here the verifier's graph-dependent challenge interacts with a deliberately biased simulator guess.
challenges.prompt: Both input graphs are isomorphic three-vertex paths, and H has center 1,2,3 uniformly regardless of its source. The verifier challenges 1 exactly when the center is 2. A defective simulator guesses source 1 with probability 3/4 and source 0 with probability 1/4, retaining only trials whose guess matches the challenge. Compute the retention probability, the conditional center distribution among retained trials, and its total variation distance from the real center distribution. Explain why this defect changes the output law rather than merely increasing runtime.
hints: The successful mass at center 2 is (1/3)(3/4); at each other center it is (1/3)(1/4).
Normalize these three masses by their sum, then use half the sum of absolute differences from (1/3,1/3,1/3).

probe.prompt: What is the total variation distance between the retained center distribution and the real center distribution?
probe.feedback: Retention is 5/12. The accepted center probabilities are (1/5,3/5,1/5), whose total variation distance from uniform is 4/15. Merely observing a constant expected retry count would not establish zero knowledge; the retained distribution is wrong.

solution: The successful masses at centers 1,2,3 are 1/12,3/12,1/12, so a trial succeeds with probability 5/12.
Dividing by 5/12 gives the retained center distribution (1/5,3/5,1/5).
The real conversation has the uniform center law (1/3,1/3,1/3). The event 'center 2' has probability difference 3/5−1/3=4/15.
The full half-L₁ calculation gives the same value: half of (2/15+4/15+2/15) is 4/15.

With a fair hidden guess every H is retained with probability one half. With this biased guess, retention depends on H through the verifier's challenge, so rejection sampling distorts the view even though expected trials remain finite.
rubric: Compute the unnormalized success masses and normalize them correctly.
Compute total variation distance, not only an expected number of trials.
Identify graph-dependent retention as the mechanism of simulation failure.
challenges.mistake: A simulator that always outputs a valid accepting transcript need not output the correct transcript distribution. Correctness of individual responses does not remove selection bias.
challenges.followup: Replace 3/4 by an arbitrary p. Determine for which p the retained center law is uniform for this verifier, and explain the role of fairness against arbitrary graph-dependent challenges.

challenges.title: Identical round marginals can conceal a wrong verifier view
challenges.skill: Distinguish matching individual transcript marginals from reproducing one verifier's correlated full view.
challenges.connection: The example fixes the verifier's tape during a round. This task makes reuse of one random bit visible across two rounds.
challenges.prompt: A verifier samples one fair bit R at the beginning and uses challenge C₁=R in round one and C₂=R in round two, ignoring the graphs for this diagnostic. A defective simulation independently resamples a fair verifier bit for each round. Its challenge in each individual round has the correct marginal law. Compute the joint challenge distributions, an optimal distinguishing event, and the total variation distance. Then explain how a rewind-based simulator should maintain the verifier's tape and accepted prefix to preserve the real correlations.
hints: The real verifier produces only 00 and 11. The defective simulation also produces 01 and 10.
Use the event C₁≠C₂ to lower-bound the distance, then check the half-L₁ formula.

probe.prompt: What is the total variation distance between the two joint challenge distributions?
probe.feedback: The real distribution gives 00 and 11 probability 1/2 each. Independent resampling gives all four pairs probability 1/4. The event of unequal challenges separates them by 1/2, equal to the total variation distance.

solution: For the real verifier, (C₁,C₂)=(R,R), so probabilities on 00,01,10,11 are (1/2,0,0,1/2).
With independent resampling those probabilities are (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4), although each coordinate is still a fair bit.
The event C₁≠C₂ has probabilities zero and one half, giving distinguishing advantage one half.
Half the sum of the four absolute probability differences is also one half, proving this is the total variation distance.

A valid simulator restores the same verifier random tape and the same accepted conversation prefix on rewinds. Fresh simulator coins are allowed; replacing the verifier's already sampled tape changes the machine being simulated.
rubric: Write both joint distributions and confirm that their one-round marginals coincide.
Give a distinguishing event and compute its exact advantage.
Explain which state is restored on a retry and which randomness may be refreshed.
challenges.mistake: Matching every separate round's marginal distribution does not match their joint distribution. A malicious verifier can retain private state precisely to correlate its later behavior.
challenges.followup: Generalize to k challenges all using the same fair R and compare with k independently sampled challenge bits. Derive the exact total variation distance.

proof.goal: Prove the hidden-source soundness gap for graph nonisomorphism and explain why malicious-verifier simulation requires the source's certification/extraction mechanism.
proof.scope: The basic hidden-bit proof establishes soundness, not malicious-verifier zero knowledge. GMW's test-pair construction and isomorphism extraction are explicit inputs; the expected-cost case split below explains why its exceptional branch cannot simply be omitted.

frames.title: Nonisomorphic inputs have disjoint honest challenge classes
frames.question: Why can the honest unbounded prover identify the source of every honestly generated challenge on a true GNI instance?

diagram.note: The two challenge classes are disjoint only on true GNI instances. A graph belonging to both would give an isomorphism between the inputs.

frames.claim: On nonisomorphic inputs, a challenge is isomorphic to exactly one input, so an unbounded honest prover identifies its source.
frames.explanation: Each honest challenge is a relabeling of one selected input. If it were also isomorphic to the other input, composing those isomorphisms would make the inputs isomorphic, contrary to the true-instance premise. Completeness does not require an efficient general isomorphism algorithm for the prover.
frames.carry: The completeness direction uses disjoint isomorphism classes, not an easily computed invariant such as edge count.

frames.title: On false GNI instances the source bit is hidden
frames.question: Why does being isomorphic imply the two honest challenge distributions are identical, rather than merely overlapping?

rows: posterior of fair b after H
diagram.note: Uniform relabeling is material. Equal isomorphism classes alone do not make arbitrary biased relabeling distributions identical.

frames.claim: On isomorphic inputs, no prover can identify the honest verifier's fresh fair hidden source with probability greater than one half.
frames.explanation: A fixed isomorphism gives a bijection between the permutations producing each labeled challenge from the two inputs. Their uniform relabeling laws are equal, so observing H leaves the independent fair source bit unbiased. This remains true for an unbounded cheating prover.
frames.carry: The basic protocol's false-input gap is information-theoretic.

frames.title: Fresh hidden sources survive conditioning on the past
frames.question: Why may a prover adapt across rounds without invalidating the sequential product bound?

lines.reason: new fair hidden bit; identical challenge laws

diagram.note: The bound is against a legal adaptive prover. It is not obtained by assuming its answers or the resulting success events are independent.

frames.claim: Sequential repetition with fresh honest secrets gives false-accept probability at most 2⁻ᵏ.
frames.explanation: Condition on all previous interaction and any fixed prover state. On a false instance the new source bit is independent of that history, and its two challenge distributions are again identical. The one-half conditional bound holds at every round; the chain rule gives the stated product.
frames.carry: Soundness amplification is established, but a malicious verifier has not yet been simulated.

frames.title: Certification makes an arbitrary challenge extractable
frames.question: What extra relation must a simulator obtain when a malicious verifier's H is not an honestly generated challenge?

diagram.note: The source's test-pair construction supplies the two compatible maps. Merely repeating the bare hidden-bit protocol does not supply them.

frames.claim: The strengthened protocol enables the simulator to compose verified isomorphisms and identify a class label without solving arbitrary graph isomorphism from scratch in the usual branch.
frames.explanation: For a malicious challenge, the basic hidden-bit analysis supplies no efficient classification method. GMW adds test pairs and challenges whose suitably different successful openings reveal compatible relations. Composing H→T with T→G_b gives the source relation needed to simulate the prover's reply.
frames.carry: Both the existence of useful openings and the cost of finding them must be analyzed.

frames.title: Separate the many-good-pattern and rare exceptional cases
frames.question: Why is 'rewind until a different good pattern appears' incomplete when there is only one good pattern?

diagram.note: In the source N=2^{n²}; the one-good-pattern fallback's expected contribution is controlled by n!/N, not by pretending another good response exists.

frames.claim: The simulator's expected-time proof must include g=0, g=1, and g≥2 separately.
frames.explanation: When g≥2, entering the retry branch has probability g/N and finding a different good pattern takes expected N/(g−1) retries, giving 1+g/(g−1)≤3 verifier calls. When g=1, that search would never succeed; the paper uses an exhaustive fallback reached with probability 1/N and bounds its expected cost. When g=0 there is no retry branch.
frames.carry: Exact simulation and expected polynomial time require a complete case analysis, including rare branches.

challenges.title: Conditional rewinding can be expensive while average cost stays small
challenges.skill: Derive the source's expected-cost cancellation without overlooking the excluded initial pattern or the unique-good-pattern case.
challenges.connection: The example's rare fallback computes one probability times one cost. This task analyzes the complete conditional retry branch and shows which denominator matters.
challenges.prompt: In a finite certification model there are N=64 equally likely patterns, exactly g=5 of which are good. The simulator makes one initial verifier call. If the first pattern is bad it finishes. If it is good, it samples patterns independently until it finds a different good pattern, counting every retry as one more call. Compute the expected retry count conditional on entering this branch and the unconditional expected total calls. Generalize the formula to g≥2 and explain why substituting g=1 into the same operational algorithm is invalid. Relate the missing case to GMW's separate rare fallback.
hints: The initial good pattern must be excluded, so there are g−1 useful targets on each retry.
Multiply the conditional retry cost N/(g−1) by the probability g/N of entering that branch, then add the initial call.

probe.prompt: What is the unconditional expected total number of verifier calls for N=64,g=5?
probe.feedback: Each retry finds a different good pattern with probability 4/64, so the conditional expected retries are sixteen. The branch is entered with probability 5/64. Therefore total expected calls are 1+(5/64)16=9/4. Using 5/64 for retry success incorrectly allows the already-known initial pattern.

solution: Given a good first pattern I, exactly four of the 64 possible retry patterns are good and different from I.
The retry count is geometric with success probability 4/64, hence expectation sixteen, counting the successful retry.
The initial pattern is good with probability 5/64. Thus the unconditional total is 1+(5/64)16=9/4.
For general g≥2, the same argument gives 1+(g/N)(N/(g−1))=1+g/(g−1)≤3.

For g=1 the desired retry event has probability zero, so the retry loop does not terminate on its entered branch. The actual source handles this rare branch separately by an exhaustive search whose probability-weighted cost is controlled.
rubric: Exclude the initial good pattern when computing retry success.
Distinguish conditional retry cost from unconditional expected cost.
Analyze the unique-good-pattern failure instead of hiding it behind a finite-looking formula.
challenges.mistake: A small probability of entering a branch does not repair an infinite conditional runtime. The branch needs a terminating fallback, and its expectation must then be bounded.
challenges.followup: Suppose the unique-good-pattern branch has fallback cost T(N). Derive the exact condition on T(N)/N required for a polynomial expected contribution.

challenges.title: Biased relabelings leak the hidden source on isomorphic inputs
challenges.skill: Compute an optimal Bayesian source-identification strategy and locate the uniformity hypothesis in information-theoretic soundness.
challenges.connection: The worked GNI example uses equal uniform relabeling laws on false instances. This task preserves graph isomorphism while changing the labeling distribution.
challenges.prompt: Both inputs are three-vertex paths, so this is a false GNI instance. The hidden source bit b is fair. A defective verifier uses biased relabelings: when b=0 the center-label distribution is D₀=(1/2,1/4,1/4), and when b=1 it is D₁=(1/4,1/2,1/4). Conditional on the center, it randomizes the two endpoints uniformly, so no other feature conveys source information. Derive the optimal prover's guessing rule and its exact success probability. Explain why the isomorphism of the input graphs is insufficient for the usual one-half soundness claim under this altered verifier.
hints: For each observed center choose the more likely source. At center 3 the two likelihoods tie.
The optimum with fair priors is half the sum of max{D₀(h),D₁(h)} over possible observations.

probe.prompt: What is the optimal one-round source-identification probability?
probe.feedback: Guess zero at center 1, one at center 2, and either bit at center 3. The success probability is (1/2)(1/2+1/2+1/4)=5/8. The two source laws have total variation distance 1/4, so the same value is (1+1/4)/2.

solution: At center 1, source zero has likelihood 1/2 versus 1/4, so guess zero. At center 2 guess one. At center 3 either guess is optimal.
With fair priors, maximum success is 1/2 times the sum of the larger likelihood at each observation: (1/2)(1/2+1/2+1/4)=5/8.
The variation distance of D₀ and D₁ is half of (1/4+1/4+0)=1/4, agreeing with the binary hypothesis-testing formula.
Both source distributions are supported on the same isomorphism class. Identical support does not imply identical probability distributions.
The ordinary GNI soundness proof uses uniform relabeling to make the source laws equal, not only the graph-theoretic fact that the two inputs are isomorphic.
rubric: Give an optimal rule based on the center and justify ties.
Compute the exact success probability from the likelihoods.
Identify uniformity of the relabeling law, rather than class membership alone, as the missing hypothesis.
challenges.mistake: Relabeling preserves graph isomorphism, but an intentionally biased label distribution can carry a side channel. Information-theoretic hiding requires equality of distributions, not just equality of supports.
challenges.followup: Run k fresh rounds of this altered verifier. Prove the best all-pass probability is (5/8)ᵏ using conditional bounds, and find the least k making it at most 1/16.

proof.goal: Separate witness reduction, binding-based edge-test soundness, and hiding-based simulation in the NP zero-knowledge construction.
proof.scope: The witness-preserving reduction to graph three-coloring and the source's cryptographic hiding/hybrid theorem are inputs. The visual proof establishes the local soundness mechanism and explains which additional privacy argument is required; it does not manufacture a commitment primitive or prove its security assumption.

frames.title: Fix a coloring before choosing an edge
frames.question: Which property prevents the prover from preparing a different endpoint coloring after seeing the challenged edge?

diagram.note: The NP reduction supplies the graph and an honest coloring. Binding fixes the chosen color values before the challenge is known.

frames.claim: Under binding, each round's challenge tests one fixed committed assignment rather than a coloring tailored to that edge.
frames.explanation: The honest witness maps to a valid coloring through the reduction. A cheating prover may commit an invalid assignment, but binding prevents switching an endpoint's value after the sampled edge is revealed. Without that order and property, every individual edge can be colored correctly even in an uncolorable graph.
frames.carry: Soundness can now count violated edges of a fixed assignment.

frames.title: Every false assignment leaves a detectable edge
frames.question: Why does counting one bad edge suffice even if the prover changes its assignment after every completed round?

diagram.note: The K₄ row illustrates a tight one-edge defect. The general statement applies anew after every previous transcript, once the new assignment is fixed.

frames.claim: On an uncolorable graph with m edges, a uniform honest edge challenge rejects a fixed invalid assignment with probability at least 1/m.
frames.explanation: An assignment with all edges properly colored would contradict uncolorability. At least one edge is therefore monochromatic, and uniform sampling hits it with probability at least 1/m.
