After conditioning on previous rounds, any new binding assignment still has such an edge, so sequential repetition preserves the conditional gap.
frames.carry: The edge-test soundness bound uses binding and the honest verifier's challenge distribution.

frames.title: Random labels explain only the opened-edge symmetry
frames.question: Why does the uniform distribution of opened color pairs not yet prove that the commitment strings hide the whole witness?

diagram.note: A transparent encoding of colors would expose global equality relations even though every single opened valid edge has the same pair distribution.

frames.claim: Fresh color permutation makes each valid opened-edge label pair uniform, but does not by itself hide unopened committed values.
frames.explanation: There are six permutations of three color names, and each maps a fixed ordered distinct pair to a different ordered distinct pair. This local symmetry explains the endpoint values a simulator can prepare. It says nothing about whether the commitment strings reveal the other colors or their correlations.
frames.carry: Simulation requires a separate hiding argument for the unopened commitment vector.

frames.title: Hiding supports the simulator against adaptive edge selection
frames.question: Why cannot the simulator simply assume a malicious verifier chooses a uniformly random edge?

diagram.note: ≈c denotes computational indistinguishability under the source's cryptographic hypotheses, not equality or statistical closeness.

frames.claim: Hiding, hybrids, and the source's rewinding analysis handle the malicious verifier's commitment-dependent challenges.
frames.explanation: A malicious verifier can choose its edge as a function of all commitment strings. The simulator prepares openings for a guessed edge and uses hiding comparisons to show that its prepared versus dummy values do not give the verifier a useful distinguishing signal. The paper separately proves adequate simulation success, expected runtime, and indistinguishability of the joint view.
frames.carry: Binding proves a sound local test; hiding and the complete simulation argument prove the intended privacy statement.

challenges.title: A stronger soundness gap from all forced defects in K₅
challenges.skill: Optimize the number of violated constraints before applying conditional repetition.
challenges.connection: The worked example finds one monochromatic edge in K₄. This task asks for the best possible cheating assignment on K₅ rather than merely reusing the generic one-edge lower bound.
challenges.prompt: Assume ideal binding and commitments to one of exactly three color labels. The false instance is K₅, which has ten edges. Prove the minimum number of monochromatic edges in any three-color assignment, exhibit an assignment attaining it, and determine the exact maximum one-round pass probability under a uniform edge challenge. Then permit an adaptive cheating prover to choose a fresh committed assignment after each previous round and derive the exact maximum all-pass probability for five fresh sequential rounds.
hints: If the color-class sizes are n₁,n₂,n₃ with sum five, the bad-edge count is Σᵢ nᵢ(nᵢ−1)/2.
Moving one vertex from a class at least two larger than another decreases this sum, so a minimizing split is as balanced as possible.

probe.prompt: What is the exact maximum probability of passing all five rounds?
probe.feedback: The minimizing class sizes are 2,2,1, producing two monochromatic edges. The best one-round pass probability is 8/10=4/5. The conditional bound applies after every transcript, and the balanced assignment attains it in every fresh round, so the exact five-round maximum is (4/5)⁵=1024/3125.

solution: A color assignment partitions the five vertices into three color classes. Every pair inside a class is a monochromatic edge, giving the stated sum of binomial coefficients.
If nᵢ≥nⱼ+2, moving one vertex from class i to j changes the bad-edge count by −(nᵢ−nⱼ−1)<0. Thus an optimal split has sizes differing by at most one.
The split (2,2,1) is optimal and has 1+1+0=2 bad edges. It is attainable, so the maximum pass probability is 1−2/10=4/5.
After any prior transcript, a newly fixed binding assignment still has at least two bad edges. Each fresh uniform challenge therefore passes with conditional probability at most 4/5.
The chain rule gives the upper bound (4/5)⁵. Reusing a balanced assignment with fresh commitments and independent edge challenges attains it, establishing equality in this ideal-binding model.
rubric: Prove the minimum bad-edge count over all assignments, rather than analyzing one candidate only.
Show an attaining class split and compute the one-round gap.
Justify repetition conditionally for adaptive assignments and exhibit an attaining repeated strategy.
challenges.mistake: The generic 1/m rejection guarantee is valid but weaker here. Counting all forced violated constraints improves soundness, and optimality needs an argument over every assignment.
challenges.followup: For Kₙ with k allowed colors, derive the balanced-class minimum Σᵢ binom(nᵢ,2) and the resulting exact one-round cheating probability.

challenges.title: Opened edges look identical while unopened commitments leak a witness relation
challenges.skill: Analyze global witness correlations and distinguish binding from hiding in a quantitative privacy diagnostic.
challenges.connection: The example notes that an opened valid edge has six equally likely ordered color pairs. This task constructs two witnesses with identical such marginals but different relations between nonadjacent vertices.
challenges.prompt: Let u−w−v be a three-vertex path. Consider proper colorings W₀=(1,2,1) and W₁=(1,2,3) in vertex order (u,w,v), and apply a fresh uniform permutation of the three color names. Use a deliberately leaky idealized commitment model: binding holds, but independently at each vertex the commitment string publicly reveals its color with probability ε=1/4; otherwise it displays a perfectly opaque marker independent of the color. Analyze only this public commitment-string view, before any edge opening. Prove that every single-vertex color marginal and every valid edge's color-pair marginal is the same under W₀ and W₁, yet derive the exact total variation distance of the complete leaky public views. Explain what this diagnoses, without claiming a complexity lower bound for this easy path family.
hints: The only graph relation that differs is whether the two nonadjacent endpoint colors are equal. It can be observed when both endpoint colors leak.

On every leak pattern not containing both u and v, the revealed colors are either one uniform color or one uniformly ordered distinct pair. On patterns containing both endpoints, the two supports are disjoint.

probe.prompt: What is the exact total variation distance of the two public commitment-string views?
probe.feedback: Both endpoints leak with probability ε²=1/16. On that event their colors are always equal under W₀ and always different under W₁, so the conditional supports are disjoint. All other leak-pattern conditional laws coincide. Therefore the exact full-view distance is 1/16, despite identical one-vertex and valid-edge marginals.

solution: A uniform permutation sends each single color to a uniform label. It sends any ordered pair of distinct colors to a uniform ordered distinct pair. Thus individual vertices and the two path edges have identical respective marginals under the two witnesses.
Condition on the public set of vertices whose colors leak. If neither endpoint pair is jointly present, that set reveals at most one color or one path-edge pair, whose laws coincide.
If both u and v leak, the public view reveals an invariant relation: equality under W₀ and inequality under W₁. This remains true whether w also leaks, so the conditional supports are disjoint.
The event that both endpoints leak has probability (1/4)²=1/16, independent of the witness. Summing total variation over the disjoint public leak-pattern events gives exactly 1/16.

This shows why local color-label symmetry and binding do not establish hiding of the full commitment view. It is a diagnostic of this deliberately leaky model, not a claim that all imperfect commitments have this leakage form or that no simulator could exploit the easiness of the path family.
rubric: Prove the identical local marginals using the uniform color permutation.
Condition on leak patterns and identify precisely when the witness relation becomes observable.
Compute the full-view distance and delimit the diagnostic claim without overstating a general zero-knowledge impossibility.
challenges.mistake: Randomly renaming colors hides their names, not equality relations among several exposed vertices. A full-view simulation must control joint correlations, including information carried by unopened commitment strings.
challenges.followup: Replace ε by an arbitrary value in [0,1]. Derive the distance and design a distinguisher that attains it using only the equality relation on the two endpoints.

proof.goal: Prove the Four Functions inequality by a valid one-coordinate compression, including cross products and zero cases.
proof.scope: This walkthrough proves the finite Boolean-lattice induction. Transfer to arbitrary finite distributive lattices also uses their set representation.

frames.title: Keep both cross products
frames.question: After splitting on one coordinate, which two products have the same union and intersection?

diagram.note: The middle two rows need one common bound; separate slice induction misses them.

frames.claim: α₀β₁ ≤ C and α₁β₀ ≤ C, where C=γ₁δ₀.
frames.explanation: The cross pairs have union bit one and intersection bit zero. This shared upper bound is exactly what couples the two slices. The diagonal inequalities alone do not compare the product of the summed masses.
frames.carry: Both cross factors C−α₀β₁ and C−α₁β₀ are nonnegative.

frames.title: Expose the nonnegative remainder
frames.question: Assume C>0. What remains after replacing the diagonal output values by their smallest permitted values?

diagram.note: All divisions occur only after C>0 has been established.

frames.claim: (α₀+α₁)(β₀+β₁) ≤ (γ₀+γ₁)(δ₀+δ₁).
frames.explanation: Multiplying the two diagonal lower bounds and expanding leaves the displayed remainder. Both numerator factors are nonnegative by the cross hypotheses. If C=0 instead, both cross products vanish, and adding the two diagonal inequalities proves the same conclusion without division.
frames.carry: The two-point theorem is now available, including its degenerate case.

frames.title: Compress actual lifts, not separate slices
frames.question: For fixed A′,B′ on n−1 coordinates, how do their two lifts become one local inequality?

diagram.note: The two-point theorem handles all four combinations of lifts together.

frames.explanation: Define each barred function by adding its two coordinate slices. Apply the two-point result to the four original hypotheses for these fixed A′,B′. This proves that compression preserves the exact local hypothesis needed for induction.
frames.carry: The compressed functions satisfy the same theorem on one fewer coordinate.

frames.title: Recover every original mass once
frames.question: Why do the barred total masses equal the original total masses?

lines.reason: each set has one lower lift

diagram.note: Compression partitions the lattice into pairs; no multiplicity is discarded.

frames.claim: The desired inequality follows by induction from the two-point base.
frames.explanation: Every original subset occurs exactly once in a pair indexed by its restriction to the first n−1 coordinates. Substituting these four sum identities into the induction conclusion completes the proof.
frames.carry: Local join/meet control survives summation because cross terms were preserved.

challenges.title: Optimize the hidden slack
challenges.skill: Sharp two-point algebra and constrained optimization.
challenges.connection: The worked family example loses multiplicities; this task measures the algebraic slack that replaces injectivity.
challenges.prompt: On the two-point lattice take α=(1,3), β=(2,4), γ₁=4 and δ₀=2. Among all nonnegative γ₀,δ₁ satisfying every Four Functions hypothesis, find the minimum of (γ₀+γ₁)(δ₀+δ₁). Prove optimality, verify both cross constraints, and compute the gap from (Σα)(Σβ).
hints: The diagonal constraints give separate lower bounds on γ₀ and δ₁.
The objective is increasing in each variable; then check the cross products 4 and 6 against C=8.

probe.prompt: What is the minimum output product?
probe.feedback: The constraints force γ₀≥1 and δ₁≥3. Their minimum gives (1+4)(2+3)=25, while the input product is 4·6=24. The gap equals (8−4)(8−6)/8=1.

solution: The bit-zero diagonal gives γ₀·2≥1·2, hence γ₀≥1.
The bit-one diagonal gives 4δ₁≥3·4, hence δ₁≥3.
The cross products are 1·4=4 and 3·2=6, each at most γ₁δ₀=8. Thus the two diagonal minima are feasible simultaneously.
Monotonicity of the positive objective makes (1,3) optimal. The minimum is 25 and the strict slack over 24 is one.
rubric: Derive both diagonal lower bounds and check cross constraints.
Justify global optimality, not merely exhibit a feasible choice.
Identify the slack with the nonnegative-remainder factorization.
challenges.mistake: Setting the output product equal to the input product assumes sharpness that the fixed cross bound C=8 does not allow.
challenges.followup: With α,β fixed, characterize all positive C for which sharp diagonal choices yield equality.

challenges.title: When can compression be sharp?
challenges.skill: Equality analysis, including the interaction of diagonal and cross constraints.
challenges.connection: The example shows that the map to union/intersection is not injective; equality must therefore come from algebra, not bijection.
challenges.prompt: Assume all αᵢ,βᵢ,γ₁,δ₀ are positive and choose the diagonal output values sharply: γ₀δ₀=α₀β₀ and γ₁δ₁=α₁β₁. Let u=α₀β₁ and v=α₁β₀. Derive the exact output-minus-input expression in C=γ₁δ₀. Under the two cross constraints, characterize equality and show why choosing C=√(uv) is generally infeasible.
hints: Expand the product after solving the two sharp diagonal equations.
Feasibility is C≥max(u,v), not C≥√(uv).

probe.prompt: For u≠v and sharp diagonal constraints, when does equality hold?
options: Exactly when C=√(uv), since the two cross terms balance.
Exactly when C=min(u,v), since one remainder factor vanishes.
Exactly when C=max(u,v), where feasibility and one zero factor coincide.
For every C≥max(u,v), since both diagonal constraints are sharp.
feedback: The geometric mean is below the larger cross product when u≠v, violating that cross constraint.
The smaller cross product leaves the larger cross constraint unsatisfied.
The slack is (C−u)(C−v)/C. Feasibility forces C≥max(u,v), so equality occurs at that endpoint.
Sharp diagonal constraints leave the two cross factors; both are strictly positive if C>max(u,v).

solution: Substituting the sharp diagonal values yields slack C−u−v+uv/C=(C−u)(C−v)/C.
Both cross constraints force C≥max(u,v). This restriction is stronger than nonnegativity of the product alone.
If u≠v, the feasible endpoint C=max(u,v) makes one factor zero. Any larger C makes both factors positive.
The proposed value √(uv) lies strictly between u and v and therefore violates the larger cross constraint.
rubric: Derive the exact slack rather than cite an equality slogan.
Use both cross constraints to restrict the feasible domain.
Explain why the geometric-mean proposal fails.
challenges.mistake: The sign of a product does not by itself ensure each original cross inequality.
challenges.followup: Remove the sharp-diagonal assumption and determine which additional equalities are forced by equality of total masses.

proof.goal: Derive positive association from log-supermodularity by constructing the correct four functions.
proof.scope: Four Functions on a finite distributive lattice is the established input. The normalization requires Z=Σμ>0.

frames.title: Put the two observables on the input side
frames.question: Which choice of α and β makes their total masses the desired expectations?

diagram.note: Start with f,g≥0; shifting real-valued observables is handled at the end.

frames.claim: The desired association is the Four Functions conclusion for these choices.
frames.explanation: The product of the input sums is Z²E[f]E[g], while the product of the output sums is Z²E[fg]. Their order will follow once the local join/meet hypothesis is verified.
frames.carry: It remains to compare α(x)β(y) with γ(x∨y)δ(x∧y).

frames.title: See exactly where monotonicity enters
frames.question: Why can both observable factors be moved to the join?

diagram.note: Both observables move upward; the measure splits between join and meet.

frames.claim: f(x)g(y) ≤ f(x∨y)g(x∨y).
frames.explanation: Because x≤x∨y and y≤x∨y, monotonicity gives the two scalar comparisons. Nonnegativity lets us multiply them. The meet does not need an observable factor in this construction.
frames.carry: The only remaining local comparison concerns the measure μ.

frames.title: Use the actual FKG measure hypothesis
frames.question: What must replace μ(x)μ(y) after the observables have moved upward?

diagram.note: Monotonicity of f and g alone cannot supply the first row.

frames.claim: Four Functions yields Z²E[f]E[g] ≤ Z²E[fg].
frames.explanation: This is the precise place where dependence is controlled. Product measures satisfy the measure inequality with equality, but arbitrary dependent measures need not satisfy it. Four Functions now transports the pointwise control to total masses.
frames.carry: Divide by the positive Z² to obtain nonnegative covariance.

frames.title: Allow real-valued increasing observables
frames.question: Why does shifting f and g not change the covariance?

diagram.note: Choose shifts large enough on the finite lattice, then cancel them.

frames.claim: The association inequality holds for all finite real increasing f,g.
frames.explanation: Finiteness supplies minima, so constants a,b can make both observables nonnegative. Expanding both sides shows that the terms aE[g], bE[f], and ab cancel, leaving exactly the original covariance inequality.
frames.carry: FKG is a statement about the measure plus the common monotonicity direction.

challenges.title: External fields preserve the determinant
challenges.skill: Log-supermodularity under reweighting and exact covariance.
challenges.connection: The worked two-bit measure has positive covariance; now perturb both marginals without assuming independence.
challenges.prompt: On {0,1}² take unnormalized masses μ(00)=1, μ(01)=2, μ(10)=3, μ(11)=12. Reweight each state x by r^{x₁}s^{x₂}, with r,s>0. Prove the reweighted measure remains log-supermodular and derive an exact covariance formula for the coordinate indicators. Evaluate it at r=2,s=3.
hints: For two bits, the only nontrivial lattice comparison is μ00μ11≥μ01μ10.
For normalized masses a,b,c,d, coordinate covariance is (ad−bc)/(a+b+c+d)².

probe.prompt: At r=2,s=3, what is the coordinate covariance?
probe.feedback: The reweighted masses are 1,6,6,72, with Z=85. The determinant is 72−36=36, hence covariance 36/85². Reweighting changes the normalization as well as the numerator.

solution: The original lattice determinant is 1·12−2·3=6>0.
External-field factors contribute rs to both products in the lattice comparison, preserving its sign.
The new determinant is 6rs, and Z=1+2s+3r+12rs, so covariance is 6rs/Z².
At r=2,s=3, Z=85 and 6rs=36. Positive association persists although neither marginal stays at its original value.
rubric: Verify the measure inequality after reweighting.
Derive the determinant-over-Z² formula.
Use the new normalization and evaluate the requested field.
challenges.mistake: Keeping the old denominator after applying external fields produces the wrong probability measure.
challenges.followup: Identify which multiplicative reweightings on a larger Boolean lattice preserve log-supermodularity exactly.

challenges.title: Pairwise correlation is not association
challenges.skill: Distinguishing coordinate tests from all increasing observables.
challenges.connection: The example tests two coordinate events; FKG promises much more than those few tests.
challenges.prompt: Let X be uniform on {000,011,101,110}. Prove that every pair of coordinate bits is independent. Then take A={X₁=1} and B={X₂=X₃=1}; both are increasing events on the whole cube. Compute their covariance, exhibit a violated log-supermodularity comparison, and explain why pairwise nonnegative covariance cannot replace the FKG hypothesis.
hints: List the four outcomes of any chosen coordinate pair.
For the lattice test, compare 011 and 101 with their join and meet.

probe.prompt: What is Cov(1_A,1_B)?
probe.feedback: P(A)=1/2 and P(B)=1/4, but P(A∩B)=P(111)=0. The covariance is −1/8 even though every coordinate pair is independent.

solution: Every coordinate pair takes 00,01,10,11 once, giving pairwise independence.
A has probability 1/2, B has probability 1/4, and their intersection is the absent state 111.
The covariance is therefore −1/8. This witnesses failure of association for increasing functions.
For x=011,y=101, both input masses are positive, but join 111 and meet 001 have mass zero. Thus log-supermodularity fails exactly where the Four Functions proof needs it.
rubric: Verify all coordinate pairs rather than just symmetry of marginals.
Check the events are increasing on the ambient cube.
Provide a concrete violated lattice inequality.
challenges.mistake: Testing only coordinate covariance misses nonlinear increasing observables such as a conjunction.
challenges.followup: Construct an analogous example using n bits with one parity constraint and determine which orders of independence survive.

proof.goal: Prove positive association on a Bernoulli product space by accounting for both within-slice and between-slice covariance.
proof.scope: The induction uses independent remaining coordinates in each pinned-coordinate slice. It does not extend automatically to conditioning on an arbitrary event.

frames.title: Isolate the last independent bit
frames.question: What remains random when Xₙ is pinned to 0 or 1?

diagram.note: Pinning one coordinate leaves the same product law on the others.

frames.claim: E[fg|Xₙ=i] ≥ aᵢbᵢ by induction.
frames.explanation: The product assumption preserves independence among the unexposed bits after a coordinate is fixed. Increasingness also survives restriction. These facts let the lower-dimensional induction apply separately in each slice.
frames.carry: Within-slice covariance is nonnegative; the slice means still need comparison.

frames.title: Average the slice inequalities
frames.question: Does averaging already give the unconditional product?

diagram.note: The two displayed expressions differ by a between-slice covariance.

frames.claim: One must retain the difference between average products and product averages.
frames.explanation: The tower property gives the first expression. Expanding the product of the unconditional means produces cross terms a₀b₁ and a₁b₀; ignoring them is the common incomplete induction.
frames.carry: Factor the remaining scalar difference before claiming association.

frames.title: Factor the missing term
frames.question: Which factorization records the common monotonicity direction?

diagram.note: The same coupling compares both slice means pointwise.

frames.claim: Both within-slice and between-slice contributions are nonnegative.
frames.explanation: Couple the two slices using exactly the same remaining-coordinate outcome. Changing only the final bit from zero to one cannot decrease either observable. The two differences therefore have the same nonnegative sign.
frames.carry: The scalar Bernoulli covariance closes the induction.

frames.title: Keep a quantitative check of the factorization
frames.question: For f=X₁∨X₂ and g=X₂∨X₃, where does all covariance come from?

diagram.note: The observables are independent inside each X₂ slice.

frames.claim: Cov(f,g)=p₂(1−p₂)(1−p₁)(1−p₃).
frames.explanation: Given the shared bit, f and g depend on separate independent bits, so the within-slice covariance is zero. The full covariance is exactly the factored between-slice term, providing a direct check of the proof mechanism.
frames.carry: Positive dependence can arise from a shared coordinate without any dependence in the base inputs.

challenges.title: Locate all covariance in the shared bit
challenges.skill: Conditional independence and quantitative equality analysis.
challenges.connection: The original example conditions on one biased bit; this task makes the entire dependence pass through a different shared bit.
challenges.prompt: Let X₁,X₂,X₃ be independent with probabilities 1/4,1/3,3/4. Set f=X₁∨X₂ and g=X₂∨X₃. Derive Cov(f,g) twice: first by conditioning on X₂ and factoring the slice means, then by computing E[f], E[g], and E[fg]. Generalize to arbitrary biases and characterize when covariance vanishes.
hints: Given X₂=0, f and g are separate bits; given X₂=1, both are one.
The between-slice term is p₂(1−p₂)(a₁−a₀)(b₁−b₀).

probe.prompt: What is the exact covariance for the stated biases?
probe.feedback: The slice gaps are 3/4 and 1/4, and p₂(1−p₂)=2/9. Their product is 1/24. E[f]=1/2, E[g]=5/6 and E[fg]=11/24 confirm it.

solution: Conditional independence makes both within-slice covariance terms zero.
The two slice-mean gaps are 1−p₁ and 1−p₃. Thus covariance is p₂(1−p₂)(1−p₁)(1−p₃).
Substitution gives (2/9)(3/4)(1/4)=1/24; direct means give E[fg]=5/12+1/24=11/24.
The general expression vanishes precisely when p₂ is 0 or 1, or p₁=1, or p₃=1. In each case the shared bit no longer transmits nonconstant influence to both outputs.
rubric: Explain why conditional covariance vanishes.
Produce both an exact joint-probability check and the factorization.
State all degenerate equality cases.
challenges.mistake: The original bits being independent does not make f and g independent: both use X₂.
challenges.followup: Replace the OR gates by arbitrary increasing functions and identify the extra within-slice terms.

challenges.title: Conditioning on an increasing event can reverse the sign
challenges.skill: Knowing when the induction hypothesis remains legal.
challenges.connection: The worked proof pins a coordinate; it does not condition on an arbitrary positive event.
challenges.prompt: Start with two independent fair bits and condition on E={X₁∨X₂=1}. Compute the conditional coordinate covariance. E is itself increasing, so explain why this is not a counterexample to Harris but does refute the claim that conditioning on every increasing event preserves association. Locate the failed step in a proposed slice-induction proof under the conditional law.
hints: The conditioned space consists of 01,10,11 with equal probabilities.
Compare P(X₁=X₂=1|E) with the product of the two conditioned marginals.

probe.prompt: What is Cov(X₁,X₂ | E)?
probe.feedback: Each marginal becomes 2/3 while the joint success probability is 1/3, giving 1/3−4/9=−1/9. Conditioning changed the base measure, not the monotonicity of the coordinate functions.

solution: Conditioning removes 00 and leaves three equiprobable states.
The conditioned marginals are 2/3 and the joint success probability is 1/3.
Their covariance is −1/9, although E and both tested coordinate events are increasing.
Harris applied to the original product law is intact. The conditional law is not a product law, so reusing the product-space induction after this conditioning is unjustified.
rubric: Compute the normalized conditional law.
Separate the validity of Harris from preservation under conditioning.
Identify loss of product structure as the missing hypothesis.
challenges.mistake: An increasing conditioning event is not the same operation as fixing a coordinate.
challenges.followup: Characterize which events on the two-bit fair cube yield an associated conditional measure.

proof.goal: Transport FKG from a pivot-relative distributive lattice of labelings to the uniform law on linear extensions.
proof.scope: The explicit lattice formulas and distributive-law verification are the key combinatorial input. The limiting argument below keeps the poset size fixed.

frames.title: Choose coordinates that make both pivot events increasing
frames.question: Why is the pivot coordinate ordered in reverse?

diagram.note: One common pivot direction makes both comparison events increasing.

frames.claim: Use the order x≤y iff x₁≥y₁ and xᵢ−x₁≤yᵢ−y₁.
frames.explanation: In these coordinates, each pivot comparison asks whether one relative gap is nonnegative. Increasing the lattice element can only increase that gap. Reversing the pivot coordinate is part of the lattice construction; ordinary coordinate order would not do this job.
frames.carry: Both events have the common monotonicity required by FKG.

frames.title: Keep order-preserving labelings closed
frames.question: Why does the indicator of a poset-respecting labeling become log-supermodular?

diagram.note: The common pivot shift cancels when comparing labels at comparable poset elements.

frames.claim: μ(x)μ(y)≤μ(x∨y)μ(x∧y) for the feasible-labeling indicator μ.
frames.explanation: If both labelings respect each poset inequality, taking coordinatewise maxima of their relative labels preserves it, and so does taking minima. The common pivot shift does not alter such comparisons. Thus feasible labelings are closed under both operations.
frames.carry: FKG is now applicable on the finite distributive labeling lattice.

frames.title: Apply FKG before passing to rankings
frames.question: Which finite probability law has just been proved associated?

diagram.note: Pₘ is uniform on weakly order-preserving labelings; ties are still allowed.

frames.claim: The pivot inequality holds for every finite label range {1,…,m}.
frames.explanation: The indicator measure is uniform on labelings satisfying the poset inequalities. At this stage equal labels may occur, so it is not yet the uniform law on linear extensions. The final deduction must explicitly remove that difference.
frames.carry: Bound the tied fraction and identify the law after conditioning on no ties.

frames.title: Count each strict ranking equally
frames.question: Why does conditioning on distinct labels give a uniform extension?

diagram.note: Every extension chooses the same increasing n-tuple of labels.

frames.claim: As m→∞, the finite-labeling probabilities converge to uniform-extension probabilities.
frames.explanation: For each extension and each chosen n-subset of labels, assigning them in that ranking gives exactly one strictly labeled outcome. Tied outcomes have one fewer free label and therefore vanishing relative mass for fixed n. Taking limits preserves the FKG inequality.
frames.carry: The XYZ conclusion follows with a uniform law, not an unspecified ranking bias.

challenges.title: A four-element poset changes all three probabilities
challenges.skill: Uniform-extension enumeration and conditional insertion.
challenges.connection: The antichain example has six rankings; adding two constraints tests whether the same covariance reasoning is actually understood.
challenges.prompt: Let P have elements x,y,z,w and only relations y<w and z<w. Enumerate its linear extensions without treating x as equally likely to precede every particular element. Compute P(x<y), P(x<z), and P(x<y and x<z), then their covariance. Explain an insertion argument that assigns the correct probability to each extension.
hints: The restricted order on y,z,w is either yzw or zyw.
Insert x into one of four slots in each of those two orders.

probe.prompt: What is the covariance of 1{x<y} and 1{x<z}?
probe.feedback: There are eight extensions. The two marginals are 3/8, while the joint event has probability 2/8=1/4. The difference is 1/4−9/64=7/64.

solution: There are exactly two legal orders on y,z,w, each with w last. Inserting x into four slots gives eight distinct extensions.
In yzw, only the first slot puts x before y; in zyw, the first two slots do. Thus P(x<y)=3/8, and symmetry gives P(x<z)=3/8.
Both comparisons hold exactly when x is in the first slot, giving two of eight extensions and probability 1/4.
The covariance is 7/64>0, consistent with XYZ. Uniform insertion is justified here because each extension has a unique restricted order and slot.
rubric: Count all extensions with equal weights.
Give both marginal counts and the joint count.
Explain why the insertion parametrization is bijective.
challenges.mistake: Symmetry between y and z gives equal marginals, not the value 1/2.
challenges.followup: Replace w by a chain of r elements above both y and z and derive the corresponding insertion probabilities.

challenges.title: The finite-label law can be mostly ties
challenges.skill: Counting the bridge between weak labelings and uniform extensions.
challenges.connection: The worked antichain enumeration hides the finite-label approximation used in the actual proof.
challenges.prompt: Use the same poset y<w,z<w and allow labels in {1,…,5}, with weak inequalities y≤w,z≤w. Count all feasible labelings, count globally distinct feasible labelings, and show that each linear extension gets the same number in the latter class. Then prove, for a general fixed n-element poset, that the tied fraction tends to zero with m; identify why fixing n matters.
hints: Choose the label of w first; the x label is unrestricted.
Distinct labelings are e(P)C(m,n), while a union bound over tied pairs costs O(mⁿ⁻¹).

probe.prompt: What fraction of the feasible five-label assignments are globally distinct?
probe.feedback: There are 5·(1²+2²+3²+4²+5²)=275 weak assignments. Distinct ones number 8·C(5,4)=40, so the fraction is 40/275=8/55.

solution: For a chosen w label j, y and z each have j choices and x has five. This gives 5Σj²=275 feasible weak assignments.
There are eight extensions and C(5,4)=5 choices of four distinct labels for each, hence 40 distinct assignments.
The requested fraction is 8/55. Ties are common at this small m, so identifying weak labelings with rankings immediately would be a serious error.

For fixed n, at most C(n,2)mⁿ⁻¹ assignments have any repeated label, whereas e(P)C(m,n) grows on the order of mⁿ. Their ratio tends to zero. If n also grows, these constants and asymptotics must be controlled anew.
rubric: Normalize using all feasible weak labelings.
Show equal multiplicity for each linear extension.
Supply the fixed-n asymptotic comparison rather than assert ties are rare.
challenges.mistake: Uniform weak labels do not directly induce a uniform extension until ties are removed.
challenges.followup: Find an explicit m(n) sufficient to make the tied fraction at most 1/10 using the crude union bound.

proof.goal: Derive Azuma from conditional exponential-moment bounds without assuming independent martingale differences.
proof.scope: The conditional one-step Hoeffding bound is the elementary analytic input. Constants here use absolute increment bounds |Dᵢ|≤cᵢ.

frames.title: Center one increment conditionally
frames.question: Which conditioning makes the increment have mean zero?

diagram.note: The past may determine the next increment distribution.

frames.claim: E[e^{λDᵢ}|Fᵢ₋₁] ≤ e^{λ²cᵢ²/2}.
frames.explanation: Apply the bounded-mean-zero exponential estimate inside each conditional probability space. This allows the increment law to depend on everything already revealed. No independence among the Dᵢ is asserted.
frames.carry: A deterministic conditional MGF bound can be pulled through the tower property.

frames.title: Carry the MGF through the exposure tree
frames.question: Why can the last conditional factor be removed even when the increments depend on each other?

diagram.note: This is conditional iteration, not a product formula for independent variables.

frames.claim: The complete martingale has MGF controlled by the sum of squared bounds.
frames.explanation: The earlier partial sum is measurable with respect to Fₘ₋₁. After conditioning, it stays fixed while the final one-step factor is bounded. Repeating removes one increment at a time.
frames.carry: Set V=Σcᵢ²; the remaining task is a scalar exponential optimization.

frames.title: Convert the MGF into a tail
frames.question: What event becomes suitable for Markov when λ>0?

diagram.note: Take t>0 and V>0; if V=0 the martingale is constant.

frames.claim: The upper tail has exponent −t²/(2Σcᵢ²).
frames.explanation: The exponential is increasing, so a deviation of at least t forces e^{λ(Mₘ−M₀)}≥e^{λt}. Optimizing the quadratic exponent gives the strongest bound available from this MGF estimate.
frames.carry: A lower tail requires applying the same argument to −M.

frames.title: Keep the two tails separate until the end
frames.question: Where does the factor two originate?

diagram.note: The two events are combined by a union bound, not by a symmetry assumption.

frames.claim: P(|Mₘ−M₀|≥t) ≤ 2 exp(−t²/(2V)).
frames.explanation: The negated process is also a martingale with exactly the same absolute jump bounds. Applying the upper-tail argument to it establishes the lower tail even when the original martingale distribution is asymmetric.
frames.carry: Conditional centering and bounded jumps, not independent differences, drive the proof.

challenges.title: A dependent-difference martingale
challenges.skill: Exact laws, conditional MGFs, and invalid factorization.
challenges.connection: The fair-coin example has independent centered increments; this perturbation keeps the martingale property while destroying that simplification.
challenges.prompt: Take fresh fair signs ε₁,ε₂. Put D₁=ε₁ and D₂=2ε₂ if ε₁=1, but D₂=0 if ε₁=−1. Show M₀=0,M₁=D₁,M₂=D₁+D₂ is a martingale. Derive the exact terminal law and MGF, exhibit dependence of D₁,D₂, and derive an Azuma upper-tail bound using c₁=1,c₂=2.
hints: Condition D₂ on ε₁ rather than on nothing.
The terminal values are 3 and −1, but they are not equally likely.

probe.prompt: What is E[M₂⁴]?
probe.feedback: M₂=3 with probability 1/4 and −1 with probability 3/4. Thus E[M₂⁴]=81/4+3/4=21. Treating the two increments as independent gives a different law.

solution: E[D₁]=0 and E[D₂|ε₁]=0, so the stated process is a martingale. Yet D₂=0 precisely when ε₁=−1, showing dependence.
For ε₁=1, the outcomes are 3 or −1, each with probability 1/4. For ε₁=−1, the outcome is −1 with probability 1/2.
Therefore E[e^{λM₂}]=(e^{3λ}+3e^{−λ})/4 and E[M₂⁴]=21.
The conditional MGF proof remains legal and gives P(M₂≥t)≤exp(−t²/10), because Σcᵢ²=5. Ordinary unconditional MGF factorization is illegal here.
rubric: Verify conditional mean zero at the second step.
Compute the asymmetric terminal distribution and its MGF.
Separate legality of the conditional proof from sharpness of its bound.
challenges.mistake: Zero covariance or zero means do not imply independent differences.
challenges.followup: Use the actual conditional range lengths to improve the MGF estimate, and compare it with the exact tail at t=2.

challenges.title: A factor of four hidden in the range
challenges.skill: Optimizing a conditional range bound instead of an absolute-jump bound.
challenges.connection: The worked four-coin martingale uses jumps ±1/2; an arbitrary Bernoulli bias changes the centered interval without changing its length.
challenges.prompt: Let X₁,…,X₁₀₀ be independent Bernoulli(0.1), and Mᵢ=Σ_{j≤i}(Xⱼ−0.1). Derive the conditional MGF using the interval [−0.1,0.9] of length one. Optimize the bound for P(M₁₀₀≥10). Compare its exponent with the valid but weaker application of the absolute-jump bound cᵢ=1, and explain the source of the factor four.
hints: The range-length Hoeffding estimate is exp(λ²(b−a)²/8).
Minimize −10λ+100λ²/8, not −10λ+100λ²/2.

probe.prompt: What is the optimizing positive λ for the range-length bound?
probe.feedback: The derivative of −10λ+12.5λ² is −10+25λ, so λ*=0.4. It yields e^{−2}, versus e^{−1/2} from cᵢ=1.

solution: Each increment has conditional mean zero and range length one, giving E[e^{λDᵢ}|past]≤e^{λ²/8}.
Tower iteration yields E[e^{λM₁₀₀}]≤e^{100λ²/8}.
The optimized exponent is −10(0.4)+100(0.4)²/8=−2.
Using only |Dᵢ|≤1 yields exponent −10²/(2·100)=−1/2. The improvement comes from preserving the actual interval length; it is not an independence correction.
rubric: Use the conditional interval correctly after centering.
Optimize λ and give both exponents.
Explain why an absolute bound loses information.
challenges.mistake: The range length is one, but the absolute-jump theorem uses an interval of length two when c=1.
challenges.followup: Repeat for nonidentical Bernoulli biases and decide when the cᵢ=max(pᵢ,1−pᵢ) bound comes closest to the range-length bound.

proof.goal: Explain how a quantile, a Lipschitz deletion statistic, and a small-subgraph coloring lemma create a four-value chromatic window.
proof.scope: For p=n^{−α} with fixed α>5/6. The small-subgraph three-colorability lemma is a separate proved input; the dense clique-packing argument is a different application in the assigned section.

frames.title: Concentrate a repair statistic, not χ directly
frames.question: Which statistic has an atom at zero at the chosen lower quantile?

diagram.note: Changing one vertex block changes Y by at most one.

frames.claim: Y is vertex-Lipschitz and P(Y=0)>ε.
frames.explanation: If two graphs differ only on edges incident to one vertex, any deletion set for one can be enlarged by that vertex for the other. This proves sensitivity one. The quantile choice gives the atom that anchors the otherwise unknown mean.
frames.carry: Azuma can compare the atom at zero to μ=E[Y].

frames.title: Use the lower tail to locate the mean
frames.question: Choose λ with e^{−λ²/2}=ε. What would μ>λ√(n−1) imply?

diagram.note: The lower-tail event would contain the atom at zero.

frames.claim: The mean repair size is at most λ√(n−1).
frames.explanation: Since Y is nonnegative, a larger mean would put zero strictly inside the lower-tail threshold, forcing its probability to be at most ε. That contradicts the quantile atom. This is the missing mean estimate in a naive concentration proof.
frames.carry: The upper tail now bounds a repair set of size O(√n).

frames.title: Color the exceptional vertices separately
frames.question: How does a deletion set of order √n become only three new colors?

diagram.note: Use a disjoint palette; edges crossing between the two parts then cause no conflict.

frames.claim: With high probability χ(G)≤u+3.
frames.explanation: The upper Azuma tail and the mean estimate make Y≤2λ√(n−1) except on a probability-ε event. The small-subgraph lemma simultaneously three-colors every set this small. Coloring the complement with u colors and S with a fresh palette proves the upper endpoint.
frames.carry: The upper window endpoint depends on the sparse structural lemma, not on Azuma alone.

frames.title: Control the lower endpoint and all failure events
frames.question: Why does minimality of u give the lower endpoint?

lines.reason: u is the least quantile integer

diagram.note: For fixed ε and α>5/6, ηₙ→0; then let the error tolerance decrease.

frames.claim: A four-integer interval captures arbitrarily high asymptotic probability.
frames.explanation: The lower-quantile failure, excessive-repair failure, and structural-lemma failure are distinct. Their sum controls the whole argument. A generic O(√n) bound on χ around its mean would not by itself imply this constant-width window.
frames.carry: Always state the sparsity range and the extra coloring lemma.

challenges.title: Optimize the packing alteration
challenges.skill: Sampling, overlapping-pair deletion, and an integer existence conclusion.
challenges.connection: The K₄ example motivates edge-disjoint triangle packing; now derive a useful lower bound instead of just counting triangles.
challenges.prompt: Let H be the disjoint union of two copies of K₄. Select each triangle independently with probability q. Compute the number of triangles and the number of unordered pairs sharing an edge. Delete one selected triangle from every overlapping pair. Derive and optimize a lower bound for the expected remaining packing, then extract an integer lower bound on the maximum packing size. Explain why every selected conflict costs at most one deletion even when conflicts overlap.
hints: Each K₄ contributes four triangles and six conflicting unordered pairs.
The alteration bound is 8q−12q².

probe.prompt: What is the optimized real-valued expectation lower bound?
probe.feedback: The derivative of 8q−12q² vanishes at q=1/3, giving 8/3−12/9=4/3. An integer packing of size at least two must therefore exist.

solution: There are eight triangles and twelve unordered overlapping pairs, with no cross-component conflicts.

A chosen triangle survives unless deleted during conflict repair; processing each conflicting pair removes at most one triangle, so remaining count is at least selected triangles minus selected conflicts.
Linearity gives expectation at least 8q−12q². Its maximum on [0,1] is 4/3 at q=1/3.
Some integer packing therefore has size at least two. This matches the actual maximum: each K₄ contributes at most one edge-disjoint triangle.
rubric: Count unordered conflicts with the correct convention.
Justify the alteration inequality despite overlapping conflicts.
Optimize over a legal q and convert expectation to an integer existence result.
challenges.mistake: Using the number of triangles as a Lipschitz statistic overlooks the much better stability of a maximum packing.
challenges.followup: For a general family with mean count μ and expected conflicting-pair count Δ/2, derive the truncated optimizer q=min(1,μ/Δ).

challenges.title: Reconstruct the quantile-to-window argument
challenges.skill: Using both concentration tails and a structural repair lemma.
challenges.connection: The finite packing example does not explain why a chromatic window has constant width; this task isolates the missing argument.
challenges.prompt: Suppose n=10001, u is the least integer with P(χ≤u)>e^{−2}, and Y is the deletion statistic from the proof. Assume the vertex-exposure Azuma bounds use n−1 steps, and the event that every set of at most 400 vertices is three-colorable fails with probability at most 0.01. Derive a lower bound on P(u≤χ≤u+3), showing the mean bound first. State why applying Azuma directly to χ would not establish the same conclusion.
hints: The two quantile/concentration failures each cost at most e^{−2}; keep the 0.01 structural failure separate.

probe.prompt: What deletion-set size does the two-tail argument guarantee before invoking the structural lemma?
probe.feedback: The atom at zero forces E[Y]≤200. The upper tail then gives Y≤400 except with probability e^{−2}. Using 200 as the deletion budget forgets the second deviation.

solution: Since P(Y=0)>e^{−2}, the lower tail at distance 2√10000=200 forces E[Y]≤200.
The upper tail yields P(Y>400)≤e^{−2}.
On the structural event, remove such an S, color the complement with u colors, and color S with three new colors.

Minimality of u gives P(χ<u)≤e^{−2}. The final success probability is at least 1−2e^{−2}−0.01. A direct concentration window for χ has width O(√n), with no mechanism producing only three extra colors.
rubric: Derive the mean bound from the zero atom.
Use disjoint palettes and the exact deletion budget.
Account for all three failure sources.
challenges.mistake: The lower-tail estimate locates a mean; it does not already give the high-probability upper bound on Y.
challenges.followup: For α=0.9, rederive the small-subgraph union-bound exponent 3α/2−5/4 and explain why it is positive.

proof.goal: Track conditional query effects through an adaptive decision tree using a worst-path variance budget and an admissible MGF range.
proof.scope: The refined small-parameter exponential estimate from §7.4 is an input. Its ε,δ-dependent deviation restriction is essential, not an optional technicality.

frames.title: Adaptivity chooses the next independent coordinate
frames.question: What distribution does an unqueried coordinate retain after previous responses?

diagram.note: The chosen index depends on the past, but its fresh Bernoulli law does not.

frames.claim: |m₁−m₀|≤cᵢ.
frames.explanation: Couple the two completions using identical values for every other unqueried coordinate. The coordinate-effect hypothesis bounds their output difference pointwise by cᵢ, hence also bounds the difference of the conditional means.
frames.carry: The martingale increment is a centered two-point variable.

frames.title: Use the biased variance cost
frames.question: If d=m₁−m₀, what are the two centered jumps?

diagram.note: The conditional variance is pᵢ(1−pᵢ)d², at most the charged coordinate cost.

frames.claim: E[D²|past]≤pᵢ(1−pᵢ)cᵢ².
frames.explanation: The current mean is (1−pᵢ)m₀+pᵢm₁, so subtracting it gives the two jumps shown. This exact centering is why rare Yes/No outcomes can cost much less than an indiscriminate cᵢ².
frames.carry: Charge this query its deterministic upper variance cost.

frames.title: Budget the entire possible line of questioning
frames.question: Which budget survives adaptive branch choices?

diagram.note: The proof needs a bound on every possible path, not merely an average-cost estimate.

frames.claim: Conditional iteration accumulates at most σ² along any path.
frames.explanation: An induction from the leaves can bound every subtree using its remaining variance allowance. Since the budget holds pathwise, an adaptive choice cannot route the calculation through an unbudgeted expensive branch.
frames.carry: The refined MGF estimate is available only for the allowed λC range.

frames.title: Keep the theorem’s admissible range visible
frames.question: Which deviations can be optimized without leaving the one-step estimate?

diagram.note: C bounds the largest coordinate effect; δ depends on ε.

frames.claim: Variance-sensitive concentration is a moderate-deviation statement here.
frames.explanation: Optimizing the exponential parameter is legitimate only while every one-step estimate remains valid. A small σ² does not imply a Gaussian tail at arbitrarily large multiples of σ. Checking this range is part of using the theorem correctly.
frames.carry: Both the worst-path budget and the deviation restriction must be verified in an application.

challenges.title: An early-stopping algorithm still has a long branch
challenges.skill: Separating expected query cost from a pathwise variance allowance.
challenges.connection: The three-bit OR example stops early; increasing the length exposes the difference between typical and worst paths.
challenges.prompt: For 100 independent Bernoulli(0.01) bits, evaluate their OR by querying in order and stopping at the first one. Derive the worst-path variance budget, the expected accumulated variance cost, and the admissible deviation threshold t for the choice ε=δ=1,C=1 in the refined theorem. Explain why substituting the expected cost as σ² is not justified.
hints: The all-zero response path queries every bit.
P(query i)=(0.99)^{i−1}, so sum a geometric series for the expected cost.

probe.prompt: What is the correct worst-path σ² for this strategy?
probe.feedback: Each query costs 0.01·0.99=0.0099, and the all-zero path uses all 100 queries. Thus σ²=0.99, even though the expected cost is 0.99(1−0.99¹⁰⁰), which is smaller.

solution: The coordinate effect is one and each fresh query costs 0.0099. The all-zero branch therefore costs exactly 0.99.
Expected total cost equals 0.0099Σ_{i=0}^{99}0.99^i=0.99(1−0.99¹⁰⁰).
Writing t=ασ, the range αC<2σ becomes t<2σ²=1.98 for ε=δ=1 and C=1.
The theorem’s premise quantifies over every path. A smaller average does not bound the cost of the long all-zero branch, so it cannot replace σ² in this argument.
rubric: Exhibit the worst branch.
Compute the expected cost using query probabilities.
Convert the α restriction into a restriction on the actual deviation t.
challenges.mistake: Stopping early in expectation does not remove the possible path that reveals all bits.
challenges.followup: Design a different statistic and strategy for which adaptive querying genuinely lowers the worst-path budget relative to revealing every coordinate.

challenges.title: A rare Bernoulli variable refutes an all-scale Gaussian claim
challenges.skill: Testing a proposed theorem outside its permitted range.
challenges.connection: The OR example has rare successes, so a variance-sized denominator can tempt an unjustified all-deviation extrapolation.
challenges.prompt: Let Y be Bernoulli(0.01). A proposed extension asserts P(|Y−EY|>t)≤2exp(−t²/[2p(1−p)]) for every t>0 merely because the one-query variance is p(1−p). Test it at t=1/2. Compute the true probability, compare with the proposed bound, and explain which restriction in the assigned theorem prevents this contradiction.
hints: Only Y=1 creates a deviation larger than 1/2.
For ε=δ=1,C=1, legality requires t<2p(1−p).

probe.prompt: What is the true probability P(|Y−0.01|>1/2)?
probe.feedback: The event is exactly {Y=1}, so its probability is 0.01. The proposed Gaussian expression is about 6.57×10⁻⁶, falsely smaller than the true probability.

solution: The two centered values are −0.01 and 0.99. At t=1/2, only the latter exceeds the threshold in absolute value.
Thus the true probability is p=0.01.
The proposed expression is 2exp(−0.25/0.0198), approximately 6.57×10⁻⁶, so the proposed all-scale bound fails.
The assigned refined result requires t<2σ²/C=0.0198 for ε=δ=1. The test t=0.5 is far outside that range, so there is no contradiction with the actual theorem.
rubric: Compute the event under the two-point law.
Compare probabilities numerically or by logarithms.
Locate the exact violated admissibility condition.
challenges.mistake: A second-moment scale can control local exponential behavior without controlling rare jumps at every scale.
challenges.followup: Find, as p→0, a deviation scale for which the proposed Gaussian exponent conflicts with the unavoidable event of probability p.

proof.goal: Choose the actual independent exposure coordinates, prove the correct sensitivity, and connect concentration to the application.
proof.scope: These frames develop the exposure mechanism and the distance-to-a-set deduction. The random-matching application additionally uses the admissible-range query theorem, not an unrestricted variance bound.

frames.title: Changing one image can affect two bins
frames.question: Why is the number of missing outputs still sensitivity one?

diagram.note: Two indicator changes have opposite signs, so their effects do not add to two.

frames.claim: Changing one independent input image changes X by at most one.
frames.explanation: Only the old and new output bins can change emptiness status. Losing the final preimage adds one missing bin; gaining the first preimage removes one. These changes cancel if both occur. A crude sum of two absolute changes would lose this structure.
frames.carry: Expose input images, not the dependent empty-bin indicators.

frames.title: Compute the center before concentrating
frames.question: Which quantities may be summed without independence?

diagram.note: Linearity locates the mean; the independent-image coupling supplies the tail bound.

frames.claim: The occupancy statistic has a valid image-exposure concentration bound.
frames.explanation: The empty-bin indicators are dependent, but linearity does not require their independence. For the martingale, couple completions using all other input images identically, which transfers the sensitivity-one bound to each exposure increment.
frames.carry: Do not confuse a convenient expectation decomposition with legal independent coordinates.

frames.title: Retain the factor two for signed vectors
frames.question: How far can one complete sign replacement move a vector sum?

diagram.note: A sign replacement is not an addition of one copy of vᵢ.

frames.claim: The norm statistic is 2‖vᵢ‖-Lipschitz in sign i.
frames.explanation: For two coupled sums differing only at sign i, the reverse triangle inequality bounds their norm difference by the norm of their difference. That difference is exactly 2vᵢ up to sign. This gives an applicable bounded-differences estimate in any normed space.
frames.carry: Exposure constants must reflect the whole replacement operation.

frames.title: An atom at distance zero locates the center
frames.question: How can a set of known measure control the mean Hamming distance to it?

diagram.note: D is one-Lipschitz in each independent cube coordinate.

frames.claim: A known mass a of A yields an explicit radius for a high-probability neighborhood.
frames.explanation: If the mean distance were too large, the lower concentration tail would make its atom at zero smaller than a. Once the mean is bounded, the upper tail controls the additional radius needed to cover most points.
frames.carry: Use both tails; an unknown mean cannot simply be set to zero.

challenges.title: Find the missing covariance in occupancy
challenges.skill: Exact second moments versus independent exposure coordinates.
challenges.connection: The four-image worked example computes the mean; now determine the variance without pretending its empty-bin indicators are independent.
challenges.prompt: Choose a uniform random function from four inputs to four outputs, and let X be the number of missing outputs. Derive E[X] and Var(X) by counting one-bin and two-bin emptiness. Then explain why a Doob martingale should expose input images rather than use the empty-bin indicators as independent trials. Prove the sensitivity-one bound with a coupling.
hints: A fixed bin is empty with probability (3/4)⁴; a fixed pair is empty with probability (2/4)⁴.
Expand X²=ΣIⱼ+2Σ_{j<k}IⱼIₖ.

probe.prompt: What is the exact variance?
probe.feedback: With a=81/256 and b=1/16, Var(X)=4a+12b−16a²=1695/4096. The covariance terms are negative and cannot be discarded.

solution: For each bin, P(empty)=81/256, so E[X]=81/64.
For distinct bins, joint emptiness has probability 1/16. Thus E[X²]=4·81/256+12·1/16.
Subtracting (81/64)² gives Var(X)=1695/4096. This is not the variance of four independent Bernoulli indicators.
Expose the four independent input images. Reassigning one image can empty its old bin and fill its new bin, with opposite contributions, so the total missing count changes by at most one.
rubric: Count joint emptiness and the ordered-pair factor correctly.
Calculate an exact variance, including covariance.
Give the sensitivity coupling and choose legal base coordinates.
challenges.mistake: The indicators are useful for expectation and second moments but are not an independent product representation.
challenges.followup: Derive the general n-bin variance formula and identify its leading-order behavior.

challenges.title: Turn a mass bound into a neighborhood radius
challenges.skill: Quantile anchoring and two one-sided concentration estimates.
challenges.connection: The finite missing-image example fixes the center explicitly; distance-to-a-set applications must first bound an unknown center.
challenges.prompt: In the uniform 64-dimensional cube, let A have measure at least e^{−2}, and let D be Hamming distance to A. Using the absolute-increment Azuma convention with 64 increments bounded by one, derive a radius r such that P(D>r)≤e^{−8}. Show the mean-distance estimate, then add the upper-tail allowance. Explain why taking only the second allowance is invalid.
hints: The atom D=0 has probability at least e^{−2}.
Solve e^{−m²/(2·64)}=e^{−2}, then solve the upper-tail deviation for e^{−8}.

probe.prompt: What radius follows from this two-tail argument?
probe.feedback: The lower tail forces E[D]≤16. An upper deviation of 32 costs e^{−32²/128}=e^{−8}; therefore radius 48 works. Radius 32 alone forgets the possible nonzero mean.

solution: Changing one cube bit changes D by at most one, by applying the triangle inequality for Hamming distance.
The zero atom and lower tail imply E[D]≤√(2·64·2)=16.
The upper-tail allowance is √(2·64·8)=32.
Thus P(D>48)≤e^{−8}. The radius is a proven bound from these estimates, not a claim that every such set needs radius 48.
rubric: Prove the Lipschitz property of D.
Use the zero atom to locate the mean.
Add, rather than substitute, the upper deviation.
challenges.mistake: Concentration is around E[D], not around the nearest point of A.
challenges.followup: Repeat with a general mass a and error tolerance η, and compare the result with a coordinate subcube.

proof.goal: Link convex mismatch geometry to the projection/fiber induction, then extract the convex-distance tail.
proof.scope: The supporting-hyperplane argument, Hölder step, and scalar optimization are displayed; this is a finite product-space proof mechanism, with all integration steps subject to the stated positive-mass conditions.

frames.title: Average repair directions, not repair lengths
frames.question: Why can three distinct one-coordinate repairs produce distance 1/√3?

diagram.note: For x=000, the mixture has squared norm 1/3 although every individual repair has norm one.

frames.claim: dT(A,x)=min{‖v‖₂ : v lies in the convex mismatch hull}.
frames.explanation: Let v minimize the hull norm. If v=0, handle that case directly. Otherwise the supporting hyperplane gives a nonnegative unit weight vector v/‖v‖ with every repair cost at least ‖v‖. Conversely, a convex mixture producing v bounds every unit-weight minimum by its scalar product with v, at most ‖v‖.
frames.carry: The distance measures a convex compromise among repairs.

frames.title: Split projection and fiber repairs
frames.question: What changes when a repair stays inside the current fiber?

diagram.note: Only the projected repair pays a last-coordinate mismatch.

frames.claim: d² ≤ (1−λ)²+λdω²+(1−λ)dB².
frames.explanation: Take a convex mixture of a repair from the fiber and one from the projection. Its last-coordinate mismatch is at most 1−λ, while convexity of squared norm bounds the old-coordinate part by the weighted squared distances.
frames.carry: Hold λ fixed while integrating over the old coordinates.

frames.title: Apply Hölder before choosing the mixture
frames.question: Where do the projection mass b and relative fiber mass r enter?

diagram.note: An x-dependent optimizer cannot be substituted into a fixed-exponent Hölder argument.

frames.claim: The induction reduces to minimizing one scalar factor for each last-coordinate value.
frames.explanation: With λ fixed, Hölder separates the two exponential distance terms. The lower-dimensional induction bounds their integrals using the projection and fiber masses. Only after this integration may λ be selected as a function of the fiber ratio r.
frames.carry: Optimize e^{(1−λ)²/4}r^{−λ} on 0≤λ≤1.

frames.title: Optimize and average across fibers
frames.question: Why does the scalar bound 2−r close the induction?

diagram.note: The final inequality uses 0<s≤1 and s(2−s)≤1.

frames.explanation: For e^{−1/2}≤r≤1 put u=−ln r. The optimized factor is e^{u−u²}. The function log(2−e^{−u})−u+u² starts at zero and has derivative 2[u−(1−e^{−u})/(2−e^{−u})]≥0, since (1−e^{−u})/(2−e^{−u})≤u. Thus the factor is at most 2−r. For 0≤r≤e^{−1/2}, choose λ=0: e^{1/4}≤4/3≤2−r because r≤2/3. Averaging b⁻¹(2−r) gives b⁻¹(2−a/b)=a⁻¹s(2−s)≤a⁻¹.
frames.carry: The exponential-integral theorem is now available for the full product.

frames.title: Convert the geometric integral into separation
frames.question: What does a distance greater than t force in the exponential?

diagram.note: The product of event probabilities is controlled without counting ambient coordinates.

frames.claim: A set of positive mass has a convex-distance neighborhood with an exponentially small outside tail.
frames.explanation: The exponential is nonnegative and increasing in squared distance, so Markov applies directly. The dimension-free form comes from the convex mismatch geometry and product induction, not from replacing Hamming distance by its square root.
frames.carry: Applications must show geometric separation in this particular distance.

challenges.title: Choose the mixture at the legal stage
challenges.skill: Calculus inside the fiber induction and the order of quantifiers.
challenges.connection: The three-repair example explains convex mixing; now optimize the mixture needed in the actual product-space proof.
challenges.prompt: In the fiber induction, let r=P(Aω)/P(B), and consider Fᵣ(λ)=exp((1−λ)²/4)r^{−λ} for 0≤λ≤1. Derive its minimizing λ, including the boundary case. Evaluate the minimum for r=e^{−1/4}, and compare the optimizer for r=e^{−1}. Explain why choosing λ separately for every old-coordinate point before Hölder would not justify the displayed integral bound.
hints: Differentiate log Fᵣ, not Fᵣ itself.
The stationary value is 1+2 ln r, then clip it to [0,1].

probe.prompt: For r=e^{−1/4}, what is the minimum scalar factor?
probe.feedback: The minimizer is λ=1/2. Its log factor is (1/2)²/4+(1/2)(1/4)=1/16+1/8=3/16, so the minimum is e^{3/16}.

solution: The log derivative is (λ−1)/2−ln r, giving stationary point λ=1+2ln r. Convexity of the log makes it a minimum when feasible.
For r=e^{−1/4}, λ=1/2 and the minimum is e^{3/16}.
For r=e^{−1}, the stationary point is −1, outside the interval; the minimizing λ is zero and the factor is e^{1/4}.
Hölder uses fixed exponents for the integration in x. One may optimize after that integration using r(ω), but an x-varying λ would require a separate argument and cannot be silently inserted.
rubric: Derive and constrain the stationary point.
Compute both interior and endpoint cases.
Explain the legal order of optimization and integration.
challenges.mistake: The unconstrained stationary formula is not a valid mixing weight when r is small.
challenges.followup: Prove the scalar inequality min Fᵣ≤2−r separately on the interior and boundary regimes.

challenges.title: Many-coordinate repairs can still have small convex distance
challenges.skill: An exact convex-hull optimization beyond the singleton example.
challenges.connection: The worked example mixes three one-coordinate repairs. Requiring several repairs simultaneously tests whether the geometry is understood.
challenges.prompt: Let x=0¹² and A be all binary strings of Hamming weight at least three. Compute dT(A,x) exactly by giving both a lower bound valid for every convex mixture and a mixture attaining it. Generalize to n coordinates and threshold r. Compare this result with the minimum Hamming distance, and explain why minimizing the norm of a repair is the wrong operation.
hints: Every mismatch vector has coordinate sum at least r.
Mix uniformly over all r-subsets to make every coordinate of the average equal to r/n.

probe.prompt: For n=12,r=3, what is dT(A,x)²?
probe.feedback: Every hull point has sum at least three, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives squared norm at least 9/12. The uniform mixture of all three-subsets has all coordinates 1/4 and attains 12/16=3/4.

solution: Every point in the convex mismatch hull has nonnegative coordinates with total at least r.
Cauchy–Schwarz yields ‖v‖²≥(Σvᵢ)²/n≥r²/n.
Uniformly averaging the indicator vectors of all r-subsets produces v=(r/n,…,r/n), attaining that bound.
Therefore dT=r/√n; for 12 and 3 its square is 3/4. The nearest individual repair has Hamming distance r and Euclidean mismatch norm √r, a different minimization.
rubric: Prove a lower bound for every convex mixture.
Construct an attaining mixture and compute its coordinates.
Distinguish Hamming distance, individual-vector norm, and hull norm.
challenges.mistake: A convex hull can contain vectors shorter than every original mismatch vector.
challenges.followup: Let coordinate costs differ; solve the analogous minimum-norm problem for a specified nonuniform family of r-subsets.

proof.goal: Use a small certificate at a high outcome to separate it from a low-value event in Talagrand distance.
proof.scope: Talagrand’s convex-distance inequality is the established input. This deduction requires a product space, a valid coordinate Lipschitz bound, and a certificate for every high outcome.

frames.title: Fix the high point before choosing its witness
frames.question: Which coordinates must all completions preserve?

diagram.note: The certificate may depend on y; it need not be chosen uniformly in advance.

frames.claim: A high-value point supplies a set I with |I|≤f(b).
frames.explanation: For a matching, reveal the b disjoint present edges of one witness. Every completion containing those edges still has matching size at least b. The rest of the graph is irrelevant to this lower-bound certificate.
frames.carry: Place the distance weights on this point-specific set I.

frames.title: Concentrate all weight on the certificate
frames.question: What weighted mismatch cost corresponds to h changed certificate bits?

diagram.note: These nonnegative weights have Euclidean norm one.

frames.claim: Distance less than t would permit at most t√|I| certificate disagreements.
frames.explanation: The convex-distance definition allows a different unit cost vector for each high point. Equal costs on I translate weighted closeness into a bound on the number of witness coordinates that would need repair.
frames.carry: Repairing only I will create a point that still certifies X≥b.

frames.title: Repair the low point and use Lipschitzness
frames.question: Why can a sufficiently low point not be close in these weights?

lines.reason: z′ agrees with y on I

diagram.note: A low point with X(z)<b−t√f(b) contradicts these three rows.

frames.claim: Every high point lies outside the t-neighborhood of the low event.
frames.explanation: Construct z′ by changing only the disagreements with y inside I; leave all other coordinates as in z. Certification forces X(z′)≥b. One-Lipschitzness says these h changes can raise X by at most h, contradicting the low-event threshold.
frames.carry: The proof has established geometric separation, not merely a small witness count.

frames.title: Apply Talagrand with the right event probability
frames.question: What can be divided out only when a high-event probability is known?

diagram.note: Without a lower bound a, the product bound is the justified conclusion.

frames.claim: Certificates improve the fluctuation scale from ambient dimension to f(b).
frames.explanation: The low event is A, and every high outcome is outside its convex-distance neighborhood. Talagrand bounds the product of their probabilities. A median or another quantile supplies a useful a; the mean cannot be substituted without further work. For the displayed non-strict threshold, apply separation at parameters increasing to t from below and take the limit.
frames.carry: Keep the Lipschitz constant, certificate size, and reference quantile explicit.

challenges.title: The Lipschitz constant must survive the geometric argument
challenges.skill: Rescaling a certificate concentration deduction.
challenges.connection: The matching example has sensitivity one. This task checks the proof when a certificate is equally small but a coordinate can have twice the effect.
challenges.prompt: Let X be 2-Lipschitz on a product space and f-certifiable with f(100)=100. Assume P(X≥100)≥1/2. Rework the repair argument to bound P(X≤60). Derive the convex-distance separation parameter rather than replacing c=1 at the last line, and state whether the resulting numerical bound is automatically useful.
hints: Repairing h witness coordinates can now change X by at most 2h.
A deficit d requires distance at least d/(c√f(b)).

probe.prompt: What upper bound follows for P(X≤60)?
probe.feedback: The deficit is 40 and c√f=2·10=20, so the distance parameter is t=2. Talagrand gives a product at most e^{-1}; dividing by the high-event probability 1/2 gives 2/e.

solution: A low point repaired on h witness coordinates can rise by at most 2h, so a forty-unit deficit requires at least twenty repairs.
With equal witness weights, the separating distance parameter is 20/√100=2.
Talagrand bounds P(X≤60)P(X≥100) by e^{−2²/4}=e^{−1}.
The probability assumption permits division, yielding 2/e<1. For a smaller deficit the same method might give a bound above one, which must be treated as vacuous.
rubric: Carry c through the repair contradiction.
Compute the distance parameter before applying the theorem.
Divide by a justified high-event lower bound.
challenges.mistake: Small certificates do not cancel a larger coordinate effect; the exponent loses a factor c².
challenges.followup: Derive the formula for general c,b,d,f(b), and identify when its divided probability bound falls below one.

challenges.title: The same graph statistic has different certificate scales
challenges.skill: Choosing independent blocks that reveal the most efficient witness.
challenges.connection: The matching example certifies by present edges. Clique number illustrates how the exposure model changes both the witness and the concentration scale.
challenges.prompt: In G(n,p), expose for each vertex j the independent block of edges {ij:i<j}. Prove clique number is one-Lipschitz under replacing one block. For a high point containing a b-clique, show that b−1 complete blocks certify it. Compare this with revealing C(b,2) individual edges. If b=25 and P(ω≥25)≥1/2, derive the block-certificate bound on P(ω≤5).
hints: Changing block j changes only edges incident to vertex j; remove j from any affected clique.
All edges of a fixed clique belong to the blocks of its vertices except its least-indexed vertex.

probe.prompt: What upper bound follows from the block certificate?
probe.feedback: The block certificate has size 24. A deficit of 20 gives exponent 20²/(4·24)=25/6, so the lower-tail probability is at most 2e^{−25/6}.

solution: Replacing one block changes only edges incident to j. Removing j from a clique leaves a clique in the other graph, proving sensitivity one in both directions.
For a chosen b-clique, pin the b−1 blocks belonging to its vertices other than the least-indexed one. They fix every edge of that clique.
Thus f(b)=b−1 is a valid block certificate, instead of C(b,2) single-edge coordinates. Each representation is a product space, but the certificate sizes differ.
Apply the deduction with b=25,d=20,f=24 and high-event mass at least 1/2 to obtain 2e^{−25/6}.
rubric: Prove the block sensitivity rather than count changed edges.
Identify exactly which blocks certify the chosen clique.
Compare the two legal coordinate representations quantitatively.
challenges.mistake: Counting all changed edges inside a vertex block misses the remove-one-vertex coupling.
challenges.followup: Determine whether any smaller fixed collection of whole blocks can certify a specified clique when unexposed edges remain arbitrary.

proof.goal: Compute the derivative parameters of a nonnegative random polynomial and verify whether the stated Kim–Vu concentration bound is useful.
proof.scope: The general Kim–Vu theorem is a deep input whose proof is omitted in the assigned text. These frames fully develop the application logic and do not claim to prove that theorem.

frames.title: Use edge indicators as polynomial variables
frames.question: Why is graph dependence compatible with independent base inputs?

diagram.note: Triangles may overlap; only their underlying edge indicators are required independent.

frames.claim: X is a multilinear degree-three polynomial with nonnegative coefficients.
frames.explanation: The random events “these triangles occur” are dependent, but the theorem works on the independent edge variables. Its derivative parameters measure exactly how a common subset of those inputs can influence many monomials.
frames.carry: Compute all derivative orders rather than just the mean.

frames.title: Differentiate every possible overlap pattern
frames.question: Which derivative expectation remains one even when p is tiny?

diagram.note: A full monomial derivative is the constant one.

frames.claim: E′=max((n−2)p²,p,1) and E=max(E[X],E′).
frames.explanation: One forced edge leaves n−2 choices for the third vertex. Two adjacent forced edges leave one required edge. Forcing all three edges of a triangle leaves no randomness at all, so its derivative is one; sparse p cannot make E′ vanish.
frames.carry: The controlling scale is the maximum across orders.

frames.title: Insert the actual number of base variables
frames.question: Which n appears in the theorem’s polynomial prefactor?

diagram.note: N is not the number of graph vertices.

frames.claim: The deviation scale and the failure probability must be optimized together.
frames.explanation: The theorem’s polynomial prefactor counts independent variables, which are edges here. Choosing λ as a large enough multiple of ln n suppresses N², but also inflates the allowed deviation by λ³. Both effects belong in a useful concentration conclusion.
frames.carry: A small failure probability is irrelevant if the deviation exceeds the mean.

frames.title: Check the relative error, not just the theorem’s legality
frames.question: What ratio must tend to zero for relative concentration?

diagram.note: The theorem can be valid yet quantitatively vacuous for a sparse statistic.

frames.claim: Relative concentration requires λ³√(E′/μ)→0 in this degree-three application.
frames.explanation: After identifying the correct regime for E, compare the permitted deviation with μ. Taking λ≈ln n often costs a polylogarithmic factor. A large derivative mean signals a shared-input bottleneck rather than a technical nuisance to be omitted.
frames.carry: Inspect overlap structure before declaring a random count concentrated.

challenges.title: A graph has n vertices but Θ(n²) variables
challenges.skill: Parameter scaling and simultaneous control of threshold and failure rate.
challenges.connection: The five-vertex calculation lists derivative values. This asymptotic perturbation tests which values dominate and how the theorem is actually applied.
challenges.prompt: Let X count triangles in G(n,n^{−3/4}). Derive μ,E₁,E₂,E₃ and identify E,E′ for large n. Apply the degree-three Kim–Vu theorem with λ=C ln n. Find the least integer C for which its displayed upper bound on failure is O(n^{−2}), remembering that the theorem counts edge variables. Then determine whether its allowed relative deviation tends to zero.
hints: The prefactor is N² with N=C(n,2), hence order n⁴.
The mean has order n^{3/4}, while the highest-order derivative remains one.

probe.prompt: What is the least integer C giving O(n^{−2}) from the displayed failure bound?
probe.feedback: The failure bound has order n⁴e^{−C ln n}=n^{4−C}; C=6 gives O(n^{−2}). Treating graph vertices as the independent variables would incorrectly suggest C=4.

solution: Consequently E′=1 and E=μ for large n.
There are N=C(n,2)=Θ(n²) independent edge variables. The degree-three prefactor N² is Θ(n⁴), so C=6 is the least integer for O(n^{−2}).
The relative threshold is O((ln n)³/√μ)=O((ln n)³n^{−3/8}), which tends to zero. Thus this application yields meaningful relative concentration.
rubric: Compute all derivative orders.
Use the edge-variable count in the prefactor.
Check that the threshold is o(μ), not merely that the failure tends to zero.
challenges.mistake: Forgetting E₃=1 or using n instead of N corrupts two different parts of the argument.
challenges.followup: Repeat for p=n^{−α} and locate every change in the dominant derivative scale.

challenges.title: One common variable can prevent concentration
challenges.skill: Detecting a derivative bottleneck through an exact law.
