challenges.connection: Overlapping triangles share edge indicators. This simpler nonnegative polynomial isolates the effect of a single shared input.
challenges.prompt: Let Z₁,…,Z₉ be independent fair bits and Y=Z₁(Z₂+⋯+Z₉). Compute E[Y], Var(Y), the largest first- and second-order derivative expectations, and the probability Y=0. Explain why a theorem whose scale involves √(EE′) should not give vanishing relative error here, despite Y being a sum of eight nonnegative degree-two monomials.
hints: Condition first on the common switch Z₁.
The derivative with respect to Z₁ is the entire remaining sum.

probe.prompt: What is Var(Y)?
probe.feedback: If W∼Bin(8,1/2), then Y=Z₁W, E[Y]=2 and E[Y²]=(1/2)(Var(W)+(EW)²)=9. Hence Var(Y)=9−4=5.

solution: Conditioning on Z₁ gives Y=0 with probability at least 1/2, while Y|Z₁=1 is Bin(8,1/2).
Thus E[Y]=2 and E[Y²]=(1/2)(2+16)=9, giving variance five. In fact P(Y=0)=1/2+1/512.
The largest first derivative mean is E[Z₂+⋯+Z₉]=4, and a derivative in {1,j} is one. Hence E′=4 and E=4.
In the version with m variables, μ and E′ are both Θ(m), so √(EE′) is Θ(m). The scale cannot be o(μ), consistent with the persistent zero atom.
rubric: Derive an exact second moment by conditioning.
Locate the common-variable derivative rather than average derivative sizes.
Relate the nonvanishing relative scale to a concrete failure event.
challenges.mistake: Many summands do not ensure concentration when all share one random switch.
challenges.followup: For Y=(Z₁+Z₂)(Z₃+⋯+Z_m), determine which derivatives and conditional atoms control the scale.

proof.goal: Separate channel atypicality from random-code confusion, then extract a fixed code under the intended error convention.
proof.scope: This is the achievability and random-linear-code mechanism. It does not supply an efficient decoder or identify average and maximum message error without an extra argument.

frames.title: Budget the noise event first
frames.question: Why choose a radius qn with p<q<1/2 rather than the exact mean pn?

diagram.note: Slack separates the channel tail from the coding collision calculation.

frames.claim: For a BSC(p), atypical noise beyond qn has vanishing probability.
frames.explanation: Independent channel flips concentrate below any fixed qn with q>p. The restriction q<1/2 is also needed for the standard entropy upper bound on Hamming-ball volume. These are separate reasons to choose q carefully.
frames.carry: Now condition on a typical received word and bound code confusion.

frames.title: Charge each possible competitor a ball volume
frames.question: What law makes one independent random competitor land in the decoding ball?

diagram.note: Competitor independence is not required by the union bound.

frames.claim: The confusion contribution vanishes if k/n<1−H₂(q).
frames.explanation: For a uniformly selected competitor, any fixed ball occupies at most the displayed fraction of the cube. Summing this probability over competitors controls their union even when competitor events are dependent.
frames.carry: Combine this with the channel-tail contribution before fixing a code.

frames.title: Average over codes, then fix one
frames.question: What performance guarantee is inherited by at least one fixed code?

diagram.note: The averaging convention includes the transmitted-message law unless symmetry removes it.

frames.claim: An ensemble error bound proves existence of a fixed code with that average error.
frames.explanation: If every fixed code had error larger than the ensemble average, averaging could not produce the stated mean. This existence step is elementary but does not automatically guarantee small error for every message or an efficient coding algorithm.
frames.carry: Maximum error requires symmetry or a separate expurgation step.

frames.title: For linear codes, work with differences
frames.question: How can dependent codewords still allow the same union bound?

diagram.note: Shift by the transmitted codeword before averaging the random generator.

frames.claim: A random linear generator permits the per-difference bound without independent codewords.
frames.explanation: Over F₂, every fixed nonzero message difference maps to a uniform vector when the generator entries are independent fair bits. Linearity shifts the decoding question to the noise around zero. Union bounding these differences avoids an unjustified claim of independent codewords.
frames.carry: Always specify what is conditioned on and which error convention is proved.

challenges.title: Dependent linear codewords still suffice
challenges.skill: Difference-based random coding and a correct entropy exponent.
challenges.connection: The repetition-code example analyzes one fixed code. This challenge reconstructs the random-linear-code argument without assuming its codewords are independent.
challenges.prompt: Take a uniformly random binary linear generator mapping 250-bit messages to length 1000. Use typical-noise radius 0.2n for a BSC(0.1). Show why each nonzero message difference has a uniform image, derive a union bound on confusion using V(n,0.2n)≤2^{nH₂(0.2)}, and explain why one should shift the received word by the transmitted codeword before this calculation. Separate rank-deficient generators and atypical channel noise from any unsupported efficiency claim.
hints: For fixed v≠0, each row dot v is an independent fair bit.
Linearity compares every rival to the transmitted message through Gv; the rivals need not be independent.

probe.prompt: What positive exponent E gives the confusion bound at most 2^{−E}?
probe.feedback: The exponent is 1000(1−H₂(0.2))−250≈28.0719051. The message-difference union bound handles dependence; atypical channel noise is a separate term.

solution: For each fixed nonzero v, a random generator maps v uniformly into the n-bit cube. This does not make all Gv jointly independent.
By linearity, subtracting the transmitted codeword leaves the channel noise, and every rival corresponds to a nonzero difference v.
For each v, the probability over G that Gv lies within the relevant radius of the noise is at most V/2ⁿ. Union bounding fewer than 2^{250} differences gives 2^{250−1000(1−H₂(0.2))}.

The exponent is about 28.0719051. A zero image of a nonzero difference is already a possible collision; one may separately bound rank failure if a full-rank code is required. Neither calculation supplies an efficient decoder.
rubric: Justify uniformity for fixed nonzero differences.
Use a union bound without asserting joint codeword independence.
State the noise, rank, and computational limitations separately.
challenges.mistake: Conditioning on arbitrary transmitted codeword information can change distributions; the difference formulation avoids that unnecessary conditioning.
challenges.followup: Derive the ensemble rank-failure bound and compare its exponent with the confusion exponent here.

challenges.title: Average error does not yet mean maximum error
challenges.skill: Expurgation with an explicit rate cost.
challenges.connection: The worked example has message symmetry. A general existence argument may only control the average over messages.
challenges.prompt: A fixed code has 1024 codewords and average message error at most 1/64 under a specified decoder. Delete every message whose error is at least 1/8. Prove a lower bound on the number retained and a maximum-error guarantee for the retained code, adjusting the decoder without increasing any retained message error. Express the finite rate loss and explain why this is different from asserting that the original maximum error was small.
hints: Apply Markov to the error value of a uniformly chosen message.
A received word decoded as a deleted message can be reassigned without removing any previously correct retained decoding.

probe.prompt: What retained-code size is guaranteed by this expurgation bound?
probe.feedback: At most 1024·(1/64)/(1/8)=128 messages have error at least 1/8. At least 896 remain, each with error strictly below 1/8 under the original decoder.

solution: Let e_m be each message error. Their sum is at most 1024/64=16.
Every deleted message contributes at least 1/8, so at most 128 messages are deleted and at least 896 remain.

Retained messages have error below 1/8. Preserve every decoding decision to a retained message; reassign other outputs arbitrarily among retained messages, which cannot spoil any previously correct retained outcome.
The rate decreases from log₂(1024)/n to at least log₂(896)/n, a loss at most log₂(1024/896)/n. No such maximum-error claim was established for the original code.
rubric: Use the correct error threshold and inequality direction.
Justify decoder adjustment for the subcode.
State the retained size and explicit rate loss.
challenges.mistake: A small average allows a minority of very bad messages; it is not already a maximum-error bound.
challenges.followup: For average error ε and retained maximum threshold τ, optimize the retained fraction and rate penalty as functions of τ.

proof.goal: Construct Carole’s nondecreasing weight strategy and explain why the weight condition is only one direction.
proof.scope: The binomial survival potential applies to fair hypothetical responses. A low starting weight does not itself construct Paul’s splitting strategy.

frames.title: Interpret the binomial weight before using it
frames.question: What does one chip at remaining lie allowance i survive?

diagram.note: The terminal value counts surviving candidates, not a probability of Paul winning.

frames.claim: W=ΣxᵢB(q,i) is the expected terminal survivor count under fair responses.
frames.explanation: Against any adaptive Paul strategy, a fixed candidate is contradicted by a fresh fair reported answer with conditional probability one half. Its lie count therefore follows the needed binomial law, and linearity adds candidate survival probabilities without independence between candidates.
frames.carry: The potential has an exact successor averaging identity.

frames.title: Compare the two possible answers to a question
frames.question: Why does every question give a response with successor weight at least W?

diagram.note: The two successor values satisfy W=(Wᵧ+Wₙ)/2.

frames.claim: max(Wᵧ,Wₙ)≥W.
frames.explanation: The binomial recurrence B(q,i)=[B(q−1,i)+B(q−1,i−1)]/2 holds chip by chip. Summing it proves the average identity for every possible question, including an adaptive question chosen from the current state.
frames.carry: Carole can choose a maximizing answer after each question.

frames.title: Carry strict weight above one to the terminal state
frames.question: Why must the initial inequality be strict in this argument?

diagram.note: An integer strictly above one means at least two surviving candidates.

frames.claim: Starting from W>1, Carole can force ambiguity.
frames.explanation: The potential never drops below its starting value. At zero questions, each live candidate has weight one. The surviving-candidate count is an integer, so a terminal value above one leaves at least two possibilities that Paul cannot distinguish.
frames.carry: The proof establishes a sufficient condition for Carole.

frames.title: Do not reverse an averaging argument
frames.question: What extra requirement would Paul need when W≤1?

diagram.note: An average ≤1 does not force both children to be ≤1.

frames.claim: Paul needs an achievable balanced question, not merely a low average weight.
frames.explanation: Question constraints and integrality determine which two successors can be realized. A state may have W≤1 but every legal question may leave one child above one. This gap is why the counting condition cannot be treated as a complete strategy theorem.
frames.carry: Analyze the feasible split, not only the parent weight.

challenges.title: A subcritical weight with no legal first split
challenges.skill: Minimax analysis of all possible first questions.
challenges.connection: The four-candidate example tests the weight obstruction; this five-candidate state shows why its converse fails.
challenges.prompt: Five candidates each allow one lie, with five questions remaining. Compute the initial weight. If a first question contains m candidates, derive both four-question successor weights in terms of m. Minimize their maximum over every integer m from 0 to 5, and use the result to prove Carole can win despite the initial weight being below one.
hints: B(5,1)=6/32; after the answer, candidates inside and outside the query have different remaining lie allowances.
The successor numerators over denominator 16 are 5+4m and 25−4m.

probe.prompt: What is the smallest possible maximum successor weight?
probe.feedback: The two successors are (5+4m)/16 and (25−4m)/16. Their continuous balance is m=2.5, but integer m=2 or 3 gives maximum 17/16>1.

solution: The initial weight is 5·6/32=15/16<1.
For one response, m candidates retain one lie and 5−m retain none, giving (5+4m)/16; the other response gives (25−4m)/16.
Their maximum is minimized at the integers nearest 2.5, namely m=2 or 3, where it equals 17/16. All other m give a larger maximum.
Carole selects that supercritical child and thereafter maintains weight above one, forcing at least two terminal survivors.
rubric: Derive both successor formulas from lie allowances.
Optimize over integer legal questions.
Connect the supercritical successor to Carole’s terminal strategy.
challenges.mistake: The fractional split m=2.5 is not a question on five individual candidates.
challenges.followup: For n candidates and one lie, determine when the first-question integrality obstruction persists near the volume threshold.

challenges.title: A biased response coin changes the potential
challenges.skill: Understanding why the fair-response interpretation is strategy independent.
challenges.connection: The worked binomial calculation uses fair hypothetical answers; replacing the coin changes the distribution of lies.
challenges.prompt: There are two candidate values, each with one lie allowed and two questions remaining. Paul asks the uninformative question containing both candidates twice. Carole independently reports Yes with probability 3/4. Compute the expected terminal number of live candidates, then repeat if both questions contain neither candidate. Explain why replacing the fair binomial weight by one fixed biased-binomial formula cannot be independent of Paul’s choices.
hints: A candidate is eliminated only after two lies.
Which answer is a lie depends on whether that candidate belongs to the query.

probe.prompt: When both queries contain both candidates, what is the expected terminal survivor count?
probe.feedback: Each candidate is eliminated only after two No responses, probability (1/4)²=1/16. Its survival probability is 15/16, so the expected count is 2·15/16=15/8.

solution: When every candidate belongs to each query, Yes is truthful and two No responses are required for elimination. Thus each survives with probability 15/16.
Linearity gives expected survivor count 15/8, regardless of the dependence between the two survivor indicators.
If every query contains neither candidate, Yes is a lie; each survives with probability 1−(3/4)²=7/16, giving total expectation 7/8.

The same initial lie allowances yield different biased survival means under different questions. A fair response has lie probability 1/2 in either case, which is what makes the original binomial potential independent of Paul’s question choices.
rubric: Identify truthful versus lying answers for each query type.
Compute both survivor expectations without assuming candidate independence.
Explain the special role of fairness in a strategy-independent state potential.
challenges.mistake: A fixed response bias is not a fixed lie bias: truthful answers depend on the candidate and the question.
challenges.followup: Describe what additional state a dynamic-programming potential would need when responses have a prescribed nonfair distribution.

proof.goal: Prove both directions of the dyadic threshold using successor averaging and the constructive splitting lemma.
proof.scope: The splitting lemma relies on finite dyadic chip weights 2^{−i} and the gluing induction. It does not hold for arbitrary positive chip weights.

frames.title: Promotion doubles the weight of the retained part
frames.question: How do the two successor values relate to the proposed split?

diagram.note: Only one part survives, but every survivor moves one level toward tenure.

frames.claim: The parent weight is the average of its two successor weights.
frames.explanation: A chip at level i has weight 2^{−i}. Promotion moves it to i−1, multiplying that weight by two, while firing contributes zero. These deterministic formulas prove the averaging identity for every split.
frames.carry: Carole can preserve W<1 by taking the lighter child.

frames.title: Below one, the target is impossible
frames.question: Why can a weight-minimizing response prevent tenure forever?

diagram.note: A level-zero chip alone would violate the maintained strict inequality.

frames.claim: For W<1, Carole wins.
frames.explanation: The smaller of two numbers is at most their average, so the maintained weight never reaches one. A tenure chip would have weight one by itself. The finite promote-or-fire game therefore terminates without tenure.
frames.carry: For W≥1, Paul needs a split with both parts of weight at least one half.

frames.title: Glue two equal chips without changing total weight
frames.question: Why must a finite supercritical position contain a repeated level?

diagram.note: If at most one chip occupied each positive level, the finite sum would be strictly below one.

frames.claim: Every W≥1 position can be split into two parts of weight at least 1/2.
frames.explanation: A repeated level must exist. Two level-one chips can be separated directly. For a repeated deeper level, glue them into a superchip one level nearer tenure, apply induction to the shorter list, then put both originals into the superchip’s assigned part.
frames.carry: The dyadic weights make the gluing operation exact.

frames.title: Use the split lemma as a strategy invariant
frames.question: What happens whichever part Carole chooses to keep?

diagram.note: Finite termination forces a tenure chip rather than an infinite avoidance path.

frames.claim: For W≥1, Paul wins by keeping the post-response weight at least one.
frames.explanation: At every nonterminal state, Paul invokes the splitting lemma. Both possible responses leave weight at least one. The game cannot end by firing every chip, and its levels strictly decrease for survivors, so the only remaining terminal outcome is tenure.
frames.carry: A strategy theorem needs both the potential and an implementable safe split.

challenges.title: How rare is a safe random partition?
challenges.skill: Constructive dyadic splitting versus a probabilistic guess.
challenges.connection: The worked 1/2,1/4,1/4 position has an evident split; the six-chip position tests gluing and exact partition counts.
challenges.prompt: Consider two chips at level two and four chips at level three. Construct a safe split by gluing, and count the probability that a uniformly random labeled partition puts each chip independently into S or its complement and is safe for Paul. Show why total weight one forces each safe part to have exactly weight one half.
hints: In units of 1/8, the chip weights are 2,2,1,1,1,1.
If S has a large chips and b small chips, its half-weight equation is 2a+b=4.

probe.prompt: What fraction of the 64 labeled random partitions are safe?
probe.feedback: The solutions give C(2,0)C(4,4)+C(2,1)C(4,2)+C(2,2)C(4,0)=1+12+1=14 safe subsets. Thus the probability is 14/64=7/32.

solution: The total weight is 2/4+4/8=1, so both parts being at least 1/2 forces exact equality.
Glue the four level-three chips in pairs into two level-two superchips, giving four quarter-weight chips; split those into pairs and unglue.
For a labeled random subset S, let a count quarter-weight chips and b count eighth-weight chips. Safety is exactly 2a+b=4.
There are 1+12+1=14 such subsets among 2⁶=64, giving probability 7/32. The gluing strategy guarantees a safe split rather than merely hoping to sample one.
rubric: Construct a legitimate unglued split.
Derive the exact half-weight equation.
Count labeled subsets with both sides included in the event.
challenges.mistake: Weight one guarantees existence of a safe partition, not safety of every partition or of a typical guess.
challenges.followup: Give an algorithm that finds a half-weight subset of any finite dyadic weight-one position.

challenges.title: Why arbitrary weights destroy the converse
challenges.skill: Identifying the structural hypothesis behind a splitting lemma.
challenges.connection: The worked proof glues equal dyadic chips; this task removes that arithmetic structure while keeping the averaging identity.
challenges.prompt: Consider an abstract one-step game with chip weights 0.4,0.35,0.25. Paul partitions them, Carole retains either part, and all retained weights double. Compute the largest minimum successor weight Paul can force. Explain why total weight one and successor averaging do not give a safe split here, and identify the precise step in the Tenure Game proof that no longer applies.
hints: List all attainable subset sums rather than split one chip fractionally.
A safe split at total one would require an attainable subset sum exactly 1/2.

probe.prompt: What is Paul’s best guaranteed successor weight?
probe.feedback: The subset sums nearest 1/2 are 0.4 and 0.6. Their smaller side weighs 0.4, so doubling gives at most 0.8; that bound is attained by separating the 0.4 chip.

solution: The attainable sums are 0,0.25,0.35,0.4,0.6,0.65,0.75,1. None equals one half.
For any split with sum s, the worst child is 2min(s,1−s). This is maximized at s=0.4 or 0.6.
The best guaranteed successor value is therefore 0.8<1, even though the parent weight is one and equals the average successor value.
The dyadic repeated-level and exact-gluing argument has no analogue for these three weights. Averaging alone proves the subcritical direction but cannot prove the supercritical converse.
rubric: Enumerate feasible subset sums.
Solve the minimax successor optimization.
Locate the failed dyadic-gluing premise.
challenges.mistake: A fractional half-half division is not a legal partition of indivisible chips.
challenges.followup: Find a condition on a multiset of rational weights that guarantees a safe half-weight subset.

proof.goal: Turn fresh randomized signs against each adaptive Pusher strategy into a deterministic strategy-existence conclusion.
proof.scope: This proves the random-walk upper-bound mechanism. The matching lower-bound potential and the zero-one reduction are additional assigned arguments, not consequences of this upper-bound proof.

frames.title: The adversary moves before the fresh sign
frames.question: What is the conditional law of one coordinate increment?

diagram.note: The vector can depend on the past; its current coordinate is fixed before the fresh coin.

frames.claim: Each coordinate has the law of an ordinary n-step fair random walk.
frames.explanation: Conditional on every past response and the current vector, vᵢⱼ is a fixed sign. Multiplying it by a fresh fair sign leaves a fresh fair increment. Repeating this conditional fact gives the usual walk distribution for any single coordinate, despite adaptive vector choices.
frames.carry: Coordinate marginals are controlled; independence across coordinates is unnecessary.

frames.title: Compute a single-coordinate failure probability
frames.question: Which binomial terms correspond to a strict discrepancy threshold?

diagram.note: For a threshold of two, only the first and last rows fail.

frames.claim: P(|Sₙ|>a) is the relevant one-coordinate tail.
frames.explanation: The strict inequality in the game payoff determines which lattice points count as failures. Exact binomial tails or a valid concentration estimate may bound this probability. The same marginal bound applies to every coordinate under the fixed adaptive Pusher strategy.
frames.carry: Sum these failure probabilities before invoking a game-theoretic conclusion.

frames.title: Find positive probability of simultaneous success
frames.question: What condition makes the union bound strictly less than one?

diagram.note: The random signs need not make the coordinate events independent.

frames.claim: Against each fixed Pusher strategy, fresh randomized Chooser play has a successful realization.
frames.explanation: A probability below one for failure proves that the fixed adversary cannot force a win against every possible sign response. This statement quantifies over a Pusher strategy first; it does not produce one universal sign sequence that defeats all adversaries.
frames.carry: The remaining step concerns strategies, not a fixed sequence of signs.

frames.title: Use determinacy with the correct quantifiers
frames.question: Why does a successful random realization against each strategy rule out Pusher’s forced win?

diagram.note: A Chooser policy can depend on the currently presented vector.

frames.claim: Finite perfect-information determinacy gives a winning Chooser strategy for this threshold.
frames.explanation: If Pusher had a forcing strategy, the randomized policy would fail with probability one against it, contradicting the strict union bound. Since the finite threshold game has no draws, Chooser must have a deterministic winning policy. This is not a claim that a nonadaptive sign list works.
frames.carry: Preserve the distinction between a response strategy and an advance schedule.

challenges.title: Find the first threshold the exact walk certifies
challenges.skill: Exact binomial tails, strict inequalities, and the union bound.
challenges.connection: The four-round example computes one walk tail; the full argument must beat the number of coordinates simultaneously.
challenges.prompt: In the 16-round balancing game in 16 dimensions, use the exact law of S₁₆ to find the smallest nonnegative even threshold a for which 16P(|S₁₆|>a)<1. Show enough binomial sums to prove both success at your threshold and failure of this criterion at the previous even threshold. Explain why failure of the criterion would not prove Pusher wins.
hints: For a=8, the strict tail corresponds to at most three positive signs or at least thirteen.
For a=6, include the fourth binomial layer as well.

probe.prompt: What is the smallest even threshold certified by the exact union-bound criterion?
probe.feedback: At a=8 the tail is 2(1+16+120+560)/65536=1394/65536, and multiplying by 16 is below one. At a=6 it is 2(1+16+120+560+1820)/65536=5034/65536, whose sixteenfold value exceeds one.

solution: For a=8, |S₁₆|>8 means the number of positive increments lies in {0,1,2,3,13,14,15,16}.
The tail numerator is 2(1+16+120+560)=1394, so the union-bound failure is 22304/65536<1.
At a=6, adding the fourth and twelfth layers gives numerator 5034; multiplying by 16 gives 80544/65536>1. Tail probabilities only grow at smaller thresholds.
Thus eight is the first even threshold certified by this argument. The failed inequality at six is inconclusive about the actual game value; it only means this union bound cannot certify six.
rubric: Use the strict tail and correct lattice endpoints.
Check the sixteen-coordinate factor.
Separate an inconclusive upper-bound method from a lower-bound strategy.
challenges.mistake: A union bound at least one says nothing about the true probability of failure.
challenges.followup: Compare the exact threshold with the one obtained from the standard two-sided exponential random-walk tail.

challenges.title: Why a strategy is not a universal sign list
challenges.skill: Adversarial quantifier order and deterministic strategy dependence.
challenges.connection: The finite random-walk example produces successful sign realizations only after an adversary is fixed.
challenges.prompt: A student reads the randomized proof as: there is one sequence of n signs that works against every Pusher policy. Refute this by giving Pusher’s response to any publicly announced sign list. Then explain why finite-game determinacy can still yield a deterministic winning Chooser strategy. Your explanation must explicitly state who sees the current vector and when the fresh random sign is chosen in the probabilistic proof.
hints: For an announced sign σᵢ, Pusher can make σᵢvᵢ point in the same direction every round.
A deterministic policy can depend on the presented vᵢ; a preannounced schedule cannot.

probe.prompt: Which conclusion correctly reconciles the probabilistic proof with the announced-list attack?
options: A Chooser response policy may depend on each current vector, although no single advance sign schedule need work.
The union bound requires independent coordinates, so the randomized argument fails before determinacy.
There is a universal advance sign schedule, but Pusher is forbidden to choose its vectors using that schedule.
Determinacy gives only a randomized strategy because Pusher is allowed to adapt to earlier signs.
feedback: Pusher can defeat any announced schedule by taking vᵢ=σᵢ·1, but a policy sees vᵢ and can choose a response to it. These are different quantifiers.
The union bound uses marginal tails only. Coordinate dependence is explicitly allowed.
The proof never establishes a universal schedule, and the game does not impose this artificial information restriction.
Finite perfect-information threshold games admit deterministic winning policies; adaptivity is part of the strategy space.

solution: Given a public schedule σ, Pusher chooses vᵢ=σᵢ(1,…,1). The actual signed increment is then (1,…,1) every round, giving final discrepancy n.
This disproves a single fixed sign list working against all Pusher policies.
The randomized argument instead fixes Pusher’s policy first and then shows positive success probability for fresh signs chosen after each vector.
Determinacy rules out any forcing Pusher policy and yields a Chooser policy that can use the entire visible history and current vector. It need not be a fixed schedule.
rubric: Construct the legal schedule-dependent attack.
State the order of choices in the random argument.
Distinguish strategies from complete advance sign strings.
challenges.mistake: Interchanging “for every Pusher policy” and “there exists a sign list” changes the theorem.
challenges.followup: Explain why evaluating the resulting deterministic policy efficiently is a separate question from its game-theoretic existence.

proof.goal: Derive the asymmetric response-path upper bound and identify the extra construction needed for matching achievability.
proof.scope: The k=1 upper-bound mechanism is developed. The nearly balanced first stage and the final chip-game strategy are separate ingredients of the lower construction; the latter is an exercise input in the assigned text.

frames.title: Count possible first lies along the truthful path
frames.question: Why is the candidate’s response set sized by its truthful No answers?

diagram.note: After a lie in an adaptive tree, later truthful answers may follow a different branch.

frames.claim: A candidate with z truthful No answers has exactly z+1 legal reported paths when k=1.
frames.explanation: Each legal nontruthful response path has a unique first lie at a No position on the original truthful path. Once that lie is used, the remaining responses are forced by truth along the resulting branch. Different first-lie positions give distinct paths. This counting does not assume fixed nonadaptive questions.
frames.carry: Assign weight W(σ)=z+1 to the candidate.

frames.title: Use disjointness of reported leaves
frames.question: Why must different candidates’ reported-path sets be disjoint under a winning strategy?

diagram.note: A shared reported leaf would leave Paul unable to distinguish two values.

frames.claim: A winning strategy must fit all asymmetric response sets into the q-bit answer tree.
frames.explanation: A q-question binary tree has at most 2^q reported answer strings. If two candidate values permit the same reported leaf, both remain possible after all questions, contradicting identification. Summing their disjoint response-set sizes gives the budget.
frames.carry: Small-weight truthful paths must be counted separately.

frames.title: Pay for exceptional truthful paths
frames.question: How many candidates can use unusually few No answers?

diagram.note: The truthful paths themselves are distinct, so binomial counting bounds exceptional candidates.

frames.explanation: Low-weight paths are cheap in the response budget, but there are few of them. Every other candidate consumes at least roughly (q−u)/2 leaves. Bounding both groups avoids the false assumption that every candidate has a typical truthful string.
frames.carry: Choose u growing faster than √q but slower than q.

frames.title: Separate the asymptotic obstruction from construction
frames.question: Why does an upper count not supply a legal winning strategy?

diagram.note: The response geometry and adaptivity still constrain realizable question trees.

frames.claim: The leading k=1 asymptotic requires a separate two-stage lower construction.
frames.explanation: The selected u makes the exceptional-path term negligible and leaves q−u asymptotic to q. Achievability then groups candidates under nearly balanced first-stage strings and invokes a controlled final chip-game strategy. It does not follow by reversing the volume inequality.
frames.carry: State which part is a count and which part constructs legal questions.

challenges.title: A volume bound misses asymmetric packing obstructions
challenges.skill: Disjoint response sets for a constant-weight family.
challenges.connection: The four-question illustration lists one candidate’s possible responses; now force several such response sets to coexist.
challenges.prompt: Consider nonadaptive four-question truthful strings with exactly two No answers, and permit at most one No→Yes lie. Determine the largest number of these truthful strings that can be used together for guaranteed identification. Prove your upper bound by analyzing when two response sets intersect, and exhibit an attaining collection. Compare with the weaker count obtained by assigning three responses to every candidate.
hints: Represent a truthful string by its two No positions.
Two distinct two-subsets sharing one position can both produce the response with only that shared No remaining.

probe.prompt: What is the largest possible number of candidates in this restricted nonadaptive code?
probe.feedback: Response sets are disjoint exactly when the two No-position sets are disjoint. At most two disjoint two-subsets fit in four positions, and {1,2},{3,4} attain it. The volume bound alone would only give floor(16/3)=5.

solution: A truthful string with two No positions S has reported No sets S and S\{i} for i∈S, hence three responses.
Two distinct two-subsets S,T share a legal response exactly when they intersect in one position: both can report that singleton No set.
A legal collection must therefore consist of pairwise disjoint two-subsets, so its size is at most two.
The sets {1,2} and {3,4} have disjoint response sets and attain two. The count 3n≤16 permits up to five and is not sufficient for realizability.
rubric: Analyze response-set intersections, not just their sizes.
Prove maximality and give a legal attaining pair.
Explain the gap between a volume obstruction and an actual code.
challenges.mistake: Disjoint truthful strings are not enough: their possible one-lie responses must also be disjoint.
challenges.followup: Solve the same restricted problem for length q and truthful strings with exactly two No answers.

challenges.title: Choose the tail cutoff without losing the leading constant
challenges.skill: Asymptotic balancing of rare paths and volume consumption.
challenges.connection: The finite response-string example hides the optimization needed to make exceptional truthful paths negligible.
challenges.prompt: Starting from n≤2^q[exp(−u²/(2q))+2/(q−u)], set u=√(c q ln q), with fixed c>0. Determine the conditions on c that make the exceptional-path term o(1/q) and keep u=o(q). Derive the resulting leading upper bound and explain what happens at the critical value c=2.
hints: The exponential term becomes q^{−c/2}.
Compare it with 1/q rather than merely ask whether it tends to zero.

probe.prompt: What is the least positive integer c that makes the exceptional term o(1/q)?
probe.feedback: The ratio q^{−c/2}/(1/q)=q^{1−c/2} tends to zero exactly when c>2. Hence the least integer is three; c=2 leaves a same-order contribution.

solution: The chosen cutoff satisfies u/q=√(c ln q/q)→0 for every fixed c.
The exceptional-path factor is exp(−c ln q/2)=q^{−c/2}.
It is negligible compared with 1/q exactly for c>2. Then 2/(q−u)=(2+o(1))/q, giving n≤(1+o(1))2^{q+1}/q.
At c=2, the exceptional contribution is 1/q and cannot be discarded; this estimate gives a leading coefficient three rather than the desired two.
rubric: Compare the exceptional term with the main term.
Verify the cutoff remains sublinear.
Explain the critical value’s effect on the leading constant.
challenges.mistake: A rare-path probability tending to zero can still dominate the main 1/q scale.
challenges.followup: Determine how slowly c(q) may approach two from above while preserving a negligible exceptional contribution.

proof.goal: Derive entropy subadditivity and use uniform family sampling to bound the size of an extremal set system.
proof.scope: All entropies are discrete and measured in bits. Equality needs genuine joint independence, not only equal or pairwise-independent marginals.

frames.title: Factor a joint probability along one order
frames.question: What becomes of the logarithm of a product of conditional probabilities?

diagram.note: Terms with zero probability contribute zero under the usual entropy convention.

frames.claim: The entropy chain rule is an identity, not an independence assumption.
frames.explanation: The joint law factors into successive conditional laws. Taking the negative base-two logarithm turns that factorization into a sum, and averaging gives the displayed conditional entropies.
frames.carry: Inequalities enter when conditioning is removed.

frames.title: Measure the information lost by using marginals
frames.question: Which divergence is the gap in subadditivity?

diagram.note: Nonnegative relative entropy gives the inequality and its equality condition.

frames.claim: H(X)≤ΣᵢH(Xᵢ), with equality exactly for the product law.
frames.explanation: Expanding the log likelihood ratio against the product of the marginals identifies the gap. Relative entropy is nonnegative, and equality forces the two full probability laws to agree. Pairwise independence alone does not identify the full joint law.
frames.carry: To count a family, make the joint law uniform on that family.

frames.title: Uniform sampling turns entropy into log cardinality
frames.question: Why is a uniform family member the correct random object?

diagram.note: The joint law is uniform, but its coordinates need not be independent.

frames.claim: log₂|F|≤ΣᵢH₂(pᵢ).
frames.explanation: Uniformity makes each family member contribute the same information log₂|F|. Each bit marginal is Bernoulli with bias equal to the proportion of family members containing that coordinate. Subadditivity then yields an explicit counting bound from these biases.
frames.carry: Additional combinatorial information can now constrain the marginal biases.

frames.title: Use concavity only after the joint bound
frames.question: What does a bound on average set size say about the sum of bit entropies?

diagram.note: The last step also uses that H₂ is increasing up to 1/2.

frames.claim: A family of average weight at most ρn has |F|≤2^{nH₂(ρ)} for ρ≤1/2.
frames.explanation: Linearity gives Σpᵢ equal to the expected set size under uniform sampling. Concavity makes equalized marginals the largest possible entropy sum at that average; monotonicity on the lower half permits replacement by ρ.
frames.carry: Track uniformity, subadditivity, concavity, and monotonicity as separate steps.

challenges.title: Pairwise independence can hide two full bits
challenges.skill: Linear constraints, joint entropy, and the equality condition.
challenges.connection: The worked family has unbiased coordinates with dependence; this construction makes every coordinate pair independent as well.
challenges.prompt: Let X be uniform on the binary solutions of X₁⊕X₂⊕X₃=0 and X₃⊕X₄⊕X₅=0. Determine its support size, joint entropy, and all one-bit entropies. Prove that every pair of coordinates is independent, yet compute the divergence from the product of all marginals. Explain why pairwise independence cannot make entropy subadditivity an equality.
hints: Use X₁,X₂,X₄ as free bits.
The five coordinates are distinct nonzero linear forms in those three free bits.

probe.prompt: How many bits is D(P_X ∥ ΠᵢP_{Xᵢ})?
probe.feedback: There are three free bits, so H(X)=3. Every coordinate is fair and contributes one marginal bit; therefore the divergence is 5−3=2.

solution: The two constraints have rank two, leaving 2³=8 equally likely solutions and joint entropy three.
With free bits U=X₁,V=X₂,W=X₄, the coordinates are U,V,U⊕V,W,U⊕V⊕W. Each is a nonzero linear form and hence fair.
Any two displayed forms are distinct and therefore linearly independent over F₂; each coordinate pair is uniform on four outcomes.
Nevertheless the joint law is confined to eight of the 32 cube points. Its entropy gap and divergence from the product of its fair marginals is 5−3=2 bits.
rubric: Identify and count the free variables.
Prove pairwise independence rather than just unbiasedness.
Connect the strict entropy gap to the nonproduct full law.
challenges.mistake: Pairwise independence controls two-dimensional marginals, not the number of independent constraints on the full vector.
challenges.followup: For a binary linear code, relate total correlation to parity-check rank and identify when every pair remains independent.

challenges.title: An average-size constraint is enough
challenges.skill: Combining uniform-family entropy, concavity, and integer rounding.
challenges.connection: The example compares entropies of one family. This task turns an average combinatorial constraint into a cardinality bound.
challenges.prompt: Let F be a nonempty family of subsets of an eight-element set, with average member size at most two. Do not assume every member has size at most two. Prove |F|≤2^{8H₂(1/4)}, simplify this expression to an exact rational number, and give the resulting integer upper bound. State the separate equality requirements in the subadditivity and concavity steps.
hints: Choose a uniform member and use Σpᵢ≤2.

probe.prompt: What integer upper bound follows after rounding down the entropy bound?
probe.feedback: The entropy bound is 4⁸/3⁶=65536/729≈89.8985. Since the family size is an integer, it is at most 89. The argument uses only average size.

solution: Uniform sampling gives H(X)=log₂|F| and Σpᵢ=E|X|≤2.
Subadditivity gives H(X)≤ΣH₂(pᵢ); concavity and lower-half monotonicity give ΣH₂(pᵢ)≤8H₂(1/4).
Exponentiating yields 4⁸/3⁶=65536/729, hence the integer upper bound 89.
Equality in subadditivity requires joint independence; equality in strict concavity requires equal biases. These are separate conditions and are not forced by an average-size constraint.
rubric: Use a uniform family member.
Apply concavity in the correct direction and justify the lower-half step.
Simplify the exponent and handle integer cardinality.
challenges.mistake: Replacing an average-size assumption by a pointwise size restriction would prove a different, stronger counting problem.
challenges.followup: Investigate whether equality in the real-valued entropy bound is possible for a uniform nonempty family at a bias other than 0,1/2,1.

proof.goal: Compare every projected entropy to one common chain expansion and then count coordinate multiplicity.
proof.scope: This is the discrete projection proof. Weighted covers follow by the same nonnegative-term counting; the measurable-body version needs an additional approximation argument.

frames.title: Fix one global coordinate order
frames.question: Why must every projection use the same inherited ordering?

diagram.note: The right-hand conditioning set is always a subset of the left-hand one.

frames.claim: H(XS)=Σ_{i∈S}H(Xᵢ|Xⱼ:j∈S,j<i).
frames.explanation: The chain rule is applied inside S using the global ordering. This makes each projected term comparable to exactly one fixed full-chain term. Arbitrary reordered expansions can obscure which conditioning sets contain which.
frames.carry: Add the missing earlier coordinates and use conditioning monotonicity.

frames.title: Use the inequality in the correct direction
frames.question: Does adding conditioning increase or decrease discrete entropy?

diagram.note: The projected entropy is the upper quantity because it knows less of the past.

frames.claim: Every occurrence of coordinate i pays for one full-chain entropy term.
frames.explanation: Adding information cannot increase discrete conditional entropy. Thus even though projected coordinates may have complicated dependence, their entropy contributes at least the sum of the corresponding fixed full-chain terms.
frames.carry: The combinatorial cover condition can now be applied term by term.

frames.title: Count each coordinate’s coverage
frames.question: What happens if each coordinate belongs to at least k chosen projections?

diagram.note: All conditional entropy terms are nonnegative.

frames.claim: ΣS H(XS)≥kH(X).
frames.explanation: Summing the previous inequalities counts a full-chain term once for every projection containing its coordinate. Since every multiplicity is at least k and terms are nonnegative, the sum is at least k times the complete chain entropy.
frames.carry: Uniform-family sampling turns this entropy inequality into a counting result.

frames.title: Use support bounds without assuming uniform projections
frames.question: Which distribution is uniform, and which need not be?

diagram.note: A uniform joint family member can cast a nonuniform projection.

frames.claim: Shearer bounds the family by the product of its distinct projection sizes.
frames.explanation: Uniformity is used for the joint entropy only. Each projected law is merely supported on its projection family, so its entropy is bounded above by the log of that support; equality there would need a uniform projected law.
frames.carry: Coordinate coverage and projection multiplicities must both be explicit.

challenges.title: More projections can give a weaker bound
challenges.skill: Choosing a useful cover rather than blindly multiplying available sizes.
challenges.connection: The box example attains a symmetric three-projection bound. An asymmetric four-coordinate instance tests whether the cover exponent is understood.
challenges.prompt: For F in a four-coordinate product, suppose the known projection sizes on 12,23,34,41 are at most 4,9,16,25. Compare the Shearer bounds from the two opposite-pair covers and from all four projections. Then allow nonnegative weights on these four projections, with each coordinate covered to total weight at least one. Show that the best bound obtainable by this weighted-cover argument is 64, not the all-four bound.
hints: The opposite covers 12+34 and 23+41 each have multiplicity one.
For an optimal positive-cost weighted cover of this four-cycle, opposite even weights can be equalized, as can the odd weights.

probe.prompt: What is the best cardinality upper bound obtained by the stated weighted-cover argument?
probe.feedback: The two opposite covers give 4·16=64 and 9·25=225. The all-four multiplicity-two cover gives √(4·9·16·25)=120. Weighted interpolation cannot beat the cheaper opposite cover.

solution: The cover {12,34} gives |F|≤64, while {23,41} gives |F|≤225.
Using all four projections counts every coordinate twice and gives |F|≤120; having more input factors has not improved the bound.

In a minimum-cost weighted cover, reduce each of the two even edge weights to their minimum a; the odd weights must then be at least 1−a. With positive costs, take both odd weights equal to 1−a and 0≤a≤1.

The logarithmic bound is a ln64+(1−a)ln225, minimized at a=1. Thus 64 is optimal within this weighted-Shearer method, without a claim that it is the actual largest realizable family under every constraint.
rubric: Apply the correct multiplicity to each cover.
Optimize the weighted logarithmic expression.
Distinguish the best bound from an assertion of realizable equality.
challenges.mistake: Multiplying every known projection size and forgetting the cover exponent can make a valid bound much weaker.
challenges.followup: Formulate the analogous weighted-cover optimization for a five-cycle of available coordinate pairs.

challenges.title: Use the actual nonuniform projected laws
challenges.skill: Entropy calculation from unequal projection fibers.
challenges.connection: The product-box example has uniform projections; most family projections do not.
challenges.prompt: Take F={000,001,010,100}, uniformly sampled, and use its three pair projections. Compute the law and entropy of each projected pair. Apply the entropy version of Shearer before replacing entropy by log support size, and compare the integer bounds obtained from these two routes. Explain why no projected law is uniform despite the joint law being uniform.
hints: Each pair projection has one outcome of probability 1/2 and two of probability 1/4.
Compare 2^{(3/2)(3/2)} with √(3³), then round down.

probe.prompt: What integer upper bound follows from the actual projected entropies?
probe.feedback: Each pair entropy is 1.5 bits. Shearer gives log₂|F|≤(3·1.5)/2=2.25, so |F|≤2^{2.25}<5 and hence |F|≤4. Support sizes alone give √27≈5.196 and only the integer bound five.

solution: Every pair projection is {00,01,10}; the zero pair has two preimages and the other two outcomes have one each.
Its distribution is (1/2,1/4,1/4), whose entropy is 1/2+1/2+1/2=1.5 bits.
Every coordinate is covered twice, so 2log₂|F|≤3·1.5=4.5. Exponentiation and integer rounding yield |F|≤4.
Using only three support sizes gives |F|²≤27, hence |F|≤5. Unequal fiber sizes explain both the nonuniform projections and the lost strength in replacing entropy by log support.
rubric: Count projection fibers and normalize them.
Compute the entropy and multiplicity factor.
Compare the two integer bounds without asserting projected uniformity.
challenges.mistake: Uniform sampling on F does not assign equal mass to projected points with different numbers of preimages.
challenges.followup: Characterize equality in the entropy-to-support replacement for an arbitrary projection.

proof.goal: Explain how farness supplies useful vertices and a bounded restriction tree controls every possible sampled coloring.
proof.scope: The list-coloring repair bound is a structural lemma from the assigned proof. The displayed s=40/ε² guarantee uses 0<ε<0.1 and n>400/ε³; small graph diagrams illustrate the mechanism, not those size assumptions.

frames.title: Lists encode every extension of a partial coloring
frames.question: What does a colorless sampled vertex certify?

diagram.note: Rejecting one partial coloring is not yet rejecting all colorings.

frames.claim: A colorless vertex kills its branch; a restricting vertex reduces lists under every feasible color.
frames.explanation: Each list contains exactly the colors still compatible with the colored sampled neighbors. An empty list proves that particular partial coloring cannot extend. A restriction tree must retain the other feasible coloring branches until they too are killed.
frames.carry: Use a minimum over feasible colors to make restriction branch-independent.

frames.title: Farness rules out too few useful vertices
frames.question: Why must many vertices be colorless or restricting?

diagram.note: δφ(v) is the minimum number of new list deletions over feasible colors.

frames.claim: An ε-far graph has many vertices useful for advancing or killing any current branch.
frames.explanation: Color each remaining vertex by a feasible color minimizing the number of compatible neighbors. The resulting monochromatic-edge bound would repair the graph too cheaply if both colorless and restricting vertices were scarce. Farness therefore forces the displayed lower count.
frames.carry: Under the sample-size hypotheses, a fresh sampled vertex is useful with conditional probability at least 0.4ε.

frames.title: A list potential bounds all branch lengths
frames.question: How many successful restrictions can a branch contain?

diagram.note: The tree can be embedded in a predetermined full ternary tree.

frames.claim: The number of possible tree locations is less than 3^{3/ε+1}.
frames.explanation: Every feasible color at a restricting vertex deletes at least εn available colors from neighboring lists. Since the initial potential is at most 3n and never increases, each branch has bounded depth. The branching factor then bounds the total collection that sampling must control.
frames.carry: Use a union bound over fixed possible tree locations, not a retrospectively chosen branch.

frames.title: Make sampling defeat every surviving branch
frames.question: How does the per-branch tail beat the number of branches?

diagram.note: The final expression is below 0.1 in the theorem’s stated parameter range.

frames.claim: With high probability all branches terminate, certifying that the sampled graph is not three-colorable.
frames.explanation: Conditional success probabilities permit a binomial lower-tail domination argument even though the process is adaptive. Its exponential decay beats the fixed ternary-tree count. Only when every branch has died does the sample give a genuine noncolorability witness.
frames.carry: Both progress under every color and simultaneous branch control are essential.

challenges.title: Find the constant that beats the restriction tree
challenges.skill: Comparing an exponential tail with exponential branch count.
challenges.connection: The K₄ example kills one branch directly; the general proof must pay for every possible branch simultaneously.
challenges.prompt: Assume the same restriction-tree argument gives depth 3/ε, fewer than 3^{3/ε+1} possible locations, and conditional useful-sample probability at least 0.4ε. Replace the sample budget by C/ε². Derive the lower-tail exponent using the estimate exp(−(μ−3/ε)²/(2μ)). Find the least integer C for which this union bound tends to zero as ε decreases to zero. Explain why this asymptotic constant does not by itself reproduce the theorem’s finite 0.1 guarantee.
hints: The mean lower bound is μ=0.4C/ε.
Compare (0.4C−3)²/(0.8C) with 3 ln3, and require 0.4C>3.

probe.prompt: What is the least integer C that makes the stated asymptotic union bound decay?
probe.feedback: For C=29 the tail coefficient is 8.6²/23.2≈3.18793<3ln3. For C=30 it is 9²/24=3.375>3ln3≈3.29584. The difference must be strictly positive.

solution: The expected number of useful samples is at least 0.4C/ε; the branch needs at most 3/ε successes.
The lower-tail bound has exponent −[(0.4C−3)²/(0.8C)]/ε, for C>7.5.
The tree count contributes +(3ln3)/ε plus the constant ln3. Direct comparison shows the first working integer is C=30.
A positive asymptotic exponent only guarantees decay for sufficiently small ε. The source’s uniform finite-range probability bound also controls constants and the stated n and ε assumptions.
rubric: Derive both exponential contributions.
Check the strict mean condition and the neighboring integers.
Separate asymptotic decay from a uniform finite-range error guarantee.
challenges.mistake: A small failure probability for one branch does not suffice when the number of branches is exponential in 1/ε.
challenges.followup: Generalize the coefficient competition to k colors with list potential kn and at most k children per node.

challenges.title: An average color loss does not control every branch
challenges.skill: The minimum-over-colors definition of a restricting vertex.
challenges.connection: The worked example follows color assignments one at a time; a general restriction step must work whichever feasible color is chosen.
challenges.prompt: A vertex v has feasible list {red,blue}. Among its still-uncolored neighbors, choosing red deletes red from one list, while choosing blue deletes blue from ten lists. The restricting threshold is five list deletions. Analyze proposed definitions using maximum or average color loss instead of minimum loss. Construct a partial-coloring/list realization of this local pattern using three fixed color anchors, and show why the potential-depth proof cannot use either proposed definition unchanged.
hints: A branch may choose the feasible color with the smallest loss.
Anchor triangles can force a neighbor’s list to be a chosen singleton.

probe.prompt: What is the correct δφ(v) for this local pattern?
probe.feedback: The correct definition takes the minimum over feasible colors: min(1,10)=1. The maximum and average exceed five but do not guarantee a five-unit drop on the red branch.

solution: The correct value is δφ(v)=min(1,10)=1, so v is not restricting at threshold five.
The maximum loss is ten and the average is 5.5, but either would label v restricting while the red branch removes only one neighbor color.

Realize the pattern with properly colored red,blue,green anchors: connect v to the green anchor; make one red-only neighbor adjacent to the blue and green anchors, and ten blue-only neighbors adjacent to the red and green anchors; connect these neighbors to v.

A feasible branch can choose red, so the asserted guaranteed drop fails. Farness is used separately to find vertices whose minimum loss is large; a favorable or average color cannot replace that universal requirement.
rubric: Compute the correct minimum.
Give a realizable list configuration.
Identify the universal branch guarantee needed by the potential argument.
challenges.mistake: The tree includes all feasible colors, so it cannot assume a favorable color choice at each restriction.
challenges.followup: Modify the local pattern so each color has large average influence but one branch repeatedly makes only a small potential drop.

proof.goal: Convert a dense-graph farness promise into many triangles, then into a justified sampling budget.
proof.scope: The regularity lemma from Chapter 9 is an input to the assigned removal proof, not an extra assigned chapter here. The regular-triple counting deduction and sampling calculation are made explicit.

frames.title: Charge every cleaning operation to the repair budget
frames.question: Why must the total edge-deletion cost be below the farness threshold?

diagram.note: Choose the regularity parameters so the combined deletion cost is strictly less than εn².

frames.claim: A cleaned triangle-free graph would contradict ε-farness.
frames.explanation: Regularity supplies an equitable partition, and the assigned parameter estimates make the four deletion categories fit inside the permitted budget. The strict inequality is what converts cleaning into a contradiction if no triangle remains; merely finding a partition does not do that.
frames.carry: Some surviving triangle must use three dense regular class pairs.

frames.title: A surviving triangle identifies a regular triple
frames.question: What structure remains around its three vertex classes?

diagram.note: A surviving triangle gives a triangle of usable partition classes, not yet the required triangle abundance.

frames.claim: A,B,C form a dense η-regular triple.
frames.explanation: Edges within classes, irregular pairs, and sparse pairs were deleted. Thus each surviving edge of the triangle belongs to a usable dense regular pair, and its three endpoints lie in distinct classes. Counting across those classes will upgrade existence to abundance.
frames.carry: Select vertices in A with sufficiently large neighborhoods in both other classes.

frames.title: Count all triangles across the regular triple
frames.question: Why do good vertices give a cubic number of triangles?

diagram.note: The neighborhood subsets are large enough for the B,C regularity estimate.

frames.claim: A usable regular triple contains a positive cubic number of triangles.
frames.explanation: At most ηm vertices fail each of the two degree estimates. For every remaining a, its two neighborhoods have size at least (d−η)m≥ηm. Regularity of the B,C pair supplies density at least d−η between them. Summing these edge counts over good a counts distinct triangles.
frames.carry: The partition-size bound converts this into a density δ(ε)>0 in the whole graph.

frames.title: Amplify a real density lower bound
frames.question: How many independent triple samples suffice once the triangle density is δ?

diagram.note: Only the structural theorem makes δ depend on ε rather than on n.

frames.claim: The tester has a sample bound depending on ε and the error target, independent of graph size.
frames.explanation: Sampling a uniformly random triple detects exactly when that triple induces a triangle. Once removal has supplied a positive density lower bound, independent repetitions yield the exponential miss bound. An isolated or sparse collection of triangles would not justify a constant budget.
frames.carry: Every rejection is a genuine triangle witness; farness is needed for frequent detection.

challenges.title: Many triangles can still be sparse for testing
challenges.skill: Exact amplification and the dense farness promise.
challenges.connection: The six-vertex example has two disjoint triangles; scaling that pattern tests whether “many” means a positive triple density.
challenges.prompt: Let G be ten disjoint triangles on 30 vertices. Compute the exact success probability of a uniform unordered triple sample and the least number of independent samples giving miss probability at most 1/3. Derive the normalized number of edge deletions needed to make G triangle-free, then generalize to n/3 disjoint triangles. Explain why the growing sampling requirement does not contradict the constant-query theorem for fixed ε-far graphs.
hints: There are C(30,3)=4060 triples and ten successful triples.
One edge per component is necessary and sufficient for repair.

probe.prompt: What is the least number of independent triple samples with miss probability at most 1/3?
probe.feedback: Each sample hits with probability 1/406. Solve (405/406)^q≤1/3 and round up; the least integer is 446.

solution: The triangle density among unordered triples is 10/4060=1/406.
Independent samples miss with probability (405/406)^q, giving q=ceil(ln(1/3)/ln(405/406))=446.
The exact repair cost is ten deletions, normalized by n² as 10/900=1/90. In general, n/3 disjoint triangles need n/3 deletions, a normalized cost 1/(3n).
For fixed ε, these graphs eventually cease to be ε-far. Their triple density is Θ(n^{−2}), so the Θ(n²) triple-sampling requirement is fully consistent with the removal-based theorem.
rubric: Normalize by the number of unordered triples.
Use independent-sample amplification and round in the correct direction.
Compare repair cost with a fixed dense-graph ε threshold.
challenges.mistake: A triangle count linear in n is not a positive fraction of all Θ(n³) triples.
challenges.followup: For a uniformly sampled r-vertex set, estimate the r scale needed to hit a triangle in the general disjoint-triangle graph.

challenges.title: Derive a regular-triple counting bound
challenges.skill: Using degree exceptions and regularity on the correct subsets.
challenges.connection: The finite example can count triangles directly; the removal proof must infer abundance from coarse pair information.
challenges.prompt: Let A,B,C be disjoint classes of 100 vertices each. Assume all three pairs are η-regular with η=0.05 and density at least d=0.4. Prove the continuous lower bound (1−2η)(d−η)³·100³ on the number of triangles across the classes. Show why each neighborhood pair is large enough for regularity. Finally round this continuous bound upward once to give an integer guarantee.
hints: Discard at most η|A| bad vertices for each of B and C.
For a good a, both neighborhoods have at least 35 vertices, exceeding η·100=5.

probe.prompt: What integer guarantee results by rounding the stated continuous bound up once?
probe.feedback: The bound is 0.9·0.35³·1000000=38587.5, hence at least 38588 triangles. This is the requested final rounding of the continuous estimate, not the sharpest possible use of intermediate integrality.

solution: In an η-regular pair of density at least d, fewer than η|A| vertices can have degree below (d−η)|B|. Apply this to A,B and A,C.
At least (1−2η)·100=90 vertices a have both neighborhood sizes at least 35.
Each such pair of neighborhoods is large enough for regularity of B,C, so it has edge density at least d−η=0.35 and contributes at least 0.35·35² triangles through a.
Summing gives 38587.5 as a continuous lower bound. Since the triangle count is integral, a single final upward rounding gives the stated guarantee 38588.
rubric: Account for both bad-vertex sets.
Verify the regularity subset-size threshold.
Count triangles once through their A vertex and handle the specified rounding.
challenges.mistake: Regularity cannot be invoked on arbitrary tiny neighborhoods; the condition d−η≥η must be checked.
challenges.followup: Express the bound for unequal class sizes and identify the parameter condition under which the same argument works.

proof.goal: Describe a hereditary property by induced obstructions and derive a one-sided bounded-sample tester from induced removal.
proof.scope: The induced-removal theorem and the general semi-hereditary characterization are deep stated inputs in the assigned text. These frames prove the elementary obstruction description and testing deduction.

frames.title: Use induced obstructions, including nonedges
frames.question: What forbidden pattern can certify that an induced sample fails the property?

diagram.note: An induced witness specifies both present and absent edges.

frames.claim: A hereditary property is exactly avoidance of a family of forbidden induced graphs.
frames.explanation: Take all finite graphs outside P that are minimal under induced restriction. A graph in P contains none by heredity; a graph outside P has a minimal induced subgraph outside P. The forbidden family may be infinite and cannot generally be replaced by a single fixed graph.
frames.carry: The structural theorem must handle both nonedges and potentially unbounded obstruction sizes.

frames.title: Invoke the actual induced-removal input
frames.question: What bounded witness abundance does farness supply?

diagram.note: The deep theorem supplies these bounds; ordinary triangle removal is not a substitute.

frames.claim: For fixed ε, a bounded random induced sample detects a violation with positive probability.
frames.explanation: The removal statement converts dense edit distance from P into an abundance of bounded induced obstructions, or equivalently a suitable bounded bad-sample guarantee. Controlling only present-edge patterns would miss the required nonedges.
frames.carry: Inspect the full induced graph on the sampled vertices.

frames.title: One-sidedness follows from heredity itself
frames.question: Why can a graph in P never be rejected by this tester?

diagram.note: A good sample does not certify that the entire graph belongs to P.

frames.claim: Rejecting only a violating induced sample gives one-sided error.
frames.explanation: The tester may be computationally expensive on its bounded sample, but it checks a finite induced graph exactly. Heredity makes every rejection sound regardless of sampling probability; removal is needed only to make detection frequent for far inputs.
frames.carry: Soundness and detection probability arise from different ingredients.

frames.title: Amplify by uniting independent samples
frames.question: Why does a bad sub-sample remain bad inside a larger induced sample?

diagram.note: If the union were in P, all of its induced subgraphs would also be in P.

frames.claim: A sufficiently large bounded sample reaches any desired fixed rejection probability.
frames.explanation: Independent repetitions need not produce disjoint vertex sets. Their union still has bounded size, and any detected obstruction is an induced subgraph of that union. Thus the one-sided guarantee survives amplification without assuming independence of vertices within the union.
frames.carry: Keep the deep removal input separate from this elementary sampling deduction.

challenges.title: Amplify an infinite-obstruction property
challenges.skill: One-sided amplification without a single fixed forbidden graph.
challenges.connection: The induced-cycle example has one small obstruction; a general hereditary property may have infinitely many forbidden sizes.
challenges.prompt: Assume a hereditary property P has the following removal consequence at a chosen ε: at least 1/16 of all eight-vertex subsets induce graphs outside P. Draw independent uniform eight-vertex subsets, take their union, and test the entire induced graph on that union. Find a vertex-budget bound giving rejection probability at least 0.95. Prove soundness and amplification even when sampled subsets overlap, and explain why no single fixed forbidden graph was required.
hints: The independent objects are the sampled eight-vertex subsets.
If any one sampled induced graph is outside P, heredity forces the induced graph on their union to be outside P.

probe.prompt: What vertex-budget bound q·8 follows from the least repetition count q?
probe.feedback: The miss probability is at most (15/16)^q. The least q with this at most 0.05 is 47, so the union uses at most 376 vertices.

solution: Each independent eight-set is bad with probability at least 1/16, so all q are good with probability at most (15/16)^q.
Solving for miss probability at most 0.05 gives q=47 and at most 8q=376 distinct sampled vertices.
If a sampled eight-set is bad but the union induced graph were in P, heredity would force that eight-set to be in P, a contradiction. Overlap does not alter this implication.
If G itself belongs to P, every induced union belongs to P and no rejection is possible. The argument uses bad induced subgraphs, not one named obstruction common to every bad sample.
rubric: Calculate the repetition count and vertex upper bound.
Prove the union implication with the correct contrapositive.
Distinguish independence of sample draws from overlap of their vertices.
challenges.mistake: Overlapping vertex sets do not destroy independence when the sets themselves are drawn independently.
challenges.followup: Compare this union-of-samples tester with a single uniformly chosen 376-vertex induced sample.

challenges.title: Ordinary copies create false rejections
challenges.skill: Induced characterization and sound witness counting.
challenges.connection: The chorded-cycle example distinguishes an induced obstruction from an ordinary subgraph. Cluster graphs give a different property where the distinction is decisive.
challenges.prompt: Prove that a graph has no induced three-vertex path P₃ exactly when each connected component is a clique. Then analyze the complete graph K₆: count its ordinary, not necessarily induced, P₃ subgraphs, counting a center and an unordered pair of endpoints. Explain why a detector that rejects on those ordinary copies would violate one-sidedness for this hereditary property. State what an induced-removal-based tester must inspect instead.
hints: If a component is not complete, choose a shortest path between nonadjacent vertices.
In a clique, every choice of center and two other vertices gives an ordinary two-edge path but also has the extra endpoint edge.

probe.prompt: How many ordinary P₃ subgraphs does K₆ have under the specified convention?
probe.feedback: There are six choices of center and C(5,2)=10 choices of unordered endpoints, giving 60. None is induced because the endpoints are adjacent.

solution: A disjoint union of cliques contains no induced P₃: three vertices in one component form a clique, and different components cannot form the path.
If a connected component is not a clique, a shortest path between nonadjacent vertices has its first three vertices forming an induced P₃, since a shortcut edge would shorten the path.
K₆ has 6C(5,2)=60 ordinary P₃ subgraphs but zero induced P₃ copies. It belongs to the property.
Rejecting an ordinary P₃ would therefore reject a valid input. A correct witness checks both path edges and the missing endpoint edge in the full induced triple.
rubric: Prove both directions of the component characterization.
Specify and execute the ordinary-copy counting convention.
Explain the exact nonedge needed for a sound induced witness.
challenges.mistake: A forbidden induced path is not the same as forbidding every path subgraph.
challenges.followup: Show how adding or deleting a single edge can create an induced P₃, and explain why arbitrary edge monotonicity is absent.
